#643. Put To The Test, Those Special Engine Cleaning Oils Do Some Lifting

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (530 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Put To The Test, Those Special Engine Cleaning Oils Do Some Lifting

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that motor oil naturally helps to flush out common contaminants, and there's a whole supply of products specifically made to keep the mechanical parts of a vehicle clean and running.
  • The Motor Oil Geek is Lake Speed Jr., of SPEEDiagnostix, known for its used oil analysis services.
  • Using those skills, he put three "cleaning" motor oils up to the test: Mobil 1 Advanced Clean, Valvoline Restore & Protect, and Pennzoil Ultra Platinum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that motor oil naturally helps to flush out common contaminants, and there's a whole supply of products specifically made to keep the mechanical parts of a vehicle clean and running. From Top Tier gasoline complete with detergents to some types of engine motor oil — these treatments and additives are designed and marketed to you, the consumer, to keep things clean internally so your car lasts. Do they really do what they claim to do, though? The Motor Oil Geek on YouTube put those "cleaning" oils to the test to see if they do make a difference.

The Motor Oil Geek is Lake Speed Jr., of SPEEDiagnostix, known for its used oil analysis services. Speed himself is a Certified Lubrication Specialist and OIl Analyst who used that expertise to help Joe Gibbs Racing for 12 years — a testing ground sometimes more brutal than the testing cars go through in-house.

Using those skills, he put three "cleaning" motor oils up to the test: Mobil 1 Advanced Clean, Valvoline Restore & Protect, and Pennzoil Ultra Platinum. There's actually a fourth oil, Valvoline Premium Blue Restore Gen2 — but that's a separate, yet important test, also included in the video. The results didn't match what real in-engine testing produced, but even in this comparable bench testing scenario, these oils managed to clean up expectations.

The Motor Oil Geek put the three oils through what's called an ASTM sequence IIIH test, which is a standard test used to evaluate engine oils at high temperatures and high speeds. Typically, these tests are conducted in an actual running engine for 90 total hours, broken down into four 20-hour test segments and one 10-hour segment. For bench test purposes, Speed ran the oils for 168 hours with varying temperatures from room temperature to 150 degrees Celsius, to better emulate real-time conditions of an engine from cold runs to high-speed performance.

He used pistons with considerable deposits from a turbocharged Mini Cooper engine, each marked with a letter code to track which one was tested in what oil. Those pistons were sent off to be professionally rated before the test, as well as after, to measure improved "cleanliness.".

Recent findings suggest that three of those pistons were then hung separately from a device so they could soak in an oil in 1000 mL beakers over a magnetic stirring hot plate. It's a way to control the notable aspects of the test concerning time, temperature, and agitation (movement), so Speed could focus on the concentration and cleaning. The fourth piston was soaked in the Valvoline Premium Blue Restore Gen2, which claimed it could clean parts just soaked in the oil.

In a recent development, in the end, all four oils cleaned some of the deposits on the pistons. The most improved was the fourth piston that soaked in the oil, which The Motor Oil Geek explained contains an agent called Ester, also used in two-stroke oils to keep things clean. And keep in mind, they perform even better in a running engine. So, if you're at all worried about buildup slowing you down, these cleaning oils might actually do the trick.

#642. Why Warming Up Your Car Unattended Is Illegal In Some States And Cities

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (673 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Why Warming Up Your Car Unattended Is Illegal In Some States And Cities

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a seasoned driver, you may be aware that some states' roads are more dangerous in winter.
  • Industry observers note that the reason behind the laws is rather simple: Those puffs of smoke in the chilly air indicate a running, usually unlocked, vehicle.
  • All is not lost for the dedicated puffer, though, as there is an exception to the rule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a seasoned driver, you may be aware that some states' roads are more dangerous in winter. Did you also know that four out of five of these states, as well as 27 others, have laws against puffing? No, not that puffing. Puffing, or "car puffing," is a slang term for the ritual of letting your car get warm and toasty before driving off. This is usually accomplished by starting your car and then heading back inside for a bit. The term comes from the telltale puffs of smoke that can be seen coming out of the tail pipe.

Industry observers note that the reason behind the laws is rather simple: Those puffs of smoke in the chilly air indicate a running, usually unlocked, vehicle. This makes it an easy target for crime. Someone can jump in and take off in your vehicle in a matter of seconds — not good for anyone involved.

All is not lost for the dedicated puffer, though, as there is an exception to the rule. Vehicles equipped with a remote starter are often exempt from these rules, as a remote start system allows you to keep your vehicle locked and your keys in your pocket.

Industry observers note that we get it — getting into a cold car sucks. But having your car stolen sucks even more. Even beyond your own personal grief, stolen vehicles are often used in subsequent crimes. Also, items left in your vehicle, such as registration information, can be used for identity theft, and a garage door opener can become easy access into your home. According to the National Insurance Crime Bureau, "By the end of 2021, just over 100,000 thefts facilitated by keys or key fobs were reported nationally. This total accounts for 11% of vehicle thefts of all types reported in the U.S. in 2021.".

Sources indicate that outside of the crime aspect, there are other reasons to avoid puffing and other forms of idling. Cold weather already hurts your gas mileage, and burning gas while you're not moving is only going to make that worse, costing you money in the long term. On the environmental side, according to the U.S. Department of Energy, "It is estimated that idling personal vehicles generate around 30 million tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) every year," which is roughly the equivalent of adding an additional 5 million vehicles to the roads.

Sources indicate that back in the olden times — sometime after the last horse and buggy but before the first DeLorean — it was common knowledge that you had to let your car warm up before driving it. So, a little puff session before work was thought to be good. That is an outdated notion today, and, in fact, experts such as AAA declare that a modern vehicle only needs a few seconds to warm up. Excessive idle time can stress the engine, as it isn't running at its preferred temperature.

Recent findings suggest that laws against puffing are clear that leaving a running car unattended is a no-no. One pro tip based on this definition is to warm up your car while you are shoveling snow out of the driveway, scraping ice off of the windows, or performing any of the other tasks that make up the unbreakable laws of winter driving. That way, you have an eye on the vehicle and are taking care of your pre-driving chores.

Puffing-specific laws are on the books in the following states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, Newly introduced Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wisconsin. If you live in one of these states, check your local statutes to see how the law may affect you. One final note to all the EV owners out there: It is recommended that you warm up your vehicles while they're still plugged in, preventing you from burning too much energy.

#641. Tech Report: Here are 7 great reasons rural drivers SHOULD embrace EVs in 2027

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1707 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tech Report: Here are 7 great reasons rural drivers SHOULD embrace EVs in 2027

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification.
  • UPGRADE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.
  • Recent findings suggest that “An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification. In fact, EVs offer rural drivers even more benefits than they do to city-dwellers!

UPGRADE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.

Recent findings suggest that “An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura. “Rural communities across the country have their own distinguishing characteristics, but certain shared characteristics such as driving distances, the type of vehicles driven, and socio-economics are factors which contribute to this larger potential to benefit from vehicle electrification.”.

Pinto de Moura went on to outline five ways rural and country drivers could benefit from going electric – but that was in 2021, and a whole lot has changed in the nearly six years since. As such, I thought it was high time we revisit some of the reasons EVs are a great fit for rural lifestyles, see if we could uncover any new ones, and outline the reasons we think rural drivers should rush to embrace electric vehicles in the coming calendar year.

According to recent reports, when you hear that line about, “the average American drives 30 to 40 miles a day,” remember that in towns like Wellington, Ohio, or Colfax, Washington, 30 miles is a grocery run. Each way. So when people trot out that old line about range anxiety, what rural drivers actually hear isn’t reassurance. It’s dismissal — a suggestion that they drive too far for an EV to work, when nothing could be further from the truth.

A recent study by Rural Climate Partnership found that rural drivers spend an average of 44% more on fuel than city dwellers, and that the top 3.6% of rural drivers — the “supermilers” who rack up the most miles — could save over $4,000 each year by switching to electric fuel.

Country guys and gals love their pickups, and arguably the biggest difference between the EV market of 2021 and 2027 is that electric trucks and SUVs are no longer a novelty. There are now battery-powered options ready to haul, handle chores, head out camping, and tow a trailer.

It has been revealed that what’s more, a new wave of more affordable electric trucks from Ford, Slate, and others is challenging the idea that you need a $50,000 half-ton pickup to get real work done. Early interest suggests there’s plenty of pent-up demand for capable, accessible electric work trucks that don’t need to be twenty feet long or cost more than what your parent’s paid for their house.

It has been revealed that with only about 45% of rural counties having access to DC fast charging, public charging still isn’t as visible as many first-time EV buyers might like, but it’s far better than it used to be — and improving fast. Still, that’s not the real EV advantage. Home charging is.

Unlike many apartment-dwelling urban drivers, most rural owners can charge right at home. More than 80% of rural households have a driveway or garage that are ideal for overnight Level 2 charging, and many already have a 240V outlet, keeping setup costs (if there even are any) to a minimum.

Plug in before bed, wake up to a full battery every morning, and do it for pennies on the dollar, especially with off-peak rates.

If disaster strikes and you lose power, your EV could be more than just a way to get around. Many electric cars and trucks have the ability to power refrigerators, freezers, well pumps, lights, and other household essentials for days, either through onboard outlets or a dedicated vehicle-to-home (V2H) system that feeds electricity directly into your home’s electrical panel. Ford’s from-the-ashes F-150 Lightning and Tesla’s Cybertruck are already among the EVs making that capability a reality, and newer, more affordable electric trucks promise to bring V2H tech to even more households.

According to recent reports, if you live in an area prone to extreme weather, where severe storms, hurricanes, or wildfires can leave homes without electricity for days, that’s a pretty compelling benefit. Keeping food cold, medical equipment running or essential medication refrigerated can be a literal lifesaver – and your EV’s battery might be the biggest backup power source you own.

According to recent reports, it’s been a few years since a working class guy could reasonably expect to get a upcoming pickup for less than $50,000. And, while much has been made of the “high cost of electric vehicles,” the truth is that thanks to killer lease deals, new tax incentives, and companies like Ford Pro and TRC that are willing to help you find even more funding to help pay for them, EVs can often be had for less than a comparable gas model.

As such, getting behind the wheel of an ultra-powerful, ultra smooth-running electric pickup truck from your favorite brand is easier than ever.

According to recent reports, at the risk of sounding like a paranoid red hat, rural Americans are proud Americans – just like rural Canadians are proud Canadians. Unfortunately, every gallon of gas burned in their pickups and SUVs came from oil drilled, refined, and traded on global markets — and that means supporting the oil business and economies of nations whose values don’t always align with, or maybe are even outright hostile to theirs.

Switching to an EV can help more of that money right here at home, especially as more and better battery recycling efforts come online and newer battery and anode/cathode chemistries are developed, reducing dependence on rare Earth metals, cobalt, and even lithium.

Even better, thanks to the rapid expansion and dramatically reduced costs of wind and solar power, you can power your EV with energy that is 100% Made in the USA, that doesn’t support foreign oil interests or involve you in a bunch of dumb oil wars (except indirectly), and which creates good-paying construction and maintenance jobs for local workers.

In my experience, rural buyers appreciate things that last, and are moved more by lasting quality than fleeting fashions – and that’s exactly why they should be looking at EVs.

We recently covered a 2019 Chevy Bolt that had put more than 470,000 miles on its odometer, along with data from Ford showing its battery packs maintain more than 90% of their battery health after 100,000 miles.

Recent findings suggest that and while we’re talking about data, it should be noted that EVs aren’t some new, unknown technology. The first modern high-voltage car battery hit the road more than 30 years ago (the Prius was released in 1996, as a 1997 model). Some of those cars are still on the road – and there are literally tens of thousands of EVs out there still performing their daily driver duties every day.

There are obviously more reasons to go electric than these, from lower cost of ownership to saving the planet to absolutely killer burnouts that would make the one-tire-fire era IROC Camaros hang their 305s in shame – but I think those kind of fade into the background as being appealing to just about everyone, instead of being especially appealing to rural drivers.

I live in rural Australia in a village that doesn't even have a fuel bowser. My shopping trip is usually around 164km (100miles). I have solar on my roof. I now have an EV (one of the Chinese brands that aren't available in the USA) and am delighted with it. I'm saving a lot of money on fuel and because the solar feed-in tariff goes negative in the middle of the day (I have to pay the utility organization to take my electricity) by charging the car at home I save money there. For rural people with roof space for solar EVs should be a no-brainer, but like many rural areas my district is incredibly conservative (do a search for Barnaby Joyce, my local member) and the populace are convinced they don't drive far enough, they'll catch on fire (mine has an LFP battery, so the risk is low) and that I'll need to replace the battery in a year (even though the battery has an 8 year warranty).

According to recent reports, that mentioned, it’s been a long time since I was back in Ohio, so maybe I’ve forgotten what it’s like. You guys are smart, head on down to the comments and let me know what I missed!

#640. Industry News: Mazda Miata Engine Swaps Ranked Best To Worst (For Your Budget And Your Patience)

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1540 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Industry News: Mazda Miata Engine Swaps Ranked Best To Worst (For Your Budget And Your Patience)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that jalopnik has long maintained that the Mazda Miata is the answer to every question.
  • In a recent development, but Miata enthusiasts are a crafty bunch, and over the nameplate's 37-year history, their quest for more power has driven the development of camshafts, turbochargers, and, of course, engine swaps.
  • Industry observers note that not all swaps are created equal, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jalopnik has long maintained that the Mazda Miata is the answer to every question. What's the best affordable convertible? Miata. What if you want a fun commuter that's reliable and sips fuel? You should consider a Miata. What if you want a car to take off-road? Surprisingly, the Miata is the answer again. Emme Hall won her class in a Baja race with her off-road modified Miata. It's an excellent sports car, relatively cheap, abundant, and just plain fun. Over four generations, the only only real critique of the venerable roadster is that it's never been particularly quick in a straight line.

In a recent development, but Miata enthusiasts are a crafty bunch, and over the nameplate's 37-year history, their quest for more power has driven the development of camshafts, turbochargers, and, of course, engine swaps. Swaps are not for the faint of heart – they often consume a lot of time and capital — but they are a great way to add power without the complexities of a forced induction setup on the factory engine.

Industry observers note that not all swaps are created equal, though. For example, transplanting an engine from a newer Miata will be easier and cheaper than shoehorning a V8 into the engine bay. However, the V8 will net you way more power for the extra effort and money. There are so many Miata swaps out there — from Honda K24 four-cylinders to Toyota V12s — so we have compiled a helpful a list of engines that go in Miatas, organized from the cheapest and easiest to the most difficult and expensive.

It has been revealed that the easiest Miata swaps involve upgrading to a larger Mazda motor within the same engine family. Early first-generation Miatas (1990 to 1993) were equipped with a 1.6-liter four-cylinder. Its output was a tepid 116 horsepower. Luckily, later first-generation cars (1994 to 1997) and all second-generation cars (1999 to 2005) came with a more powerful 1.8-liter four-cylinder that will bolt up to the factory transmission. Flyin' Miata sells an affordable kit that makes the swap to the 1994-to-1997 engine essentially plug-and-play. The later engines make more power, but they still require some effort to work in the 1.6 cars. To get the most power for your money and effort, look for a 2001-to-2005 Miata engine donor. They have variable valve timing and provide 142 horsepower .

According to recent reports, similarly, third-generation Miatas (2006 to 2015) have an easy path to more displacement and power. A 2.5-liter Duratec four-cylinder engine from a Ford Fusion, Mazda3, Mazda6, or Mercury Milan fits in place of the Miata's 2.0-liter four-cylinder with minimal effort. The larger engine is plentiful in junkyards and can be had for as cheap as $350. The swap isn't completely plug-and-play — the Miata's lower intake manifold needs to be modified to fit the 2.5 — but most of the 2.0-liter's accessories fit the larger engine without matter. A stock 2.5 makes about 10 more horsepower and 35 more pound-feet of torque over the factory Miata engine. But with upgraded cams and a freer-flowing exhaust, Grassroots Motorsports made 196 hp at the wheels with its 2.5 swap.

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, the Miata has never had much more than an economy-car four-cylinder turned sideways. By contrast, when Honda decided to make a roadster of its own, the automaker equipped it with the F20C four-cylinder — an engine with a 9,000-rpm redline that held the title for the most naturally aspirated horsepower per liter until the Ferrari 458 came along. Intrepid engine swappers may think a Miata with an F20C could be a good way to create a low-buck, bootleg S2000. But S2000 engines aren't exactly affordable or easy to come by.

Industry observers note that however, there is another Honda option that can rev almost as high as the F20C and makes similar power. Enter the K24, the budget friendly and readily available alternative. The K24, like its name might suggest, is a 2.4-liter four-cylinder with dual-overhead camshafts and Honda's i-VTEC system. The high performance variants of the engine found in the Acura TSX and Honda Civic Si make around 200 horsepower in factory trim. But the aftermarket for the engine is immense, and with the right combination of parts, the K24 has the potential to make nearly 300 hp without boost.

It has been revealed that although it was only available in front- and all-wheel-drive cars, tuners like KPower Industries recognized the engine's potential for rear-wheel-drive applications. As such, KPower Industries makes kits to swap a K24 into all four generations of Miatas. It's not a simple or cheap swap. Bits like a transmission adapter plate and a standalone ECU are needed to make it all work, and the most comprehensive kits start at around $6,000. But for a powerful, lightweight engine that doesn't mess with the balance of the Miata chassis, the juice is worth the squeeze.

The next rung on the Miata-swap ladder is the V6. A V6 swap is an exercise in more — more cylinders, more power, more effort, and more money. There are three V6 engines that have readily available Miata swap kits: the 3.5-liter Honda J35 found in the Odyssey and various Acuras, the direct-injected 3.6-liter GM LFX found in the Chevy Camaro and Cadillac CTS, and the 3.0-liter Jaguar AJ30 V6 found in the S-type and XJ. Each option has an aluminum block and heads, and depending on the variant, outputs roughly 40 to 100 more horsepower than a stock K24.

Industry observers note that no matter what engine you choose, the kits are not cheap. Luckily, with a kit, you don't have to fabricate your own front subframe, motor mounts, and other swap-related parts. The Honda J35 kit from Mini Tec is the most affordable at $3,350, and it utilizes the factory Miata transmission and differential. But that doesn't include any provisions for the cooling, power steering, and fueling systems. The next kit on the list is the $7,260 GM LFX V6 conversion from V8Roadsters, which requires a Camaro transmission and other GM donor parts. This adds more complexity to the swap, but the GM parts are more durable than the factory Miata stuff. Rocketeer Cars takes the most comprehensive approach to V6 swaps. It will sell you everything you need for the conversion, including a refreshed Jaguar AJ30 V6. But that will set you back roughly $22,040. If you are going to spend all of that money on a V6, you might as well go for the gusto and consider our next swap option.

It has been revealed that if the Miata is the universal answer to any sports car question, the Chevy LS is the the answer for any engine swap inquiry. The V8 LS-series engines are still such a popular swap for a reason. They're compact, powerful, readily available in junkyards, and have massive aftermarket support. The LS engine is available in many configurations, from 4.8-liter truck engines to 7.0-liter sports car screamers. Even the wimpiest 4.8-liter LS can make 400 horsepower without much effort. That type of power is a tantalizing prospect for those looking to make a modern version of a Shelby Cobra with a Miata. Fortunately, for those with enough capital and bravery, the massive V8 can be stuffed into every generation of Miata. Although Colorado-based tuner Flyin' Miata stopped doing V8 swaps years ago, other manufactures like Monster Miata and V8Roadsters will sell you the parts to roll your own.

There are many tradeoffs involved in putting an LS in a Miata, first of which is the car's balance. Monster Miata says the weight distribution moves from a perfect 50/50 to a nose-heavy 53/47 with a significant V8 under the hood. Also, the rest of the Miata's driveline can't hold up to V8 power, so it needs to be swapped as well. You'll need parts like a T-56 six-speed transmission, fresh driveshaft, and a differential from a fith-gen Camaro. Costs are highly variable depending on which engine you choose, but they generally fall somewhere around $20,000 for the average completed swap.

Industry observers note that A Miata with more than eight cylinders is like an automotive cryptid. There's evidence that it exists, but it can only be found in the murky depths of internet forums and YouTube. During our dive into the internet swamps, we found a Miata with a Viper V10, one with a Jaguar V12, and another with a Toyota 1GZFE V12 from a Toyota Century.

The efficacy of these swaps is questionable, as there are no off-the-shelf kits for them. And more cylinders means more weight over the nose of the Miata, even further messing up the roadster's weight distribution compared to an LS. Plus, an LS can make just as much power or more power than the engines above. The LS also fits in the engine bay a whole lot better. The guy who did the Jaguar V12 swap said he had to cut the firewall and move it 6 inches back. But if you're crazy enough to try one of these swaps, you'll certainly have the only Miata at the Cars and Coffee with more than eight cylinders.

As a red wave of Chinese-built electric vehicles breaks over Europe and Canada, Xiaomi is selling its electric cars outside of China for the first time ever – and its starting its push for global growth with the UAE in 2027.

Xiaomi is selling its electrified vehicles to buyers outside of China for first time this week, with the SU7 sedan, YU7 crossover, and Skynomad SUV now listed for sale throughout the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The company isn’t going it alone, however.

Xiomi is working local distributor Gargash Prime Automotive, rather than operating its own retail network, with Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun confirming that the tech giant would officially enter Western car markets next year at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen held 17NOV.

CarNewsChina reports that Gargash Prime Automotive is offering 13 variants across the Xiaomi SU7 sedan, YU7 SUV, and Skynomad extended-range electric SUV lineup, with retail prices starting at 169,900 AED ($~46,200 US) for the SU7 Standard and climbing all the way up to 375,900 AED ($~102,000 US) for the range-topping SU7 Ultra.

Not to lump a bunch of nations with their own rich heritage and car culture together, but it’s fair to say that drivers in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait love their supercars – and the brand’s Xiaomi SU7 Ultra might be one of the most super of them all, thanks to fully 1,548 hp from three high-torque electric motors, the SU7 Ultra can sprint from 0-100 km/h (62 mph) in under two seconds on its way to a towering, 217 mph top speed.

Industry observers note that it’s not just a straight-line speed machine, either. Xiaomi gave its go-fast flagship a serious track-focused makeover on its way to becomig the “Utlra,” complete with carbon-ceramic brakes, an aggressive (if controversial) composite aero package, an enormous rear wing, and a chassis tuned to tackle the turns the Green Hell of the Nürburgring.

And, at a relatively reasonable $102,000 equivalent price, I’d be willing to bet that a lot of the hypercar-loving Emiratis will be eager to get their hands on one.

The first customer deliveries of the Xiaomi SU7 Standard and Ultra, YU7 Standard, and Skynomad N70 Pro models are scheduled for December of this year, with deliveries of the remaining variants scheduled for February 2027.

#638. Every Car Brand That's Put Rotary Engines In Production Cars (There Aren't Many)

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1148 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Every Car Brand That's Put Rotary Engines In Production Cars (There Aren't Many)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, beyond the realms of car enthusiasm, most normies wouldn't have actually heard of a rotary engine – also known as a Wankel engine (after Felix Wankel, the man who patented the design in the first place).
  • When it comes to street cars, the most coveted example is Mazda's famous RX-7.
  • Industry observers note that but Mazda isn't the only car brand to have ever used a rotary engine in its production cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, beyond the realms of car enthusiasm, most normies wouldn't have actually heard of a rotary engine – also known as a Wankel engine (after Felix Wankel, the man who patented the design in the first place). These are fondly called "spinning Doritos" because at their heart is a triangular rotor that whizzes around a central shaft and makes power in a similar way to how a regular piston engine does. There are many pros and cons to rotary engines, and the cons are why they have seldom been used in automobiles.

When it comes to street cars, the most coveted example is Mazda's famous RX-7. The same brand was also responsible for arguably the most mythical race car ever created: the quad-rotor 787B. It won the 1991 edition of the famed 24 Hours of Le Mans and leaves a lasting impression on anyone who hears it, thanks to the orgasmic, high-pitched wail it generates as it climbs toward 9,000 rpm.

Industry observers note that but Mazda isn't the only car brand to have ever used a rotary engine in its production cars. The very first instance came from a German company called NSU (which eventually became part of Audi), and there were also examples from Citroën and the Russian brand Lada. Maxton, a low-volume sports car maker from the U.S., also briefly used rotary engines in the Rollerskate. But since it used Mazda engines and was built in such small numbers, it is often discounted.

Industry observers note that in fact, the famed Japanese brand is estimated to have built around two million rotaries between 1967 and 2012, starting with the much-loved Cosmo sports car and ending with the equally adored RX-8 coupe. It has since resurrected the rotary, but only as a generator that forms part of a hybrid package in the MX-30 electric SUV, so it hardly counts.

In a recent development, mazda really did try it all at the height of its rotary days, even building the now highly collectible Rotary Pickup. It was — and is — humanity's sole rotary-powered pickup truck, equipped with a 110-horsepower 1.3-liter Wankel unit, and made purely for the U.S. and Canadian markets. The manufacturer built around 15,000 examples, and well-maintained, low-mileage trucks still go for close to $30,000. Further afield, ardent enthusiasts will also remember the Mazda Furai concept, which is among the weirdest one-off cars ever built.

According to recent reports, before Mazda's love affair with Wankels, NSU rolled out the very first rotary-powered production car, the Spider, at the 1963 Frankfurt Auto Show. Its single-rotor, 500cc engine wasn't hugely powerful: it produced just 50 hp when it debuted, and maxed out at 54 hp in its most powerful guise. Despite getting positive reviews from the automotive press, the Spider never really took off. Just 2,400 units are estimated to have been built before production ended in 1967.

NSU replaced it with the Ro 80, which was a sleek, four-door sedan with a 115-hp twin-rotor motor and a fancy independent suspension. It was so good that European Car of the Year jurors voted it as their winning candidate for 1968 – making it the first German vehicle to ever win the coveted prize. It enjoyed a 10-year run rolling off the production lines, with NSU building around 37,000 examples before retiring it in 1977.

It was in 1964 that Citroën struck up a partnership with NSU to develop rotary engines. While NSU went on to join the VW Group, Citroën stayed the course and eventually unveiled the M35 in the late '60s — its first true rotary-powered car, built in a limited run of 267 examples. Based on an Ami 8 – the same model James May used during the "Top Gear" classic time trial rally challenge in Mallorca – the M35 even had Citroën's super-soft hydropneumatic suspension, with 49 rampant French horses under the hood.

Then came the GS Birotor in 1973, whose twin-rotor setup produced an even mightier 106 hp and allowed for a top speed of 109 mph. Citroën eventually dropped its rotary experiment by the late '70s, in part due to low sales volumes, but also because of the world's oil crisis. The latter is significant here because rotary engines, by nature, guzzle fuel. They burn a lot of oil, too.

Yes, who'd have thought it? Little about these cars ever made it past the Iron Curtain, but Lada started its Wankel journey in 1978 with the VAZ-21018. Though it may have shared model codes with a fax machine of some kind, the 21018 did have a pretty prominent place in society. The four-door sedan used a 71-hp rotary engine that was basically reverse-engineered from either an NSU or a Mazda engine, depending on who you ask, and proved horribly unreliable. Some accounts say these engines couldn't manage more than 12,000 miles before succumbing to issues such as seal and bearing failures.

According to recent reports, lada took another crack at it in 1982 and created a twin-rotor engine with two outputs: 115 and 140 hp. These were fitted to the VAZ-21019 sedan, and provided a notable step up in performance from "regular" Ladas. They proved slightly more reliable too, at the cost of poorer fuel economy. Lada did stick by its rotary engines all the way until the early 2000s, albeit on an increasingly small scale, before wrapping up production entirely.

Industry observers note that citroën, Mazda, Lada, and NSU aren't the only manufacturers to have dabbled with rotary cars. General Motors was at the height of its power in the '70s, and saw an opportunity to reinvent how vehicles were engineered by placing rotaries at the heart of its prepares. It had intended to offer its then-new Vega compact car with a Wankel engine, and committed $50 million just to license the technology. There was even the Aerovette: the best-looking Corvette of all time that never made it out of the concept stage and had a rotary engine. Unfortunately, as would soon happen with Citroën and the GS Birotor, the global oil crisis forced GM to ditch its rotary plans by the end of 1974.

Recent findings suggest that mercedes-Benz also got in on the act with its jaw-dropping C 111 experimental vehicle, first previewed at the 1969 Frankfurt Auto Show. It seemingly had everything a discerning celebrity would've wanted back then: a funky wedge-shaped body, a striking orange metallic paint job, and gullwing doors. Whereas the very first experiment had a three-rotor configuration, the second cranked it up to four rotors and was claimed to have a top speed of 186 mph. It all sounds super exciting, right? Well, Mercedes chose not to put it into production. Sorry to burst your several-second dream of owning one. But of the rotary-powered cars that did make production, which would you most like to own?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the last time Hyundai revealed a newly introduced work truck was 22 years ago, and the Hyundai Porter has proven itself as a dependable workhorse throughout Korea and Southeast Asia – but only the pyramids and the Chevy Express can last forever. Hyundai is reportedly getting ready to pull the wraps off an all-new Porter pickup. This time, it’s electric.

Distinct from the Piaggio-branded Porter pickup that’s already sold in Europe, the Hyundai Porter is a conceptually similar, work-focused vehicle with a dropside pickup “bed” trailing a box-like passenger cab and a serious, professional-grade payload capacity.

Carscoops recently published photos of a heavily camouflaged Hyundai Porter prototype last month, along with claims that Hyundai means to follow up the success of sister brand Kia’s multifunctional PV5 electric vans with a globally available electric version of the truck as early as next year. This week, the wraps came off, giving us our best look yet at what the truck might look like when it makes its official debut.

After feeding as many spy shots as I could into some AI models, we ended up with the images you see here. If they’re accurate, they show a commercial-ready EV that’s meant to attract new fleet buyers looking to ditch diesel in Western markets while serving as a direct, 1:1 replacement for domestic fleet operators already putting Porter pickups to work.

Those operators will probably feel a little safer behind the wheel of the fresh truck, too. Hyundai has worked a short hood and crash structure into the bodywork where a conventional “flat” cabover now sits – a move that seems to point both to a commitment to provide better front-end protection to the truck’s occupants and an intent to at least take an honest run at the Euro NCAP crash standards.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, we don’t really know anything about the upcoming Korean pickup – but it’s a safe bet that the next-generation Porter will benefit from some of the technology that’s been baked into the Hyundai Motor Group’s E-GMP.S commercial vehicle platform that underpins the Kia PV vehicles. Those ship with 51.5 and 71.2 kWh battery options sending electrons to 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motors, and while that’s far from a guarantee, it’s not nothing, either.

That’s my take, anyway – what’s yours? Will the Hyundai Porter EV make its way to the West on an AWD version of the E-GMP.S platform, or will it remain a regional model running on one of the company’s hybrid platforms? Let us know in the comments.

SOURCES: SH Proshots, Baldauf, via Carscoops, SEMA News.

According to recent reports, toyota's Corolla hatchback is already a pretty lovely car, but I adored driving the all-wheel drive turbocharged Corolla GR. You can imagine how great it must be with more power and less weight, as found in the GRMN. That initialism isn't just the stock ticker symbol for Garmin, it's an extremely fancy $64,000 Toyota hot hatch, and it allegedly stands for Gazoo Racing Masters of the Nürburgring. Maybe the hottest hatch of all time? I haven't yet had the pleasure of slipping behind the wheel, but my delightful (and extremely tall) colleague Logan absolutely loved their time driving it, and recommended buying one.

The Corolla isn't the first GRMN product in the world, as that honor belongs to the Yaris GRMN which isn't sold here. That remarked, this definitely got me thinking about what else Toyota could build if it wanted to get super serious about performance cars. Don't get me wrong, I think Toyota is building more cars for enthusiasts today than any other automaker, and there are more in the pipeline, but what's the harm in offering pumped up versions?

In a recent development, given my druthers, I'd absolutely love to see an amped up Prius GRMN. The all-wheel drive Prius is already quite quick and powerful, given its economy car bent. The current generation is also quite a fetching design. I want something economical that looks good, but when I put my foot down, I want something a little quicker than the current 7-ish second 0-60 time. The AWD Prius right now uses a 150-horsepower 2-liter four-cylinder engine mated to a 111 horsepower electric motor at the front, plus a tiny 40 horsepower electric motor at the rear axle. What if Toyota wanted to get serious about acceleration and ditched the gas motor for the GRMN Corolla's 300-pony 1.6-liter three-cylinder instead? And maybe that puny rear motor could be supplanted by the 165 horse electric motor found in the base model bZ electric. Keep the same electric motor that the current Prius has in the front, you're still looking to at least double the power output from standard Prius to theoretical GRMN Prius. I like it, how about you?

It has been revealed that toyota makes a whole lot of different cars. I want to hear what your favorite hypothetical GRMN silk purse from a base model sow's ear might be. Pick a model that Toyota at the moment makes and give us your idea for how it could be GRMN-ified. Given that the GRMN Corolla is a two-seater with the rear seats stripped out, you can kind of go hog wild with it. Do you want to see a Sienna with aggressive track-focused aerodynamic bodywork? How about a Toyota Sequoia V8 stuffed under the hood of a GRMN-86?

This is your dream workshop, and you're playing with whatever toys are already in the Toyota (or Lexus) arsenal. Because GRMN is a track-focused operation, these creations should also be intended with the dual purpose of fun driving dynamics and fast lap times. Try to keep it to a parts bin special, if you please, because there's no good game in the world without a few rules to it. Maybe you want to go hog wild with it and bring the Lexus LFA's V10 out of retirement to shove under the hood of a track-oriented Tundra sport truck? Now that would be a whole lot of street style. It's Saturday, you don't have to leave dream world just yet, so you have the entire Toyota research and development team at your beck and call, what wild track-oriented automotive monstrosity would you make them create?

I don't know about you, but I'm still thinking about that time attack bZ that Toyota brought to SEMA last year. That could make a pretty cool GRMN EV.

#635. Breaking: Why Cars Need To Be Driven To Stay In Peak Condition

Breaking: Why Cars Need To Be Driven To Stay In Peak Condition

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Sources indicate that humans anthropomorphize cars in many different and often goofy ways, but there is one thing we have in common: sedentary lifestyles are bad for both of us.
  • Industry observers note that of course, life happens and sometimes that extra project car that you're "definitely going to have running next week" sits for weeks, months, or even years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Sources indicate that humans anthropomorphize cars in many different and often goofy ways, but there is one thing we have in common: sedentary lifestyles are bad for both of us. Much like neglecting to stretch those hammies can add strain to certain movements, leaving your car untouched can cause components to seize up, and both can be a major pain in the butt. While time comes for us all and everything will eventually deteriorate from age, keeping active can still help keep us in peak shape and prevent additional challenges from arising.

Industry observers note that of course, life happens and sometimes that extra project car that you're "definitely going to have running next week" sits for weeks, months, or even years. However, this can have real consequences. Leaving your car stationary too long can result in brake corrosion, battery problems, fuel system issues, and leaks. All can lead to reduced performance or potentially costly repairs.

Industry observers note that thankfully, many of these problems can be mitigated by simply using your vehicle for what it is designed for — regular driving! Taking a weekly cruise that lasts about 20 to 30 minutes, per AAA guidance, will help keep your vehicle's fluids flowing, parts lubricated, and battery charged. Turns out, hitting those favorite back roads is actually good for both you and your car.

Sources indicate that so what does regular driving help prevent? Well, in as little as a day or two, a thin layer of rust can form on the brake rotors of a parked car. Fortunately, this is mostly cosmetic and normal driving clears this up after a few stops, but over extended periods of time corrosion can set in and seize up braking components.

According to recent reports, fuel that sits in your gas tank lasts about three to six months before it starts to break down. In older cars with metal fuel tanks, condensation can collect and start to rust the tank out from the inside. Aged fuel and moisture in your fuel system can lower octane, gum up fuel injectors, and lead to reduced performance. Keeping your fuel tank full (in this economy?) and cycled through every few months will help mitigate fuel system complications.

Sources indicate that an glitch that may require immediate intervention is a weak crank or no start from a dead battery. Batteries naturally lose charge with time, and even more so depending on battery age or if there are any parasites drawing current when the vehicle is off. Additionally, cold weather reduces a battery's cranking power on top of the natural battery discharge. Routine driving helps keep your battery topped off via the alternator so your car is ready.

Industry observers note that tires and belts will eventually need replacing. You may even find a flat spot in a tire that's sitting for too long. Seals and gaskets that keep fluids in place can dry up and crack when not driven enough to keep everything conditioned, soft, and flexible, which can cause leaks throughout your vehicle's powertrain. Depending on the seal and severity of the leak, this may require repair and keep your vehicle stationary even longer.

According to recent reports, if you know your car is going to be sitting for a while, there are a few steps you can take to protect your car. I grew up in the Northeast, where it's common to put away the "nice" car for a few months over the winter so it doesn't get destroyed by road salt. Indoor storage is optimal for protection from the elements, but I'm no Rockefeller and my cars get parked outside.

The annual ritual involves topping off the tank and adding a fuel stabilizer to prevent fuel degradation. Attaching a trickle charger keeps a low current fed to the battery and helps it stay ready to go. Changing the oil prior to storage will remove contaminants from the engine as an added layer of protection. A good cleaning inside and out can keep blemishes or stains from setting in. With that prep out of the way, you should be safe to get through the season.

Recent findings suggest that when the time comes to start your car after it has been sitting for a while, do a quick visual inspection. Check for underinflated or flat tires, the presence of animals, and any upcoming leaks. If the tires are okay, fluids are at normal levels, there aren't any pools below your car or new inhabitants, and your battery isn't dead, you should be good to go. Drive it easy until the engine comes up to temp and listen for any new or unusual sounds. Just like humans, keeping your car in peak shape requires attention. Doing so will keep both you and your car happier and healthier for many more miles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that while many Americans are struggling to meet their basic needs, automakers are moving further upmarket. Porsche's mid-engined Mission S supercar concept, for example, is aimed at an ultra-wealthy clientele, with an estimated $500,000 starting price for the production model. And Jay Leno has something to say about this.

Industry observers note that during an interview with TBPN on YouTube, Leno noted Porsche was "moving upscale" with the Mission S: "They want to be like Ferrari. Sell fewer cars [for] more money to fewer people." In the old days, he noted, "A Ferrari had 800 miles and Porsche had 60,000. A Corvette, same thing." And back then, when people used to hold shootouts to find out which car was the fastest, "the only ones that indicated up would be Corvette and Porsche. Everybody else just didn't." Nowadays, Leno continued, people "buy a GT3 and [say,] 'I'm putting it away.'" He added, "Porsches have always been expensive, but they're not rare. There's a lot of them around.".

And while Leno mentions how someone reasonably financially successful could still aspire to own a Corvette, the lineup has gone fairly upmarket, especially with the ZR1X in the mix — although the ZR1X's starting price of roughly $230,000 is considerably lower than those of most modern Ferraris and Lamborghinis, it's still a pretty expensive automobile.

Recent findings suggest that leno concluded that this strategy of selling fewer but pricier cars is spreading across the auto industry and, more broadly, the economy as a whole. "You're either Motel 6 or the Four Seasons. ... We have no middle class anymore. And that's the sad thing.".

According to recent reports, there's no official definition of the middle class, at least not one that's widely agreed upon. The Pew Research Center defines middle-income households as those with an income (adjusted for household size) that's between two-thirds and double that of the U.S. median household income. Upper-income households earn more than double the median, while lower-income households earn less than two-thirds of it. By that measure, 61% of Americans were part of the middle class in 1971, with that share dropping to 51% by 2023.

In fact, the share of household income held by the middle class has fallen in almost every decade since 1970. Middle-income households held 62% of all U.S. household income in 1970, but just 43% in 2022. Upper-income households, meanwhile, saw a massive gain in their share, jumping from 29% to 48%.

The middle-class decline can also be attributed to the pace at which income grew. Inflation-adjusted incomes across all tiers improved between 1970 and 2022, but not at the same rate. Upper-income households saw 78% growth, compared with just 60% for middle-income households. Lower-income folks saw the least growth (55%). In 2024, the median income of an upper-income household was $278,800, versus $115,900 for middle-income and $38,400 for lower-income households, according to Pew's 2026 report. And while upper-income households had 6.8 times the typical income of lower-income households in 2001, that number had risen to 7.3 by 2024.

It's deeply concerning how new car sales are booming for the rich and falling for everyone else. Some of our readers have shared how their finances are holding them back from buying a new car in 2026, and they are certainly not alone.

It has been revealed that perhaps Jay's take on the middle class being nonexistent is a bit of a stretch. But as you can tell, income inequality is real. According to the Economic Policy Institute, between 1979 and 2023, the average annual earnings of the bottom 90% of workers saw cumulative growth of 44%, while the top 0.1% posted staggering growth of 354%. Although Americans earning an hourly wage were getting bigger paychecks than in the '70s, their purchasing power had remained largely unchanged after you factor in inflation, per a 2018 study from Pew. And according to data gathered by Statista, average real wages were down 0.8% in July 2026 compared with January 2021.

No wonder there's an affordability crisis. The data shows that President Trump's repeated claims of it being "fake" and a "hoax" couldn't be further from the truth, and plenty of working families can attest to that.

#633. What Are Drivers Supposed To Do When Encountering A 'Narrows' Road Sign?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (557 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

What Are Drivers Supposed To Do When Encountering A 'Narrows' Road Sign?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Road signs are short, sweet, and sometimes downright goofy.
  • Various warning signs are used for narrowing roadways.
  • It has been revealed that the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), which is managed by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Road signs are short, sweet, and sometimes downright goofy. However, they're not always easy to understand. When a picture is worth a thousand words, deciphering signage with diagonal black-and-yellow stripes or arrows pointing in opposite directions is akin to playing Pictionary with toddlers: what is that shape supposed to mean?! Adding a few words can create even more ambiguity, like Pennsylvania's contribution to the worst road signs list. Which brings us to the narrows.

Various warning signs are used for narrowing roadways. The self-explanatory ones are emblazoned with the phrases "road narrows" and "narrow bridge." Less informative is the pictorial variation featuring an hourglass-like outline that may or may not be accompanied by vertical dashes down the middle — the figure's "hips" reference the road narrowing. Regardless of which version you see, the rules of engagement remain the same: proceed with caution.

It has been revealed that the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), which is managed by the U.S. DOT's Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), sets the standards for all traffic-flow-related communications, including road markings, signs, and signals. Per the MUTCD, Road Narrows signs are part of the W5 series, which includes cautions for underpasses. Standardized to be yellow, warning signs will vary in shape. For the W5s, the MUTCD settled on a diamond.

You'll also find them only in specific places. Plenty of driving lanes narrow and widen, but only when the path is shrunk to a certain width will you come across a W5 sign. The exception is low-volume local streets with speed limits of 30 mph or less. At those speeds, you're likely able to see oncoming traffic.

It has been revealed that according to the MUTCD, a road's width must diminish so abruptly and sharply that opposing traffic cannot simultaneously pass at posted speed limits. For bridges, culverts, and underpasses, warnings are issued following the surface-street rules, as well as when the two-way road's clearance is 16 to 18 feet across. This measurement includes the shoulder, if there is one.

The guidance suggests warnings be posted roughly 155 to 325 feet ahead of narrowings in 25 mph sections and up to 990 feet in 55 mph sectors. If visibility is impaired due to curves or grades, those distances can be adjusted. In construction zones, especially dangerous highway work, the W5s switch to work-zone orange and should appear prior to lane tapers, while a second reminder can be placed closer to the work area.

In a recent development, so, what should you do when you see a narrows sign? Because it's not a road closure and the number of lanes can be unchanged, you simply continue on. Just keep your vehicle centered and take things slow and easy, especially if there's oncoming traffic. If a large vehicle approaches, like a bus or truck, consider yielding and letting it through. Room to pass will be limited, even if there is a shoulder.

On bridges, stick to your side of the road, reduce your speed, and definitely watch out for outside mirrors. If the bridge is too narrow for two vehicles, the rule of thumb is whoever arrives first gets dibs. If there's no room, there's no point in forcing your way through. Although these signs don't say how long the road narrows, the early heads-up gives you time to prepare.

#632. 6 Fuel-Sipping Motorcycles That Will Make Your Commute Less Exorbitant

6 Fuel-Sipping Motorcycles That Will Make Your Commute Less Exorbitant

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the skyward surge in gas prices in 2026 has hit our wallets pretty hard, even more so for those who commute within city limits.
  • These are manufacturer-claimed figures, of course, but they should still translate to some pretty awesome mileage in the real world, which can help ease your concerns regarding gas prices.
  • Sources indicate that kicking things off is the WR125R, which, at $3,999 (plus a $400 destination fee), is the most affordable street-legal motorcycle Yamaha offers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the skyward surge in gas prices in 2026 has hit our wallets pretty hard, even more so for those who commute within city limits. And if you use a gas-guzzling sportbike or a heavyweight cruiser to get around town, things are likely even worse for you. Fear not, though, as we've compiled a list of six commuter motorcycles presently on sale (spoiler alert: the overwhelming majority of them are Hondas), all of which claim impressively high fuel efficiency figures — specifically, more than 100 miles per gallon.

These are manufacturer-claimed figures, of course, but they should still translate to some pretty awesome mileage in the real world, which can help ease your concerns regarding gas prices. What's also great about these motorcycles is that they're very affordably priced. However, don't expect scintillating performance out of them, as they're powered by small-capacity single-cylinder engines. Consequently, these motorcycles are best suited to urban commuting rather than zipping down a highway or freeway. That said, some of them are dual-sport bikes, which means you can take them to off-road trails on the weekends, if you're into that.

Sources indicate that kicking things off is the WR125R, which, at $3,999 (plus a $400 destination fee), is the most affordable street-legal motorcycle Yamaha offers. The WR125R comes with a 125 cc single-cylinder fuel-injected motor that's liquid-cooled (the only liquid-cooled engine on this list) and develops 14 hp and 8.3 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel through a six-speed wet-clutch gearbox. Yamaha touts an estimated fuel economy of 105 mpg for the WR125R, and the bike features a 2.1-gallon fuel tank, with Yamaha quoting a maximum range of around 200 miles.

Pretty good for a city commuter, right? It doesn't end there, though, as the WR125R is a dual-sport motorcycle. As part of its off-road trappings, the WR125R packs a 41mm (1.6-inch) KYB front fork with 8.5 inches of travel, a linked-type rear Monocross shock with 7.3 inches of travel, and a generous 9.4 inches of ground clearance — all of which can make for a fun ride off the beaten path. At 304 pounds (wet), the WR125R's weight should be easy to manage for rookie riders, though some may find the 34.4-inch seat height on the taller side.

It has been revealed that priced at $2,199 (plus a $300 destination fee), the cute Honda Navi is the most affordable motorcycle on this list. The word "motorcycle" does do a bit of heavy lifting here, as the Navi's styling features a dose of scooter influence. Within its chassis sits a 109 cc single-cylinder engine that uses a carburetor, which is simple and easy to repair, but prone to hard starting in colder weather. The engine is also air-cooled instead of liquid-cooled, so it can run hot during long traffic halts.

Recent findings suggest that the Navi makes an estimated 8 hp and 6.5 lb-ft of torque, which is ample for trundling around city blocks at leisurely speeds. Notably, it remains the cheapest new major-brand motorcycle you can buy with an automatic gearbox, specifically a CVT, which furthers the case for the Navi being an ideal city bike. It also weighs just 234 pounds and has a 30-inch seat height, so beginners can get to grips with it quickly. However, Honda has fitted the bike with a teeny-tiny 0.9-gallon fuel tank, so at Honda's claimed 110 mpg, the range works out to around 100 miles. The Navi, therefore, is best suited for those who have short daily commutes.

Like the Yamaha WR125R, the XR150L is Honda's entry-level dual-sport motorcycle, priced at $3,399 (plus a $300 destination fee). It's powered by a 149 cc single-cylinder engine, which is carbureted and air-cooled, and makes 12.6 hp and 9.6 lb-ft of torque. A five-speed manual gearbox transmits that grunt to the rear wheel. As for fuel efficiency, the XR150L is quite a step above the WR125R, and even the smaller-engined Navi. Honda's figures work out to 124 mpg, and the bike offers a 2.8-gallon fuel tank — the largest-capacity tank on this list.

Recent findings suggest that so, even though the XR150L doesn't tout the highest fuel efficiency here, its relatively massive tank enables a claimed range of 346 miles on a single tank. If your commute is on the longer side, this is the motorcycle to go for. Since it's a dual-sport bike, the XR150L additionally features a 31mm (1.22-inch) front fork with 7.1 inches of travel, a single rear shock with 5.9 inches of travel, and 9.6 inches of ground clearance. While the wheel travel is shorter than that offered by the WR125R, the XR150L has more ground clearance, and, at 282 pounds, is a decent bit lighter too. Its seat height is also noticeably lower (32.8 inches), which can make mounting and dismounting easier.

Industry observers note that if you find yourself less interested in dual-sport bikes and motorcycle-scooter hybrids, and lean more toward retro-inspired styling, the Honda Trail125 might just be the bike for you. Priced at $4,199 (plus a $300 destination fee), the Trail125 features a distinctive design that draws on Honda's trail-bike heritage, with a high-mounted exhaust, a step-through steel backbone chassis, a rear luggage rack, and spoked wheels. The Trail125 comes fitted with a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder engine that's air-cooled and produces 9 hp and 8.1 lb-ft of torque.

Recent findings suggest that A four-speed semi-automatic transmission — meaning you never have to work a clutch lever — is equipped as standard, and the fuel tank measures 1.4 gallons, which translates to nearly 220 miles between fill-ups, at about 157 mpg. The seat height is 31.5 inches, which is slightly taller than that of the Navi, and the Trail125 weighs 256 pounds, making it heavier than the Navi as well.

Industry observers note that honda's quirkily named Grom is yet another small and cute motorcycle. It's powered by a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder motor that's air-cooled and belts out nearly 10 hp and 7.7 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel via a five-speed manual gearbox. The Grom is rated for a stellar fuel economy of 161 mpg, and its 1.6-gallon fuel tank means that it can theoretically cover 257 miles before needing a refill.

Industry observers note that the Grom is styled much like a downsized conventional motorcycle, so if you're not a fan of the Navi's scooter-like look or the XR150L's dual-sport design, it would likely appeal to you. It also weighs 224 pounds, making it lighter than the Navi, and it even matches the Navi's 30-inch seat height. As for price, the Grom is available in three trim levels, namely the Base ($3,599), SP ($3,699), and ABS ($3,799) — all three carry a destination fee of $300. The Base and SP trims are differentiated by color and graphics (the SP comes solely in a black finish, while the Base trim is offered in red, white, and blue), and the aptly named ABS trim adds front-wheel ABS.

Taking the top spot on this list is the Monkey — one more whimsically named motorcycle from Honda. Much like the Trail125, the Monkey is a retro-inspired motorcycle, but instead of a trail bike, it resembles an old-school scrambler. Pretty cool, right? As for mechanicals, the Monkey comes equipped with a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder mill that uses air cooling and develops all of 9 hp and 8 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel via a five-speed manual transmission.

In a recent development, despite the Monkey's impressive 163-mpg claimed fuel economy, its 1.5-gallon fuel tank is good for around 244 miles — less than the Grom's. The seat height is also a tiny bit higher at 30.5 inches, and, at 231 pounds, the Monkey is a few pounds heavier than the Grom too. That noted, the Monkey does come with front-wheel ABS as standard. As for the price, the Monkey is available for $4,399 (plus a $300 destination fee), making it the most expensive motorcycle here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, over the last few years, Flock cameras and other AI-powered automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have steadily spread across the United States, and until recently, the spread was relatively silent.
  • Over 100 public school systems have let Flock Safety expand its private spy network onto their campuses, according to The 74, leaving hundreds of thousands of students nationwide surveilled without their consent.
  • Recent findings suggest that if having your kids being spied on from the moment they enter the campus isn't concerning enough, there's also Flock Safety's track record to worry about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, over the last few years, Flock cameras and other AI-powered automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have steadily spread across the United States, and until recently, the spread was relatively silent. Today, Flock Safety has over 145,000 cameras deployed throughout the nation, though their prevalence hasn't made the public any safer. And it's not just major roads being spied on and license plates being tracked.

Over 100 public school systems have let Flock Safety expand its private spy network onto their campuses, according to The 74, leaving hundreds of thousands of students nationwide surveilled without their consent. This is affecting students of all ages, too. Some 150 colleges and universities have introduced mass surveillance to their campuses through Flock cameras, too, per Policing and Society: An International Journal of Research and Policy.

Recent findings suggest that if having your kids being spied on from the moment they enter the campus isn't concerning enough, there's also Flock Safety's track record to worry about. Flock cameras are notoriously easy to hack, and they collect an absurd amount of information, some of which lives unencrypted on the camera itself. In the past, Flock cameras have even been caught streaming on the open web, according to a report by 404Media.

It has been revealed that one question when looking at how many schools are targeted by Flock cameras may be, "Why?" Flock says its cameras "help communities deter crime, respond to emergencies, and investigate safety incidents." And law enforcement is supposed to use Flock data to help solve crime and aid investigations. But Flock cameras also have huge abuse potential, even beyond their numerous security problems. We know that cops are looking up stuff on Flock and putting "LMAO," "WEIRD KID," and "sexy" as reasons for the searches, and we know that in Georgia alone, 17 cops have been arrested for using Flock to stalk civilians.

In a recent development, we also know Flock info isn't entirely accurate and has led to the detention of auto journalists, wrong cars being towed, and traffic stops and tickets based on incorrect information. Couple that with Flock Safety's attempt to shut down DeFlock, a website that maps Flock camera's in public, and the fact that police don't like Flock-inspired cameras tracking their own movements, and the intent behind installing Flock cameras at schools seems less altruistic than the marketing material might suggest. Surprise.

What ALPRs at schools definitively can do is build and deepen profiles on cars that frequent the area, namely those driven by parents and students. And while Flock Safety claims that its cameras aren't capable of tracking people (or cars, for that matter), a recent hack of a Flock camera revealed that the cameras do at least detect people and save images of them. Some have rightfully voiced concerns over the privacy concerns this presents near schools and questioned how accessible this information becomes once it's on Flock's servers.

It has been revealed that after public and student pushback, some schools are canceling their Flock contracts and removing the offending cameras. Take the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee, which canceled its contract in September and called for Flock to remove the company's 20-plus cameras from campus. This came on the heels of two other UW schools discontinuing their use of Flock cameras.

This is part of a bigger trend of cities across the country dumping Flock en masse, and hopefully this trend continues to spread until not just Flock, but also Axon and all other privately owned cameras are off the streets. Or at least well-regulated enough to not threaten massive security risks, and not give police warrantless access to the public's data.

It has been revealed that for now, though, the unfortunate reality is that canceling a Flock contract doesn't necessarily remove the concern, and it certainly doesn't undo damage already done. See, like many stalkers and creeps out there, Flock refuses to take no for an answer. The company doesn't always remove cameras after a contract ends, sometimes opting to keep them in service instead. Some officials have taken to removing the cameras themselves, while other discontinued Flock cameras are covered with garbage bags after contract termination.

Until the cameras are actually fully removed, there's no guarantee that they're not continuing to collect data still. Maybe if we're lucky, Republican U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie's anti-Flock bill will ban automated traffic enforcement and we won't have to worry about this mess anymore.

#629. Why Automakers Call Their Early Prototype Cars Mules

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (856 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Why Automakers Call Their Early Prototype Cars Mules

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The hybrid equine offspring of a male donkey and a female horse is known as a mule.
  • Surely you're familiar with the concept of a pre-production development car, and you'll likely have seen some of these cars wearing heavy camouflage in spy photography over the years.
  • You may recall that Porsche cobbled some 911 bodywork around the hybrid drivetrain of a 918 Spyder back in 2012.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The hybrid equine offspring of a male donkey and a female horse is known as a mule. These animals have traditionally been useful pack animals and beasts of burden because they tend to be larger, stronger, and faster than a donkey, while tougher and able to endure longer days than a horse. Because mules are typically sterile, they almost always represent the end of their bloodline. Many of these attributes also apply to pre-production cars, which might explain why they're frequently known as "test mules.".

Surely you're familiar with the concept of a pre-production development car, and you'll likely have seen some of these cars wearing heavy camouflage in spy photography over the years. Automakers use these pre-production testers to help develop the driving and chassis dynamics and guide them through the parts-selection process. Usually they're used in the development of new hardware, whether that be a new engine, early electric motor prototyping, or a new suspension design. They are often cobbled together from existing componentry, and hidden under the skin of an existing production car in an effort to hide their true intent.

You may recall that Porsche cobbled some 911 bodywork around the hybrid drivetrain of a 918 Spyder back in 2012. That thing looked weird. Or maybe you remember the extra-long-wheelbase 348 Ferrari used to develop the now-iconic Enzo. Another favorite is the Holden Maloo ute Chevrolet imported from Australia to use as a development chassis for the mid-engine C8 Corvette, stuffing that V8 right in the truck bed (photo below). There are thousands of slightly less exciting examples, of course.

Industry observers note that before a vehicle reaches production, automakers have to spend thousands of hours and miles making sure the components are up to snuff. Sometimes these cars are used for years ahead of their scheduled production manufacture, letting engineers make changes on the fly in the development phase. Sometimes these mules end up going nowhere, as the engineers figure out their ideas weren't viable. Sometimes they're used for final validation of simple things like weight distribution, or setting ride and handling tweaks.

Like the animal mule, automotive mules are frequently hybrids of a few different cars, keeping costs down by using stuff automakers already have in the parts bin. The word has frequently been used to allude to anything made in a hybrid manner. Additionally, like the mule, these are cars that are putting in the work for the manufacturer. They may be philosophically sterile, never to produce offspring, but they can help move the heavy load of getting a car closer to production. Perhaps that's why these cars have been dubbed "mule.".

Industry observers note that however, pre-production prototype mules are likely called that because of the role of a mule car in motorsport. Italian race teams frequently referred to their spare or test cars as "mulettos" or little mules (also a slang term for forklifts in Italian). Here's a brief explanation from Pirelli Tires: "It originates from the 1930s, when cars that were used for training racing drivers or testing new parts needed to be strong and reliable rather than necessarily fast: a bit like mules, especially when contrasted with the capricious thoroughbreds that were the actual race cars.".

After decades of use in motorsport, the concept of a test car being called a mule seems to have spread to the road car engineers as well.

Consider, for a moment, this rather innocuous looking 1980s Ford Transit van. You probably wouldn't suspect from the outside that this is effectively a test bed for Jaguar's exciting 542-horsepower XJ220 supercar. That's exactly what it is, though. Right in the middle of the white van's load floor is the 3.5-liter Tom Walkinshaw Racing-built twin-turbo V6 cribbed directly from TWR's Jaguar racing program. In an effort to swiftly work out all the bugs in the XJ220's drivetrain, Jaguar engineers slapped this van together.

In a recent development, the story goes that Jaguar not only could get plenty of road testing miles on the engine without attracting much attention, but could also position an engineer in the back of the van to directly monitor the engine while it was driving, tuning for turbo lag and the like. In an effort to disguise the van further and convince passersby that it was just a regular white van, Jag engineers put newspapers and candy wrappers on the dashboard to make it look like the work vehicle of a plumber or construction worker.

Perhaps I don't speak for everyone when I say this, but I believe this test van is perhaps even cooler than the XJ220 that it muled for. To get an XJ220, you merely had to be a wealthy person in the late 1980s, but this van has a story, and stories are what make cars cool. I feel the same about pre-production prototypes of pretty much any supercar ever made. There's an engineered necessity here that makes the prototype cooler. Mules are just plain cooler than the horses or the donkeys they're derived from — it's a real "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts" situation.
