#628. Electric cars are finally mainstream in GTA 6, and Vice City is full of them

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1347 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Electric cars are finally mainstream in GTA 6, and Vice City is full of them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Electric vehicles have finally gone mainstream in Grand Theft Auto.
  • It’s a major change for a series that spent over a decade treating EVs as a Tesla joke.
  • I’ve been playing GTA 6 since it launched on Thursday, partly for fun and partly because I wanted to see how Rockstar would handle EVs this time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric vehicles have finally gone mainstream in Grand Theft Auto. In GTA 6, EVs are just part of everyday traffic in Vice City, from Tesla and Porsche lookalikes to a parody of Electrify America’s charging network.

It’s a major change for a series that spent over a decade treating EVs as a Tesla joke. After a few days of playing, I’d say Rockstar nailed the vibe.

I’ve been playing GTA 6 since it launched on Thursday, partly for fun and partly because I wanted to see how Rockstar would handle EVs this time. The answer: a lot better than I expected.

The game starts you in the Keys, Rockstar’s take on the Florida Keys, and it’s a rougher part of Leonida. Lots of older cars and beaters, and you won’t see many EVs.

Recent findings suggest that that changes as you head north to Vice City, the game’s version of Miami. The closer you get, the more electric cars show up in traffic, and the more charging stations you pass. By the time you’re in the city, EVs are just normal cars.

That’s pretty much how EV adoption looks in the real world, concentrated in significant, wealthier metro areas while rural areas lag behind.

Here’s what I’ve run into so far:.

According to recent reports, that last one got me. Gas cars blocking chargers has been a complaint for as long as public charging has existed, and we’ve covered EV owners blocking a gas station in protest over ICEing. Rockstar recreating it tells me someone at the studio has actually tried to charge an EV in public. Probably even in Florida, which they tried to recreate here.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 is the first mainline GTA where energy matters. Gas cars burn fuel and need a pump, and EVs have a battery level and need a plug.

Rockstar could have used that to make EVs a pain. It didn’t. In my testing, the EVs have about the same range as the gas cars, charge just as fast as a fill-up, and cost the same or less to top up.

Kotaku’s range test backs that up. On the same highway loop, a Tesla Model 3 lookalike lasted 20 minutes and 23 seconds on a charge, longer than the Banshee sports car at 18 minutes and 31 seconds, and not far off an old pickup at 29 minutes and 8 seconds. Crossing the whole map by highway takes under 15 minutes, according to Kotaku.

In a recent development, and finding a charger isn’t a problem. Wccftech counted 120 EV chargers marked on the map, against just 57 gas stations.

In a recent development, rockstar’s EV history starts with Coil, the series’ Tesla stand-in, named after the Tesla coil. GTA V, released in 2013, gave us the Coil Voltic, a copy of the original Lotus-based Tesla Roadster, alongside oddballs like the Cheval Surge and the Fisker Karma-inspired Khamelion.

The Voltic was quick off the line and slow everywhere else. It had the lowest top speed of any supercar in the game, which fan lore pins on its battery overheating at speed. That’s pretty much how a lot of people thought about EVs in 2013.

Industry observers note that GTA Online added more electric cars starting in late 2017: the Rimac-inspired Coil Cyclone, then the Model S-based Coil Raiden and the Taycan-inspired Pfister Neon around the Doomsday Heist update. That same update introduced Avon Hertz, a tech billionaire whose AI tries to end the world. Rockstar never stated who he was based on. Players didn’t need the help.

Industry observers note that but those were rare, expensive toys. Nothing in GTA V needed fuel, so an EV was just a gas car without the engine noise, and you mostly saw them in the garages of players who bought them.

It has been revealed that electrify America noticed its in-game twin fast. The Volkswagen-owned network put out a statement on Friday saying it “will stick to charging vehicles in the real world” and adding, “We wish ReVolt America well.”.

It’s a good-natured response, and probably the best free marketing the network has had in years. EA has spent most of the last decade fighting a reputation for broken chargers, even though reliability across US fast-charging networks has improved this year. Every ReVolt station I’ve used in the game worked. Not a perfect parody, then.

GTA has always been a parody of American life. With EVs, it’s now slightly ahead of it.

Florida is one of the strongest EV markets in the country, with a 9.4% share of latest passenger vehicle sales in Q2 2026 versus 7.4% nationally, according to the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. Electrify America alone runs more than 350 chargers at over 60 Florida stations, including its biggest station yet near Orlando’s theme parks.

In a recent development, but real Florida still has roughly three gas stations for every public charging location, based on the Alliance for Automotive Innovation’s count of 3,267 charging locations and xMap’s count of more than 10,500 gas stations. Leonida flips that ratio.

There’s one piece Rockstar hasn’t nailed, at least not yet. You can’t install a charger at your place, but early in the story you’re renting. I’m not far enough in to own a property, so I don’t know whether that changes later.

It matters, because home charging is the biggest real-world advantage of an EV. Most owners leave every morning with a full battery and rarely use public chargers. If owned properties in GTA 6 come with a plug, EVs become the more convenient choice in the game, just like they are in real life for anyone with a driveway.

Recent findings suggest that I also haven’t hit a mission built around EVs yet. If I find one, I’ll revision this post.

Sources indicate that GTA works as a mirror. In 2013, the EV was a punchline: a Tesla parody that overheated if you drove it too fast. In 2026, it’s just another car in Vice City traffic, and the joke is on the guy in the pickup parked in the charging stall.

According to recent reports, that’s a good sign of where EVs actually are. Satire goes after what’s common, and Rockstar decided EVs are common enough to be part of everyday Leonida, more so in the city than in the Keys, just like real life. And that message is reaching a huge audience. Take-Two says GTA 6 did $3.79 billion in first-day sales. Tens of millions of people are now driving EVs that charge as fast and as cheaply as gas cars, with no range anxiety. No automaker ad campaign gets close to that.

In a recent development, so EVs aren’t a statement in GTA anymore. They’re normal, which is exactly the point the industry has been trying to make for years.

The real Florida just needs to catch up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you're into cars, it's basically common knowledge at this point that both Yamahas — the two independent companies that make musical instruments and motorbikes – helped put engines into several brands' cars. Yamaha also helped Lexus out when it came to making the LFA's engine sound just right and aided in creating that car's ancestor, the Toyota 2000GT.

In fact, if you look into it, Yamaha has a long history of working with Toyota on various car parts, engines, and even e-bikes way before e-bikes became a whole thing. However, one Yamaha-Toyota collab you may not know about is a lot more pedestrian than making a V10 supercar sing: The musical instrument firm supplied dashboard wood trim for the fifth-generation Toyota Avalon sedan.

From the Toyota press release that accompanied the car's debut in 2018: "Upon opening Avalon's doors, an overarching simplicity and a purposeful placement of amenities and controls welcomes passengers. Authentic materials, such as the available Yamaha-sourced wood trim and authentic aluminum pieces, accent armrests, center console, and instrument panels." In case you forgot, the Avalon was Toyota's full-size sedan that used to slot above the utilitarian Toyota Camry. The final, fifth-gen car was made for the 2019 to 2022 model years. The Yamaha wood came in the top Limited trim.

Recent findings suggest that as Alan Schneider, the senior principal designer at Toyota's CALTY design studio, shared with CorollaCrossUS on YouTube, the Avalon uses Sapele wood, chosen because it's easy to bend into the tight, curved shape that it needs to be to fit the Avalon's swoopy dash design. "We wanted a wood that had a very beautiful and consistent linear pattern and also had the strength and ability to be able to form in this type of application," stated Schneider. "[Yamaha] recommended Sapele as the species, and also it met a lot of requirements as well; it's highly sustainable, it's renewable, it has great strength and great consistency.".

Industry observers note that speaking to MotorTrend on the topic, Schneider said "[Yamaha's] process allows us to have a compound bend" — also known as a compound curve, which is a woodworking term for when the material is curved across multiple planes simultaneously. And actually looking at the inside of the 2019 Avalon Limited, that wood really does look sharp. It's dark, rich-looking, looks like it'd feel great to touch, and coming out in an era when "piano black" was all the fingerprint-y rage in car cabin design, the Avalon's piano wood trim feels like a flex that isn't talked about nearly enough.

#626. I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3767 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living.
  • It has been revealed that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work.
  • In a recent development, in other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living. I’ve been working with e-bikes for nearly two decades, professionally covering the e-bike industry for most of that time, testing hundreds of different models and traveling around the world to ride latest e-bikes in some pretty incredible places. Yeah, it’s a tough job – but someone’s got to suffer it.

It has been revealed that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work. I ride them recreationally. I ride them for exercise. I ride them for transportation. My family doesn’t even own a car, meaning two wheels handle the vast majority of our transportation.

In a recent development, in other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk. Or perhaps more accurately, I ride the ride.

According to recent reports, and while most of the time all you really need for a good ride is an e-bike and a direction to go in, there are a handful of pieces of gear that I’ve come to rely on over the years. Some keep me safer. Some keep my bikes out of the hands of thieves. Some make rides more comfortable or convenient. And some are just neat little things that I’ve discovered along the way.

According to recent reports, this isn’t a list of every bike accessory I’ve ever tested, nor am I saying these are necessarily the absolute best products in every category. These are simply the things that I actually use. Some are a bit pricey, some are dirt cheap (several pieces of gear below are under $5!), but they’re all things I personally rely on and that I recommend to my friends and family. And now, to you.

Industry observers note that if you own nice e-bikes, you’re eventually going to spend a lot of time thinking about locks. Your lock may even be your most important accessory. Or perhaps I should say “accessories”, because the best way to ensure your e-bike is still there when you get back is to use more than one solid lock.

My go-to options that I grab basically every day for the last couple of years have been Seatylock’s FoldyLock Forever folding lock and Mason 220 U-lock.

Recent findings suggest that for reference, the Foldylock Forever is the world’s strongest folding lock. That’s not just their marketing speak, but rather it’s confirmed by independent testing and certification. It’s the only folding lock in the world to achieve an ART 3-star security rating awarded by the Stichting ART Foundation, an independent Dutch organization that tests and certifies anti-theft locks. It earned that certification three years ago, and no other folding lock has been able to reach that level yet. The only higher ratings ART gives are for locks rated for motorcycles.

Personally, I like folding locks because they pack relatively neatly on the bike while still giving me enough flexibility to work around different racks and poles, or even larger things like trees.

The FoldyLock Forever is the one I reach for when I want serious security matched with more flexibility, while the Mason 220 gives me another beefy option when I know a U-lock will fit what I’m locking to.

The Mason is great as a strong U-lock, but I also like how large it is, letting me lock to wider poles and also a tad bit farther from the pole itself, leaving room for pannier bags and other things that get in the way. Amazingly, it’s also one of the few U-locks I have that can fit over the beefy battery-filled downtube on most of my e-bikes.

I also use the smaller FoldyLock Compact when I want something easier to carry and don’t need quite as much lock.

It’s more affordable and lighter, though it doesn’t have quite the same security level as the bigger and beefier options above.

The Compact does have one other advantage, though: it comes in all sorts of bright colors and even a rainbow option where each link is a different color. That might not be a huge security concern, but it’s fun when you can choose a color to match your bike or mood!

No bike lock makes a bicycle theft-proof. Given enough time and the right tools, a determined thief can defeat virtually anything. The idea is to make your bike enough of a pain in the butt to steal that the thief decides someone else’s bike looks easier. And if they still want your bike (because let’s face it, you’ve probably got an awesome e-bike), then the multiple locks better be good ones so its takes them long enough that they eventually give up.

Industry observers note that I also covered Seatylock’s upcoming angle grinder-proof U-locks that I saw at the Milan Motorcycle Show, so I’ll likely switch to those once they come out this Spring. They’re designed to keep motorcycles safe, and come in two sizes: one for motorcycles and a smaller one for bikes.

Let’s continue with what may actually be the most notable piece of gear for an e-biker: a helmet.

I’ve tested plenty of helmets over the years, but lately I’ve been gravitating toward UNIT 1’s helmets. They’re comfortable, they look good, and I appreciate the extra safety features beyond simply putting a layer of impact protection around my skull.

I particularly like having integrated lighting built right into my helmet, putting lights up high where they’re easier for drivers to see. On models like the FARO, I also appreciate the inclusion of MIPS as well as the handlebar-mounted remote for activating the helmet’s turn signals.

Industry observers note that I recently started using UNIT 1’s NEON helmet too, which is lighter and has a really slick magnetic face shield. You barely have to line the shield up; get it close enough and the magnets practically snatch it out of your hand and put it into place. It’s clear enough for night riding but darkens in bright sunlight, and the helmet is rated for faster 28 mph e-bike riding.

There are cheaper helmets out there, of course, but considering how much time I spend on two wheels, a good helmet is one area where I don’t mind spending a bit more.

You can actually see the FARO helmet in the clip below, along with the TriEye glasses coming up next.

Sources indicate that triEye glasses are another accessory that sounds a little gimmicky until you actually start using them. Sunglasses with a built-in rearview mirror? I was sure they were going to be a gimmick but they just looked too interesting to pass up, so I offered to test them out.

As it turns out, they’re now the first sunglasses I reach for when I’m riding. They really do work!

They have a tiny rear-view mirror integrated into the glasses, giving me a quick view behind me without having to turn my head all the way around.

It takes a little time to get used to looking into such a small mirror, but once your brain figures it out, it becomes surprisingly natural. I can quickly check what’s approaching from behind while still keeping most of my attention pointed forward.

It’s especially useful when riding on roads where I’m regularly interacting with traffic, though I still give an old-fashioned head check before making any major lateral move.

They’re $99, which isn’t bad for decent sunglasses, though you can get them for 10% off with the discount code EBIKE at checkout.

I love listening to music and podcasts while riding, but I’m not a fan of plugging my ears while sharing the road with cars.

That’s why I’ve become a substantial fan of H2O Audio’s bone-conduction headphones. They sit outside my ears and transmit sound through bone conduction, meaning my ears themselves remain open to the world around me. I’ve been testing out the newly introduced TRI ULTRA PRO model, and it’s pretty dang amazing! I can hear my music perfectly, but I can still hear all the road sounds, pedestrians, other cyclists, etc.

It has been revealed that of course, that doesn’t mean you can crank the music and magically retain perfect situational awareness. But at reasonable volumes, I can enjoy something in the background while still hearing cars, horns, bells and everything else happening around me.

Sources indicate that for longer recreational rides especially, they’ve become one of those things I really appreciate having along. I’ve done rides as long as 3 hours with them and they haven’t felt cumbersome or made my ears sore, so the fit seems great for me.

I really like the Knog Oi Prima as a bike bell. It looks good, has a nice low-profile design and does what a bell is supposed to do without looking like you bolted a miniature doorbell onto your handlebars.

Industry observers note that despite its small size, it’s also super loud. And unlike the older ratcheting-style bells (krr-krr-krr-krrring), this is a single thumper, meaning I can ding once promptly for a polite “hello, I’m here!” or several hard and rapid DINGs for a “wtf do you think you’re doing, guy?!”.

The bell absolutely disappears on my handlebars, which is good because there’s not much real estate left up there. Really, the only downside I can find is that it’s not cheap, at around $32 depending on current sales.

But I also have another favorite bell that costs a fraction as much.

Sources indicate that I found cheap bike bells on AliExpress that have a hidden compartment for an Apple AirTag. From the outside, it just looks like a boring bike bell. Inside, it’s secretly helping me keep tabs on my bike.

Industry observers note that and for $4, they’re a pretty awesome deal for a loud bell that hides a tracking device. Of course, you’ll have to fork over another $20 or so for the AirTag tracker, but your e-bike is certainly worth that much.

Which brings me to another part of my bike security strategy.

I don’t necessarily stop at one AirTag. One AirTag is for amateurs. I go with multiple. A four-pack is $79, or around half the cost of a solid e-bike lock.

It has been revealed that there are all sorts of clever AirTag hiding accessories available now. In addition to the bell, I’ve used a $5 water bottle-style AirTag holder as well as an $8 rear reflector with a hidden AirTag compartment.

According to recent reports, the reflector isn’t the most inconspicuous AirTag hider, but the water bottle holder definitely doesn’t scream “guess what’s actually inside of my molded plastic body!” And for added security, the water bottle holder is held on with Torx bolts. It’s not exactly a security key, but even if a bike thief carries hex wrenches with them, they’re unlikely to have Torx wrenches, meaning that the AirTag will stay on the bike a bit longer while it’s in the hands of a thief.

Industry observers note that airTags aren’t dedicated anti-theft GPS trackers, and Apple intentionally includes anti-stalking features that can eventually alert someone that an unknown AirTag is traveling with them. But I still think they’re a useful additional layer of security, especially because they’re cheap enough to use redundantly.

According to recent reports, A bike thief might know enough to search for an AirTag and remove it. But are they going to keep searching after they find the first one? What about the second? Are they expecting three?

That’s the idea, anyway. And since I keep pretty good tabs on my e-bikes, I’ll know pretty rapidly if one goes missing. From there, it’s a race between me getting to the thief and him finding all of my AirTags. Good luck, buddy.

I’m a major believer in wearing proper protective gear when riding faster electric two-wheelers, but I also don’t particularly want to look like I’m headed to a motorcycle race every time I leave the house. That’s one of the reasons I’ve really come to appreciate my Beyond Riders protective riding hoodie.

Industry observers note that it looks and feels much like a regular casual hoodie, but it’s designed with motorcycle-style protection in mind, including abrasion-resistant materials and removable impact protectors. Believe it or not, there’s flexible CE Level 2 armor in there on the elbows, shoulders, chest, and spine.

I like that I can throw it on before a ride and get an extra layer of protection without having to wear a bulky motorcycle jacket. It’s particularly nice for faster e-bikes and electric mopeds, where the speeds are high enough that I’d rather have something more substantial than a regular sweatshirt between my skin and the pavement.

Recent findings suggest that of course, no protective hoodie is going to make a crash harmless, and I still choose my gear based on the type of riding I’m doing. But I love products that make it easier to incorporate safety into everyday riding without adding a bunch of hassle. If protective gear is comfortable, convenient, and looks good enough that I actually want to wear it, that’s a significant win in my book.

Recent findings suggest that tannus tire liners are perhaps one of the less exciting products on this list, right up until they save you from fixing a flat on the side of the road. And then they’re the one thing on this list you’ll be ready to open-mouth kiss.

I’ve used Tannus products for years as an extra layer of flat protection, and I’m a big believer in them.

No tire protection system is going to prevent every possible flat, but anything that reduces my chances of sitting on the side of a road pulling a wheel off an e-bike is worth considering.

That’s particularly true with e-bikes, where hub motor wheels can be more complicated to remove thanks to heavy motors, annoying cables, clumsy torque washers, and other hardware.

It has been revealed that tannus tire liners are annoying to install, but you do it once and forget about it. Then you’re almost guaranteed to not get a flat.

And even if you do happen to get a 3″ nail going through it at the perfect angle, they serve as runflats so you can still ride home (albeit a bit slower and more carefully) instead of doing the walk of shame next to your bike.

I don’t want to carry an entire bike shop with me, but I do want enough tools to deal with the common things that can happen during a ride.

The Topeak Ratchet Stick hits a nice sweet spot for me. It’s small enough that I’ll actually bring it along, yet useful enough for the various bolts and adjustments that tend to crop up on bikes.

All of the important bits fit right inside the handle, so I don’t have any extra sleeves or clips to keep tabs on.

This is exactly what I want from a ride tool: something small but effective. The giant tool kit sitting at home isn’t particularly useful when something starts rattling 20 kilometers away.

Industry observers note that at $48, it’s not cheap. But I’ve had mine for around 6 years, and it’s still going strong, so at least it’s well made! At around 8 bucks per year, I’d call it a good investment.

This is one of my more recent cheap finds.

I picked up a waterproof-style pannier bag from AliExpress for around $25, and I’ve been surprisingly impressed with it.

It isn’t quite as big as the pannier I have from Priority Bicycles, but it still holds a useful amount of cargo and feels much nicer than I expected for the price.

It has been revealed that I particularly like that there are two ways to close it. You can use it as a traditional roll-top pannier and clip the sides together, or you can use the strap that comes over the top when you have too much stuff in there to close it the normal way. I use that second option anytime I have my yoga mat in there since it sticks out the top, but I can still close it relatively tight to keep the mat from swinging around while riding. Depending on how much stuff I’m carrying and how I’ve packed it, having both options is quite convenient.

It’s not the fanciest pannier I own. But for around 25 bucks, it’s one of those cheap accessories that turned out to be much better than I expected.

These might have the highest usefulness-to-price ratio of anything here.

Sources indicate that I bought a pair of tiny plastic handlebar jacks on AliExpress for barely more than a dollar. They clip onto the handlebars and provide little stands for when I need to turn a bicycle upside down.

Recent findings suggest that anyone who has ever flipped a modern e-bike over to change a tube knows the problem. Your handlebars are probably covered in displays, buttons, brake levers, bells, phone mounts and who knows what else. Turning the bike upside down means resting all of that expensive stuff directly on the ground.

According to recent reports, you can loosen everything and rotate it out of the way. Or you can use two $1 pieces of plastic.

Sources indicate that the jacks hold the handlebars slightly above the ground so my accessories don’t get scratched or crushed. Simple problem, simple solution.

If you have a 3D printer, you can probably just print your own version of these. There’s a rubber O-ring-style keeper on it, but you can probably just use a rubber band if you wanted to DIY these yourself.

Another recent addition has been a ZOOM suspension dropper seatpost that I installed on my Ride1Up Roadster V3.

I love the thing now that it’s installed. It gives me suspension to take some of the sting out of rough roads while also providing the convenience of a dropper post.

Getting it onto my particular bike, however, was another story.

In a recent development, it took me nearly two hours, largely because the Ride1Up Roadster V3 wasn’t set up for the internal cable routing I needed. I got the cable most of the way there through the downtube’s very narrow wire run, but then I ultimately ended up drilling a small hole in the seat tube to make the last bit of my installation work.

To be very clear: I do not recommend doing that.

Drilling holes in bicycle frames can compromise their structural integrity, void warranties and generally create problems you don’t want. As a mechanical engineer with a lot of bike experience, I was comfortable making that decision on my own bike because I knew exactly where the frame is least stressed, but it’s definitely not something I’d advise others to copy.

The lesson here isn’t “drill your frame.” It’s to check whether your bike is actually designed for an internally routed dropper post before ordering one. Had I done that first (basically by shining a flashlight down the empty seat tube and realizing there wasn’t a hole to access the bottom bracket), I could have saved myself quite a bit of trouble and just gotten a dropper post with an external cable run.

Recent findings suggest that but now that it’s installed? I love it!

And finally, here’s one that isn’t really normal bike gear at all, but that I LOVE bringing on my rides.

I spend a lot of time taking photos and videos of bikes, which presents an obvious problem when I’m both the cyclist and the photographer.

In a recent development, the HOVERAir X1 Pro Max has become one of my favorite solutions. It’s a tiny autonomous flying camera that can follow me around without requiring someone else to pilot it. I used the previous version of this drone for a while until this version came out, and then I immediately upgraded.

In a recent development, it folds down small enough that I basically forget that I even have it in my bag. Despite its small size, it still can automatically track and follow me, even at speeds of over 20 mph (32 km/h). That means I can pull it out during a ride, send it up (it takes off from my palm!) and get tracking shots that would normally require another person riding or running alongside me with a camera.

I especially like the Dolly Track mode, which can create some fantastic moving shots while automatically following me from the sides or the front, instead of just the boring old follow-behind-me drone shots you usually see.

Just be aware that its obstacle avoidance isn’t great when flying sideways or backward, meaning I’ve flown it into walls, fences, and street signs plenty of times already. But I can also report back that somehow the little guy is still working fine. I’m not suggesting that’s part of the official durability testing procedure, but it has certainly become part of mine. Now it’s my go-to drone, and I especially like bringing it on my travels for all the same reasons.

After a list this long, I should probably point out that you don’t actually need most of this stuff.

That’s one of the things I love about bikes. You don’t need a pile of expensive gear to have a good time. Most days, give me an e-bike, a helmet and a direction to point the front wheel, and I’m happy.

But after years of riding e-bikes professionally, recreationally, for exercise and simply to get around, these are the products that I’ve found myself continuing to use.

It has been revealed that sure, some of these are expensive pay-to-play things that are a lot of fun but might not be worth it for the casual rider. And some are just $1 pieces of plastic that keep me from smashing my bike computer into the pavement.

But they’ve all found their way into my life after being battle-tested… and passing!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that are you a port or rail terminal operator looking for a latest electric material handler that can move serious cargo without sacrificing maneuverability? Do you wish it had tank treads? If that’s you, the Mantsinen 200 might be just the thing.

According to recent reports, designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks. And, yes: I stated tracks.

By far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw. And while, yes – most massive material handlers have similar form factors, there’s something about the 200 that really sells the whole Dragon Walker vibe.

Sources indicate that the Mantsinen 200 is powered by a 380 kW (~510 hp) grid-connected electric motor running at 1,800 rpm. Power comes from a 460V electrical connection as standard, with other voltage options available to suit local site requirements.

According to recent reports, mantsinen says its electrically powered machines deliver the same performance as their diesel counterparts, while eliminating exhaust emissions at the machine and reducing operating noise, energy consumption and maintenance costs. Power is delivered through a load-sensing hydraulic system featuring four variable-displacement piston pumps and a separate closed-loop swing circuit.

Mantsinen also fits the 200 with its proprietary HybriLift energy-recovery system. HybriLift works a lot like regenerative braking by capturing potential energy as the main boom is lowered, but instead of storing that energy as electricity in a battery, the material handler stores it in hydraulic accumulators for reuse during the next lift. The company claims HybriLift improves the big machine’s energy efficiency by up to 50%, effectively giving the machine an additional 300 (ish) hp of lifting assistance at average lifting speed.

In a recent development, and, while the machine normally draws power from the grid, operators aren’t necessarily tethered to an outlet. Mantsinen offers an optional PowerPack that allows the machine to disconnect from its main power supply and still travel around the worksite, with some basic hydraulic systems still functional. The PowerPack is currently diesel-powered, but a battery-backed version isn’t out of the question. It’s a useful bit of flexibility for terminal operators who want the benefits of electric material handling without giving up the ability to reposition the machine when a fixed electrical connection isn’t available.

#623. Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this week, Jackery unveiled a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP).
  • The plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets.
  • As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this week, Jackery unveiled a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP). The program starts with Fresh York City apartment residents. I went to the RE+ in Las Vegas to meet with leaders from Jackery and Every Electric to learn more.

The plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets. For the customer, the process is simple:.

That’s it. As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery. Over the 11-year rated lifespan, purchasing the battery could increase the total net payback, although the upfront cost would be a little higher.

It has been revealed that it seems almost too simple and convenient for the customer. However, a lot of complex work and coordination is happening behind the scenes. The Jackery battery is in communication with Every Electric, who automates power management to charge when electricity demand is low and discharge to run the air conditioner when electricity demand is high. This kind of active demand response can go far beyond the typical TOU blueprint to directly mitigate utility demand shifts. Every Electric monitors data for each battery. The demand response of the combined storage across thousands of individual batteries is aggregated and sold to the utility, in this case Con Edison. Then the benefits are divided up and distributed to customers based on their contributions. Over 2000 batteries were in the initial trial phase, with a larger scale rollout planned next year. I am already on the waitlist, along with over 15,000 other NYC households.

Because it does not feed electricity back into the grid, implementation is much simpler. No electrician needed. The system monitors the amount of energy being stored and deployed at the point of use with no need for user intervention. Unlike traditional demand response that turns off appliances, there is no inconvenience to the user. Thermostats do not need to be adjusted. Smart appliances are not needed. The battery simply provides power when grid demand is high, shaving off the peaks.

Recent findings suggest that you may still be asking “what’s the catch?” Presently, the system needs to coordinate a large number of relatively small batteries under the same utility to have enough combined capacity to sell to the utility. To start, it is only being offered in New York City, which sets the blueprint. In the initial application, the batteries will be used with 120V air conditioners, up to around 12,000 BTU. This is a common size for NYC apartments, letting one battery size serve a wide range of customers, simplifying initial rollout. It also offers clear return on investment based on how much electricity is used, when that electricity is used and when demand peaks for the utility. However, I wouldn’t expect it to stop there.

In a recent development, the batteries being used are led by the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. This battery has 2042 Wh of capacity and up to 2200 W of output with 4400 W of surge power. A total of three outlets are on the front panel, as well as two USB-C and a USB-A port. Due to the UPS function, the portable power station adds protection and would be ideal to plug in a computer or sensitive electronics, in addition to the air conditioner. Although the VPP is based on air conditioner use, using all the outlets can potentially add to the amount of load shifted by the VPP and, as a result, increase the amount of payback for the customer. Plugging in other forms of energy consumption could also extend the benefit beyond the times of year when the air conditioner is being used.

Recent findings suggest that at 40% smaller and 34% lighter than the previous generation model, the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 weighs 39.5 lb. That’s less than a 5-gallon water cooler bottle but less bulky to carry. Due to the plug and play nature, people changing apartments within the city can easily take it with them at 13.2” x 10.4” x 11.5”. Multiple levels of safety protections and a ruggedized portable design using automotive-grade LFP batteries ensure safe operation even if apartment occupants bump into it.

That portability also contributes to the emergency preparedness capability of the battery. For the months of the year when the air conditioning isn’t running, the battery could provide backup power for a refrigerator in a power outage, for example. Of course, Jackery also offers batteries specifically for refrigerators. Those batteries are not a part of the initial program… yet.

Recent findings suggest that this also gets to a limitation of the current program. To keep the program manageable as it scales up, only one size of battery in one use case is initially being offered. Right now, the biggest challenge is scaling up. Making it too complicated at the start would make scaling up more difficult. However, once the program reaches scale, more options can become available. Jackery also offers batteries with greater aesthetic appeal, like the slim FridgeGuard, which may be a better fit for the homes of some customers. As the program scales up, the applications have the potential to diversify.

Sources indicate that much of RE+ focused on supplying power and storage for data centers. While residential clean energy tax credits (25D) have been cut, data centers can still benefit from the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit that can add up with bonuses to cover half the cost of the project. With additional state and federal incentives piled on top, the majority of the cost of data center ESS can be covered by subsidies. With the heavily subsidized storage and large-scale contracts with the utility, data centers can access benefits not typically available to residential customers.

Sources indicate that however, the plug-in VPP changes the energy storage dynamic. People get credit for energy storage deployment at the point of use. AI technology, rather than just being a consumer of resources, is being used to automate the VPP system and let the benefits flow to more families. By starting with small window air conditioners, the system also tends to provide relief to people living in typically older apartments, rather than the sleek new high rises with multi-million-dollar apartments.

There is no need for home electrical upgrades. In fact, by taking some of the load off the circuit, the potential for my wife to trip the breaker from ironing in the living room while the TV and air conditioner are running on the same breaker is reduced. As the energy monitoring comes directly from the battery, it also isn’t dependent on smart meters.

According to recent reports, for the system to have enough total capacity to sell to the utility, the plug-in VPP needs to connect thousands of batteries to provide multiple MWh of storage. This scale can easily be accomplished in urban areas. In addition, the value of the system will heavily depend on the local price of electricity and the variability in price. In NYC, electricity is significantly more expensive than in most of the US.

New York City apartments are a perfect starting place. While apartments tend to be far more energy efficient than detached houses and have lower net emissions overall, many of us living in apartments have traditionally felt a bit left out on clean tech. We don’t have roofs for rooftop panels. We typically do not have attached garages to place large permanent batteries or access to modify the electrical panel. If we do have the ability to make electrical modifications to the apartment, they can be prohibitively expensive in NYC. As such, a plug-in VPP is an exciting development for those of us living in apartments.

Sources indicate that A plug-in VPP also makes the benefits of battery energy storage more accessible to urban areas. Often, there is not room for container-sized batteries. In places like New York City, the fire regulations are so strict, and the permitting is so complicated that large-scale BESS becomes exceedingly difficult to execute. Large-scale BESS, if approved, could take years to deploy.

In a recent development, according to NREL, the national average full installed price of utility scale BESS was $334/kWh of capacity in 2024, with hardware making up roughly two thirds of the total. However, the cost would undoubtedly be higher in NYC. For comparison, the discounted Explorer 2000 v2 in this program (which avoids retail markup) comes in at $318.32/kWh, with no added permitting or installation cost. That is also significantly less than the installed cost of many home batteries used in traditional VPPs, like Tesla Powerwall. Once delivered, it can be online within minutes.

At the moment, plug-in VPP is the fastest, easiest and least expensive way to add battery capacity that shaves peak demand on urban grids in the US.

Sources indicate that as high draw usage like air conditioning increases, more stress is placed on the grid. Transformer and other electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure upgrades can be expensive. Having storage at the point of use reduces the amount of electricity that needs to flow through the grid during peak periods. As plug-in VPP is deployed more broadly, the benefits will be experienced more broadly. And CO2 emissions can drop in the process.

According to recent reports, while the benefits of the program are already attractive, the initial program may just be the tip of the iceberg. In New York City, buildings over 25,000 square feet must reduce their greenhouse gas emissions under Local Law 97 (LL97). This includes many apartment complexes and offices. The deployment of batteries at the point of use has the potential to reduce emissions.

While the current batteries and air conditioners in the program are 120V, Jackery also makes batteries that are 240V. For appliances that have intermittent use but high draw, like heat pumps, hot water heaters, ranges, etc., 240V connections are often needed to provide the necessary power. The electrification of applications that were previously run on gas or fuel oil can greatly reduce building emissions. But many apartment buildings do not have 240V outlets available. However, larger Jackery models can charge on 120V, accumulate charge and discharge at 240V for intermittent use. There is potential for batteries to support the higher voltage electrification without expensive electrical upgrades while also providing VPP benefit. The math would have to work out and it hasn’t happened yet. But the potential is clearly there.

In a recent development, overall, the potential applications for this approach are massive. Already, I can see the potential to transform energy storage in NYC. In talking with Jackery and Every Electric, I started thinking about where the technology could go from here. Plug-in VPP could apply far beyond just Latest York City. However, that is for a follow-up article.

The Pros And Cons Of Importing A Japanese Mini Truck

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that models such as the Honda Acty, Suzuki Carry, Daihatsu Hijet, Subaru Sambar, and Mitsubishi Minicab all have decades of production behind them, along with a knack for toughness and reliability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, japan's tiny kei trucks have become a massive novelty in the U.S. — even for road-tripping — with 7,500 imported in 2023 alone. Whether bringing one home makes sense, though, depends on what you want to do with it.

It has been revealed that the most glaring pro here is the low entry price. Since they have to be 25 years old or older to be imported, it's perhaps unsurprising that — depending on condition — these used mini trucks generally sell for $4,500 to $10,000, before shipping and registration fees . The price lets enthusiasts from any tax bracket enjoy the amenities of the simple, durable — and, importantly, mechanically uncomplicated — trucks.

Industry observers note that models such as the Honda Acty, Suzuki Carry, Daihatsu Hijet, Subaru Sambar, and Mitsubishi Minicab all have decades of production behind them, along with a knack for toughness and reliability. And their small footprint makes them handy for farms, trade jobs, and urban delivery runs that would frustrate a full-size pickup, while also offering low fuel consumption.

It has been revealed that but despite the benefits of these kei trucks on paper, know that legal and regulatory adversities can vary from state to state. There also can be unforeseen costs and safety concerns that present a real challenge for prospective buyers.

It has been revealed that the notorious 25-year federal law applies to kei trucks, counted from the month of manufacture rather than the model year. Being mindful of build dates before you buy can help avoid any holdups. Even when your mini truck clears customs, though, that doesn't guarantee license plates.

California is the hardest case, with most kei trucks that satisfy the federal age rule still unable to be registered because they don't meet emissions and safety regulations. Elsewhere the rules vary — states like Wyoming and Arkansas bar use on interstate highways while others like Georgia refuse road registration outright. Concern over how these trucks fare in a collision has led several states to crack down.

Shipping costs, customs and registration all add a few more thousand dollars on top of the sticker price — finding a reputable importer takes legwork, and the wait for shipping and customs clearance can last months. Once you've navigated that, insurance can pose another hurdle as some agents and systems may not be able to accommodate kei trucks. And though these tiny trucks are touted for their robust builds, sustained stateside highway speeds wear down parts faster and finding replacements is hard, as those parts aren't stocked at ordinary auto parts stores.

For a farm, estate, or enthusiast collection in a state with friendly rules, a kei truck can be a rewarding purchase, so long as you confirm your state's registration rules first. If all you need is a cheap light-duty pickup, however, several other examples are readily available. Perhaps a Ford Maverick might just be what you need.

#621. Latest Update: Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (849 w)

Latest Update: Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, toyota is getting into electric bikes.
  • The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.
  • And when Toyota says compact, it means it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, toyota is getting into electric bikes. Well, sort of.

The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.

And when Toyota says compact, it means it. The little electric ride can reportedly fold up in around 30 seconds and become small enough to fit inside the trunk of the brand’s GR86 sports car. Think of it like Toyota’s take on the Motocompacto.

The BKE Concept was unveiled as part of the newly revived Scion by Toyota brand, which the firm is positioning less as the return of the quirky youth-oriented car brand many Americans remember and more as a sort of experimental mobility laboratory.

Sources indicate that toyota calls the newly introduced Scion a “freedom lab” where the organization can explore vehicles and mobility concepts that don’t necessarily fit neatly into its conventional automotive lineup. Alongside the BKE, Toyota showed its KEI-01 ultra-compact utility truck and a hybrid side-by-side.

But perhaps unsurprisingly for me, it’s the tiny electric two-wheeler that caught my attention.

And I should point out here that while Toyota refers to it as an “electric bike” in its own brand literature, the lack of pedals means that the cute little two-wheeler is not going to qualify as an electric bicycle in Europe or North America. The moniker means it merely slots into the broader electric bike category that encompasses everything from electric bicycles to scooters and motorcycles. In essence, the BKE is more or less a small seated e-scooter, sometimes referred to as a “no-ped”.

Despite looking like the kind of concept vehicle that might have been whipped up for an auto show, Toyota states the BKE has actually been under development for several years.

A small team of chassis and electrical engineers has reportedly been testing and refining the design based on real-world use and feedback.

The basic idea came from a fairly simple question: How could Toyota make short-distance mobility easier and integrate it more seamlessly into everyday life?

The result is essentially a secondary vehicle designed to travel inside your primary vehicle.

Toyota specifically highlights camping, errands, last-mile transportation, and even using the BKE as a pit bike alongside a GR86. The bike can also be recharged from the 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles, meaning the car carrying it can effectively serve as its mobile charging station.

Believe it or not, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda has apparently been involved in the testing process himself. Toyoda attracted attention after riding a similar small electric mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, and Toyota says his experience riding prototypes has even resulted in design changes.

After Toyoda complained about getting splashed while riding through puddles, for example, engineers enlarged the rear fender.

It’s a small detail, but it’s also a pretty textbook example of Toyota’s famous kaizen philosophy of continuous improvement.

Here’s where things get a little frustrating for those of us who want to know what the BKE can actually do.

It has been revealed that toyota hasn’t announced the motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed, or even the vehicle’s weight. There’s also no pricing because, for now, there’s nothing to buy.

Toyota is referring to the BKE strictly as a concept and hasn’t announced production intends or a timetable for bringing it to market.

But the fact that Toyota states a small engineering team has spent several years developing and testing the BKE makes it more interesting than your typical one-off styling exercise.

And the underlying idea makes a lot of sense.

Recent findings suggest that I’m obviously a significant believer in matching the vehicle to the trip. Taking a 4,000-pound car several miles to move one person isn’t always the most efficient solution, and a compact electric two-wheeler gives drivers an easy way to leave the larger vehicle behind for those shorter trips.

Toyota itself makes essentially the same argument, saying that using smaller vehicles for shorter journeys could reduce emissions by better matching the vehicle to the task.

There’s also something amusingly circular about one of the world’s largest automakers arriving at the conclusion that sometimes the best vehicle for a trip is a tiny electric bike.

But hey, I’ll take it. Now Toyota just needs to actually build the thing – and preferably tell us how fast it goes first.

  • Tesla is rolling out an enhancement that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.
  • It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla plans to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.
  • According to recent reports, tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is rolling out an enhancement that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.

But there’s a catch. It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla plans to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.

According to recent reports, tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path. “Even tighter turns now rolling out to upcoming Cybertrucks,” the account wrote.

In a follow-up post, Tesla noted the improvement requires software version 2026.44 or newer and “only applies to model year 2027 Cybertrucks.”.

It's not the size … it's how you maneuver itEven tighter turns now rolling out to newly introduced Cybertrucks pic.twitter.com/FuNoox4ax0.

Sources indicate that tesla didn’t share a newly introduced turning circle figure. In the video, the “after” circle is visibly smaller than the “before” one by what looks to be at least a foot.

The Cybertruck’s maneuverability comes from its rear-wheel steering paired with steer-by-wire. At low speeds, the rear wheels turn opposite to the fronts, which shrinks the space the truck needs to make a U-turn. We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s four-wheel steering since the prototype days, when Tesla was showing it off in parking garages.

Recent findings suggest that even before this upgrade, the results were impressive. Tesla’s owner’s manual lists the Cybertruck’s curb-to-curb turning circle at about 43.5 ft (13.25 m). That beats the Ford F-150 Lightning at roughly 47.8 ft and the Rivian R1T at 44.9 ft, and it’s within about 4 ft of a Model Y. Not bad for a 6,600-lb truck that’s nearly 19 feet long.

And Tesla always remarked there was more to come. At launch, the rear wheels turned only about 3 degrees. In early 2024, a Tesla engineer said a software revision would push that to 10 degrees, and Elon Musk said the manufacturer had improvements in the works to “tighten the turning circle significantly.”.

Tesla hasn’t noted whether this update delivers the full 10 degrees, or why it’s limited to 2027 trucks. If it comes down to hardware, owners of earlier Cybertrucks who were counting on this as an over-the-air upgrade are out of luck.

In a recent development, credit where it’s due. The turning circle is one of the best things about the Cybertruck, and anyone who has driven one knows it. Steer-by-wire combined with rear-wheel steering is real engineering, and other vehicles are just starting to get that combo a couple years after Cybertruck had it. Making it even better is a nice revision.

But it’s hard to get excited about it.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, Musk announced that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab. He has since pushed the end date to the end of summer 2027 to work through an “order backlog.” We estimate Tesla is delivering about 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks a quarter, roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year it planned for.

Recent findings suggest that so Tesla is improving a 2027 model year truck that it will stop making next summer. And since Tesla now only sells the $109,990 Cyberbeast, the people getting this upgrade are the few still buying the most expensive Cybertruck in its final months. It does nothing about what actually sank the truck: pricing that never came close to the $39,900 promised in 2019, range and towing that fell short, and a design most truck buyers never warmed up to.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a cool engineering flex on a product with an expiration date. If Tesla had delivered this kind of polish on the $40,000 truck it promised, would we be writing the Cybertruck’s obituary right now?

#619. Tech Report: These 7 Porsches Have A Reputation For Being Nearly Indestructible

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1979 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Tech Report: These 7 Porsches Have A Reputation For Being Nearly Indestructible

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For many, owning a Porsche is something of a dream.
  • It's models like the 996-generation 911 that might give buyers a reason to pause, as while the right advice could save 996 buyers from getting screwed, the model is still plagued with complex complications.
  • That need not end the dream for Porsche fans, though, as there is still a plethora of used Porsches that have proven pretty much indestructible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For many, owning a Porsche is something of a dream. However, keeping one running as it should year after year without having to spend thousands in preventative maintenance or labor-intensive repairs might not be all that easy. Sure, the automaker enjoys a reputation for engineering excellence, but that doesn't mean each model from its back catalog is as capable as the last when it comes to covering moon mileage.

It's models like the 996-generation 911 that might give buyers a reason to pause, as while the right advice could save 996 buyers from getting screwed, the model is still plagued with complex complications. Problems such as failed intermediate shaft (IMS) bearings and cylinder bore scoring swiftly make the 996 look less of a tempting proposition for those who need something they can rely upon.

That need not end the dream for Porsche fans, though, as there is still a plethora of used Porsches that have proven pretty much indestructible. Some are cheap, like the 987.2-generation Boxster, and some are far from it, such as the iconic "widowmaker" 930 Turbo. What they all prove, however, is that with the correct maintenance and know-how, a secondhand Porsche really can run forever. Here are seven of our favorites, listed from the oldest through to the newest, and justified via high-mileage examples, owner reviews, and expert opinions.

It can be difficult to deduce whether the Porsche 924 was a success. It sold rather well, with a total of 152,082 finding homes across its full production window, 1976 to 1988. However, it sat unloved for decades, with many enthusiasts citing its lackluster performance and what they erroneously called its van-derived engine as solid proof that it wasn't a "proper" Porsche.

Industry observers note that the eventual 924 Turbo and homologation special 924 Carrera GT models did much to align the little coupé with enthusiasts, but for our purposes here, it's the naturally aspirated 2.0-liter inline-4-powered model that appeals the most. The Classics World 924 Buyer's Guide describes it as remarkably robust, and says "simple DIY maintenance" is often all that's required to keep it running. The guide adds that 924 spare parts are available directly through the automaker via Porsche's Classic program, and are frequently quite affordable.

Numerous enthusiasts on owners forums are happy to boast that their own pride-and-joys have been able to surpass 100,000 miles, and often by some serious margins. One post on Porsche Club Great Britain details both a 168,000-mile and 272,000-mile example, and that post is almost 20 years old, so many more examples may well have hit such achievements since. Owner reviews further back up the 924's claim to indestructibility, saying that, in spite of its age, the little Porsche largely proves very dependable across long ownership windows.

While the Porsche 924 is impressively reliable and durable, it probably isn't the adrenaline-fueled sports car that springs into most minds when the word "Porsche" is uttered. Instead, something like the original 930 Turbo is far more appropriate.

In a recent development, it was produced between the 1975 and '89 model years, and throughout that time the engine evolved from a turbocharged 3.0-liter flat-6 with 256 horsepower into a boosted 3.3-liter unit that produced 296 horses. U.S. versions received slightly less power, but these were still very formidable sports cars for the era.

Turbochargers do add extra complexity into engines, and they can fail prematurely, so it might be reasonable to assume the 930 Turbo doesn't fall into the "indestructible" category. Well, you'd be wrong to assume that, and one man alone proves that point impeccably. His name is Bill MacEachern, and he ordered a 930 Turbo back when they were newly introduced in '76. He's kept it ever since, and racked up in excess of 826,000 miles during that time. Yes, its engine has been rebuilt, but he's had it tuned to produce in excess of 550 horsepower, and it's still managing its daily duties without stress. Here he is on Magnacars telling the story:.

In a recent development, those seeking to find themselves an indestructible 930 Turbo for piling on the miles should head for a 3.3-liter model. These received internal improvements over the earlier cars, like different sealing rings that could deal with heat more effectively, enabling the engine to handle its performance more reliably. Also, the addition of an intercooler massively reduced intake temperatures on 3.3-powered cars, as well as helping to bring that extra grunt.

According to recent reports, if a boosted Porsche 911 from the late '70s is capable of punching out 800,000-plus miles, it stands to reason that a less performance-focused 911 of the same era also makes for a pretty dependable companion. The SC introduced fresh technologies and developments in the engine bay that really helped boost reliability.

The previous model was powered by a 2.7-liter mill, the last evolution of the 911's original engine. By this point, it was at its limit, and with thermal reactors used to help reduce emissions in line with new legislation, heat was a major problem. This heat buildup caused head stud and valve concerns, and while fixable via the aftermarket route, such issues plagued the reliability reputation of early '70s 911s. The later SC rectified this issue with an all-aluminum engine casing that could better handle the engine's higher temperatures, and those thermal reactors were replaced with catalytic converters, which ran far cooler.

It has been revealed that it's well-documented that these 3.0-liter SC models are good for 200,000 miles or more between engine rebuilds, as long as they are suitably maintained. So if it's an early 911 with built-in indestructibility that you're seeking, this is a far better starting point than any pre-'77 car. In fact, Porsche Club GB describes the 3.0-liter as "probably the most reliable Porsche engine ever" and "simple to work on." Just be prepared for the prices commanded; we recently found a 164,000-mile 911 SC selling for close to $75,000, so even with high mileage, these cars are still a significant investment.

Sources indicate that this next entry steers us back away from Porsche's legendary line of rear-engined flat-6-powered models, and once again to a four-cylinder front-engined sports coupé. The Porsche 944, much like the 924, was available in a variety of guises, but for reliability and durability, the simple naturally aspirated models appeal the most.

Its 2.5-liter engine (displacement grew throughout production) is derived from the V8-powered 928, and it's known to have a remarkably strong bottom end. While the Turbo cars aren't exactly fragile, these later boosted engines are more complex, and failures can and do occur, as both turbo exhaust manifolds and wastegates can crack. In terms of what a base 944 can achieve, it's well-documented that these engines are good for in excess of 250,000 miles before a rebuild is necessary, provided necessary maintenance is kept up with along the way.

Looking at owner reviews, the 944 experience seems to be mostly trouble-free. Across 127 reviews on CarSurvey, the 944 received a 7.5 out of 10 score for reliability. One owner of a high-mileage example noted that, while certain items like locks, alarms, and other accessories were beginning to fail, they were easily DIY-able, and no power train concerns were noted, despite the car having north of 160,000 miles.

Some owners would say a 160,000-mile 944 is still just being broken in. In 2023 a 571,000-mile example was spotted at an auto auction, and even boosted models have been seen with 400,000 miles on the clock, who knows how far a well-maintained 944 can go?

In a recent development, the 3.2-powered Carrera models follow on from the SC, which is a textbook example of an indestructible Porsche. The Carrera 3.2 is less bulletproof than the earlier 3.0 SC, with some experts suggesting it may need top-end work by 130,000 miles, whereas SC cars can exceed that mileage and more without having to come apart. That doesn't mean, however, that the Carrera 3.2 isn't worthy of a place here.

In fact, the 3.2-liter engine received a plethora of updates that 3.0-liter engines miss out on. Upcoming pistons, hydraulic timing chain tensioners, and a new Bosch Motronic engine management system were chief among the updates, bringing more power, efficiency, and reliability, especially in the timing system.

It has been revealed that regardless of whether the Carrera 3.2 is as bulletproof as its 3.0-liter SC predecessor, it's a fine place to look for a durable classic Porsche. While some do argue the top end may need work by 130,000 miles, others say 200,000 miles is perfectly possible before a rebuild is required. A very smart 218,000-mile example sold this year at auction in the U.K., described by Historics Auctioneers as "One of the best maintained G Series cars we have offered." Admittedly, it had been treated to an engine rebuild and glass-out repaint in recent years, so both its engine and body should be good for another 200,000 miles or so.

The last two entries on our list bring things back up to date, at least a little. While the latest batch of Porsches very well could be the holy grail of reliability and indestructibility, they simply haven't been on the road long enough to prove it, which is why most models here are far older. They've had the chance to accumulate hundreds of thousands of miles and demonstrate their strength.

In a recent development, one such model is the first-generation Porsche Cayenne, specifically the 3.2-liter model. It's powered by Volkswagen's 30-year-old VR6 engine, which was already well-known by the time Porsche's 955-generation Cayenne debuted as a 2004 model. Why the 3.2? Well, it boasts a strong cast-iron block, whereas the V8 models sported aluminum blocks, and serious engine concerns are quite uncommon.

The 3.2-liter VR6 engine is certainly capable of completing 200,000 miles with basic maintenance covered, and what's just as reassuring, is that the rest of the Cayenne seems built just as tough. One owner on Pistonheads thoroughly detailed every expense during their 51,000-mile and five-year ownership of a Cayenne 3.2 that was already 100,000 miles and 10 years into life when purchased. Apart from general servicing, some tidying up, and a few minor repairs, the Cayenne wanted for nothing, and was sold on to continue its service. Porsche's brand-newly introduced Cayenne Turbo Electric might be an impressive $200,000 powerhouse of excellence, but if robust dependability is called for, perhaps its nameplate forefather is the better bet.

We called the 2024 Porsche 718 Boxster GTS 4.0 perfection on wheels, and while it's not a model that's attracting much negative attention to itself, it's barely old enough to call reliable yet, let alone indestructible. The 987.2-generation of Boxster and Cayman, though, is another matter altogether, especially in base 2.9-liter flat-6 guise. While the 3.4-liter "S" model is a better performer, it has been known to suffer bore-scoring, while the 2.9-liter lump seems to avoid that costly concern. Porsche specialist LN Engineering says it has "never seen a case of cylinder bore scoring with these models," when referring to the 987.2 Cayman and Boxster.

Industry observers note that it's also notable to detail why it's the 987.2 cars which deserve a spot here, rather than the 987.1 models. The later models employed an all-upcoming 9A1 engine, which did away with the troublesome IMS bearing altogether. All previous iterations of the Boxster and Cayman were motivated by M96 and M97 engines, which did suffer from IMS problems.

It has been revealed that it would appear most owners find the rest of the car to be just as dependable. Across 12 reviews on Cars, specifically for 2010 model-year Boxsters, owners rated the drop-top a respectable 4.4 out of 5 on reliability. Most comments commended the car's sublime road manners, but some did point out their Boxster had been nothing but reliable, which should reassure potential future owners.

#618. Breaking: Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica

Breaking: Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Europe’s industrial hydrogen looks have a buyer problem.
  • It has been revealed that the central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg.
  • Recent findings suggest that at a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Europe’s industrial hydrogen looks have a buyer problem. A factory cannot make its products competitive by paying whatever a latest hydrogen plant needs to recover its investment. Its maximum hydrogen price is set by the cost of making the same product, or delivering the same useful heat, another way.

It has been revealed that the central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg. That starts with electricity at €60/MWh and 53 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, so the electricity alone costs €3.18/kg. Electrolysers, capital recovery, maintenance, stack replacements, water and other plant costs bring the total to €5.70. Getting hydrogen to a customer can cost more.

Recent findings suggest that at a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel. With 94% heating efficiency, delivering one MWh of useful heat requires roughly 31.9 kg of hydrogen. The fuel bill reaches €182/MWh before the burner, maintenance and other equipment costs. In the model’s central 2050 comparison, suitable direct-electric heating sets a hydrogen price ceiling of €2.07/kg. At that ceiling the same hydrogen heat costs about €66/MWh. The hydrogen production case overshoots the customer’s competitive input price by €3.63/kg.

Industry observers note that the mismatch is not a prediction that hydrogen makers will never lower costs. It is the actual commercial test investors should apply before financing supply. Reducing the cost of production from €7 to €5 a kilogram achieves little if the relevant industrial customer can pay €2. Production-cost targets are meaningless without a corresponding market price ceiling.

The International Energy Agency’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 has made customer cost acceptability part of its assessment. Across most sector and region comparisons, the IEA finds maximum acceptable hydrogen prices below US$2/kg without policy support. Some incumbent-steel comparisons yield negative acceptable prices. The IEA examines a 2035 horizon and a different set of competitors; the same buyer-side arithmetic exposes the problem.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment calculates the maximum hydrogen input price for industrial heat, ammonia and ironmaking and compares it with distinct European supply cases. It also links to the underlying European hydrogen research and interactive model.

Industry observers note that european ammonia illustrates how demand for a product differs from demand for European-made hydrogen. Ammonia remains necessary for fertilisers and industrial chemicals. The buyer’s real choice is where to produce it. In the central 2050 TFIE model, making qualifying green ammonia inside Europe can compete with imported green ammonia only when its hydrogen input costs roughly €2.62–€4.00/kg, depending on the origin and production route. The €5.70/kg onsite supply case misses those thresholds. Europe can keep consuming ammonia without building every electrolyser locally.

Ironmaking has a similar sourcing decision. The model’s hydrogen input-price ceiling versus qualifying imported hydrogen-reduced or hot-briquetted iron ranges from €2.28 to €4.45/kg. Against a European electrochemical iron process, the central ceiling is approximately €1.43/kg. Where enough suitable scrap can deliver the required steel grade, the hydrogen-based route can lose even at a zero price for hydrogen. Steel quality, industrial integration and the commercial maturity of electrochemical iron matter to those comparisons. They do not entitle a hydrogen supplier to ignore the alternatives.

Hydrogen used as a chemical reagent deserves a different assessment from hydrogen burned for heat. Chemical production may need the molecule. Industrial heating needs temperature, pressure, reliability and useful energy, all of which can be delivered directly from electricity for many applications. Manufacturing hydrogen from electricity and then burning it adds conversion losses and fuel-system costs before the plant receives the heat it needs.

Sources indicate that the supply cases have defined boundaries. The central onsite cost is €5.70/kg. A generic delivery allowance takes that case to €6.95/kg. The model’s separately configured hub-and-pipeline case is €5.81/kg. Those are different cost structures, not interchangeable price quotes for the same customer. Even the favourable 2050 case, at €3.46/kg with its specified delivery allowance and €28/MWh electricity, clears some industrial thresholds but still misses others.

It has been revealed that policy can create demand that market prices do not support. Carbon pricing, procurement mandates, subsidies and carbon contracts for difference can raise willingness or obligation to pay. That may be a deliberate industrial or climate choice, but governments should disclose the premium, who will finance it and the contract duration. Describing a regulated purchase as competitive demand hides the cost rather than eliminating it.

In a recent development, the EU energy regulators’ market monitoring points in the same direction. ACER reported 4.2 GW of committed electrolyser capacity in November 2026, including operating plants, projects under construction and those with final investment decisions. Roughly 49% was associated with refining, where renewable-fuel mandates provide a strong demand signal. The remaining industrial sectors face a harder test when policy does not compel the same purchases.

For lenders, the consequence is immediate. A proposed hydrogen plant costing €5/kg has no viable commercial case when its intended industrial buyer can afford €3/kg. A memorandum of understanding cannot close that €2/kg gap. Developers need buyers with enforceable contracts at prices that cover supply costs, lower production costs, or identified support durable enough to finance the difference.

Industry observers note that industrial and public procurement should start with the product the customer must deliver, calculate the best eligible competing route, and determine the maximum hydrogen price that route permits. Only then should investors consider electrolysers, pipelines and capacity targets. Suppliers do not set the market by drawing cheaper future cost curves. Industrial customers set the ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that the full TFIE Briefing and open European hydrogen assessment contain the industrial route comparisons, scenario assumptions and research submitted to the European Commission. The next Briefing examines the competing routes for sourcing green ammonia and iron.
