#607. 7 6.2-Liter V8s Ranked From Least To Most Horsepower

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1601 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

7 6.2-Liter V8s Ranked From Least To Most Horsepower

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the 6.2-liter V8 holds a special place in the hearts of modern muscle-car fans.
  • Sources indicate that true, some V8-powered supercars can top the horsepower output from these 6.2-liter units.
  • Industry observers note that we do have a disclaimer, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the 6.2-liter V8 holds a special place in the hearts of modern muscle-car fans. After all, a motor that size was under the hood of the dearly departed third-generation Dodge Challenger — in which it showed off a horsepower rating well into four-figure territory — and Dodge isn't the only automaker to use a beefy 6.2-liter V8.

Sources indicate that true, some V8-powered supercars can top the horsepower output from these 6.2-liter units. The Hennessey Venom F5, for one, touts 1,817 horses from its 6.6-liter twin-turbo V8. But 6.2-liter V8s, whether they're naturally aspirated, turbocharged, or supercharged, are among some of the most powerful and most well-liked powerplants of all time. We'll get into the details below, but there are all sorts of rides like the Ford F-150 Raptor, the first mid-engine Chevrolet Corvette, the Chevy Camaro ZL-1, and various Mercedes-Benz AMG models ranging from the C 63 to the SLS AMG that use impressive 6.2-liter V8s.

Industry observers note that we do have a disclaimer, though. Engine displacement is generally displayed in cubic liters today, but many automakers do their measuring in terms of cubic centimeters. Then they round up to get to liters. For instance, Dodge's 6.2-liter Hemi V8 actually displaces closer to 6,166 cubic centimeters, so the numbers aren't hyper-precise, but we figure it's close enough.

According to recent reports, the trail-ready Ford F-150 SVT Raptor hit dealerships in 2010 with an optional 6.2-liter unit capped at 400 hp. Ford then made that engine standard, with 411 ponies, the following year. Known by Blue Oval fans and insiders as "the Boss" – though it was unrelated to the V8s of the Boss Mustangs — it could propel the Raptor from zero to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds.

Industry observers note that ford started the engine's development with a goal of producing a so-called Triple Seven – a 7.0-liter V8 capable of 700 hp with a redline of 7,000 rpm. The single example made, many years later, would find its way into a 2005 Ford Mustang dragster that could get through the quarter mile in under 9 seconds. Who knows what kind of numbers the Raptor would have put up if Ford's 7.0-liter ended up under the hood? Even without it, though, the massive-power pickup truck was an impressive rig.

For a certain subset of AMG enthusiasts, this is where it all started. The naturally aspirated 6.2-liter M156 V8 was the first motor ever developed from scratch by MB's in-house performance division. All previous AMG vehicles had relied on modified Mercedes-Benz production engines. Of course, many of those engines were built by hand. The Mercedes-AMG philosophy of "one man, one engine" goes back to at least 1976, when the tech giant had relocated to Affalterbach, Germany.

As for the first car with the M156, that distinction goes to the 2007 Mercedes-AMG E63, which won Car and Driver's German Sports Sedan Comparo that same year. No doubt impacting the decision, the naturally aspirated engine kicked out a healthy 507 hp and 446 pound-feet of torque. When C&D put that output to the test, the car introduced to 60 in a mere 4.2 seconds, dispatching the quarter mile in 12.6 seconds at 115 mph. By 2010, the E63's M156 came with 518 hp complemented by 465 lb-ft of torque.

The M156 would end up motivating the likes of the R230 SL 63 AMG, the CLK 63, CL 63, CLS 63, and ML 63, but it's crucial to note that the "63" attached to these machines was a bit of a misnomer. The M156's displacement remained at 6.2 liters in all these applications.

The M159 started out with healthy horsepower, and it increased in output over the years. When the car premiered in 2010, its engine could make 563 horsepower, and the AMG SLS GT could serve up 583 horses from 2013-2015.

Industry observers note that the 6.2-liter V8 powering the 2020 Mercedes-AMG SLS Black Series made 622 horsepower, which might seem meager by modern supercar standards, but that power output comes from a naturally aspirated mill. What's more, this engine wasn't simply an updated version of the M156 6.2-liter V8. The significant updates ranged from dry-sump lubrication to redesigned camshafts to the kind of lightweight forged pistons needed by some high-performance rides. In all, some 120 of the M159's components were upgraded compared to the M156.

In a recent development, it's further worth pointing out that Mercedes refers to the engine as having 6.3 liters of displacement. You can chalk that up to marketing, however. To honor Mercedes' first post-war V8, the 6.3-liter M100, the organization decided to also call the M156 a 6.3-liter mill — despite it displacing 6,208 cubic centimeters. That, obviously, should be rounded down to 6.2. Anyways, the naming strategy then carried over to the M159.

It has been revealed that as Chevy's high-performance halo car, it makes sense that the Corvette — especially in its ZR1 variants — has been the showcase for some of the brand's most powerful engines. So we're going to talk about two different versions of the Corvette's 6.2-liter V8: the LT5 from the 2019 ZR1, and the LS9 that came in the 2009 ZR1. First, it's the LS9.

According to recent reports, putting out a stout 638 horsepower, the LS9 is part of GM's long-running LS lineup, which is considered a totally different engine generation than the LT roster. One core practical difference is that the former featured port injection and the latter had direct injection, cylinder deactivation, and variable valve timing. Drilling down into the details reveals the LS and LT families are set apart by much more than that — there's practically zero parts interchangeability between the two.

The LS9 proved its performance credibility on the road with zero-to-60 sprints of 3.4 seconds and a top speed of 205 mph. When it debuted, it was Chevy's most powerful production motor.

According to recent reports, when Chevrolet ended production of the front-engine Corvette, it sent the car out on top: The 2019 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 debuted as the fastest, most powerful model to ever wear the Crossed Flags badge. Yes, both benchmarks have since been obliterated by the record-setting Corvette ZR1X, but the '19 ZR1 was no slouch. During testing at Car and Driver, the ZR1 covered the quarter mile in 10.7 seconds, reaching 135 mph along the way, and along the way it went from zero to 60 in 2.9 seconds.

In a recent development, the engine backing those results was Chevy's supercharged 6.2-liter LT5 V8. Now, GM has a tendency to re-use its engine codes, so keep in mind that this is a totally different mill from the 5.7-liter LT5 V8 that Lotus developed for the 1990 ZR-1.

According to recent reports, oh, and the hand-built 2019 LT5 also set a record itself. The LT5's 755 hp and 715 lb-ft represented the most output ever offered in any production Chevy up to that point. Another milestone — the premiere of GM's first dual fuel-injection system — was a key contributor to the output. With that on board, the LT5 had both direct and port injection working for it.

According to recent reports, before it was adapted to be fueled by ethanol and got a huge horsepower bump as a result, the "regular" Demon spent time as the most powerful muscle car in the world. Despite its street-legal status, the Demon was purpose-built for the dragstrip. There, it could make the most of its supercharged 6.2-liter V8 and enter the record books. The Demon tapped into 840 hp to cover the quarter mile in 9.65 seconds at 140 mph, making it the fastest production car in the quarter mile at the time.

The Demon was plenty different from its Hellcat predecessor. To be more specific, while it was technically the same engine, the Demon's V8 shared fewer than 40% of its components with the standard Hellcat. Notable enhancements here extended to a reinforced block with upgraded main caps and deck surfaces, along with a forged alloy crankshaft, forged pistons, and powder-forged connecting rods. Compared to the Demon's 840 hp, the standard Hellcat's 707 hp output seems almost pedestrian.

Dodge first debuted a supercharged 6.2-liter Hemi V8 for the 2015 Challenger SRT Hellcat, setting a template for the increasingly insane Dodge V8s that followed. The basic progression was from the Hellcat to the aforementioned Demon, and eventually to the Demon 170, with each set of changes massive enough to count as a different engine.

Consider the 2023 Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170. The most powerful muscle car in the world when it rolled out — according to Dodge – this street-legal stunner can spit out 1,250 hp and 945 lb-ft when drinking E85 ethanol fuel. On E10, it still offers up a hefty 900 horses. And although its supercharged 6.2-liter V8 shares its displacement with its predecessors, that's about all it shares. With the exception of the camshaft, just about every internal component on the Demon 170 was changed.

According to recent reports, for one thing, to maximize its fluid intake, newly introduced fuel injectors capable of delivering more than 2.7 gallons of fuel per minute were used. On the air side of the fuel-air mixture, the 3.0-liter supercharger benefited from enhancements to its throttle body, pulley, intake valves, valve guides, bearings, connecting rods, and more. The outcome was a machine that could sprint to 60 in an EV-like 1.66 seconds on a race-prepped surface — just as fast as the Rimac Nevera R that set 24 new performance records in 2025.

#606. 2026 Genesis GV80 Coupe Is An Appeal To Your Heart, Not Your Head

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1309 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

2026 Genesis GV80 Coupe Is An Appeal To Your Heart, Not Your Head

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like just about everything Genesis makes, the GV80 Coupe is a fabulous-looking vehicle, perhaps the best-looking in its class with its distinctive front end, lovely silhouette and ducktail spoiler out back.
  • Sure, it runs on low-profile all-season rubber, has seat bolsters that hug you in corners, and is powered by a twin-turbocharged and electronically supercharged 3.5-liter V6.
  • Full Disclosure: Genesis was kind enough to lend me a 2026 GV80 Coupe with a full tank of fuel to do with as I pleased for a week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like just about everything Genesis makes, the GV80 Coupe is a fabulous-looking vehicle, perhaps the best-looking in its class with its distinctive front end, lovely silhouette and ducktail spoiler out back. And like most crossover coupes, the GV80 Coupe promises to lean more into the sporty side of things than its normal-backed brother. The thing is, it doesn't quite deliver on that.

Sure, it runs on low-profile all-season rubber, has seat bolsters that hug you in corners, and is powered by a twin-turbocharged and electronically supercharged 3.5-liter V6. It even has bright red seatbelts, but the GV80 Coupe is by no means a sports car. Hell, it's barely sporty and is certainly lacking a bit in the body control area when compared to stuff like the BMW X6 and Mercedes-Benz GLE Coupe. However, if you take the idea of sporty pretentions out of your head, you're in for a much better time, because the GV80 Coupe is a wonderful, delightfully comfortable cruiser with a well-thought-out interior, lots of top-notch luxury gizmos, and practicality that punches far above what you'd expect from a crossover coupe.

Full Disclosure: Genesis was kind enough to lend me a 2026 GV80 Coupe with a full tank of fuel to do with as I pleased for a week.

There are two engine options for the GV80 Coupe. A twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 that pumps out 375 horsepower comes as standard, but those who aren't lilbabybois can step up to the more powerful (and certainly more interesting) twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 that has a 48-volt system with an electric supercharger. This funky motor throws down 409 hp and 405 lb-ft of torque while also getting slightly better gas mileage than the standard motor. Don't worry, it's still not good fuel economy. The EPA rates it at 17 mpg city, 22 mpg highway and 19 mpg combined. It's a thirsty beast, but that's a small price to pay for all of this modest sportiness.

Granted, the GV80 E-SC, fitted with a Genesis-built 8-speed automatic that sends power to all four wheels, can get a move on in a straight line. It'll hit 60 mph from a standstill in 5.2 seconds, according to Car and Driver's testing, which is solid for a 5,132-pound crossover. The GV80 doesn't feel like it's in much of a rush to accelerate, though, and it also lags behind its competition. Without a doubt, it's a smooth powertrain, but it's not exactly sporty — not in the way the red seatbelts would imply.

The lack of sportiness becomes incredibly obvious when hustling the GV80 Coupe around a corner. It's almost as if those seatbelts are red not to denote sportiness, but to show how miffed the car is that I dare push it. The lack of athleticism is evident almost immediately, as the suspension and brakes have a tough time keeping up with the beefy curb weight. There's just too much body roll and not enough steering feel to make for any sort of fun-spirited driving no matter what drive mode I was in, including the E-Supercharged-exclusive Sport+ mode.

According to recent reports, what I learned promptly is that this car really shines as a cruiser. I've noted in the past that crossover coupes are the personal luxury coupes of the modern age, and that's true again with the GV80 Coupe. This thing is wonderfully comfortable to eat highway miles in or blast around town as the Ergo Motion driver's seat works on that knot in my back and HMG's wonderful suite of driver-assistance aids keep me in my lane and out of the rear bumper of the car in front of me. The engine, while interesting in its operation, doesn't provide the most inspiring noise, so it's not the end of the world when it shuts up as I drive in quiet, calm luxury through the streets of Latest York.

In a recent development, beyond those lovely quilted leather seats, the interior of the GV80 Coupe is a fantastic place to be that also goes toward its cruising pretensions. Sure, there's some carbon-fiber-look trim, but it doesn't exactly scream sportiness. Neither does the wood, metal, glass, and swaths of suede. Do ya know what that does scream? Nice. Pleasant. Chill. Good.

Another nice, pleasant, chill, and good element of the GV80's interior is its 27-inch OLED touchscreen that serves as both a digital gauge cluster and center infotainment display. Inputs can be made with either fingers or an iDrive-style control knob. I'll admit, the system feels a bit clunky to use the first day or so, a step behind BMW and Mercedes-Benz's upcoming systems, but after a bit of learning where everything else is, it becomes second nature. Using wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto fixes that problem quickly, too. Adding to the simplicity is the secondary touchscreen below it that has all of the car's climate controls housed within it, and between the two screens is a row of buttons that can pull up core vehicle controls. It's certainly welcome for the Luddites among us.

Aside from the sloping roofline, not too much else was changed on the inside or outside for the Coupe, which isn't a bad thing as the GV80 is a lovely-looking vehicle from the get-go. The GV80 Coupe carries the same 116.3-inch wheelbase as the regular GV80, but overall length increases by an inch to 195.5 inches, and the rakish roofline drops overall height by 0.2 inches. Rear seat occupants probably aren't going to miss the 0.8 inches of headroom they've given up, and if they are ones to complain, ditch them. You don't need that sort of negativity in your life, anyway. You're going to need to trim the fat regardless, because there's no third row in the Coupe.

Sources indicate that the GV80 Coupe is no exception when it comes to crossover coupes being a bit silly. No truly practical person would buy one over the normal crossover they're based on simply because they're an exercise in style over substance. They're innately compromised products, and on top of that, they almost always cost more.

A base-base GV80 2.5T RWD starts at $59,195 including destination, but that's not really a fair comparison, so let's look at the GV80 3.5T Advanced AWD — that's the trim level where the Coupe starts from. The regular GV80 in that spec starts at $77,445, while a comparable GV80 Coupe is going to be $83,345. That means you, dear buyer, need to fork over an extra $5,900 for the pleasure of having fewer seats and worse visibility out the rear. I, however, would contend that that is a small price to pay for such a pretty car. Argue with a wall.

According to recent reports, the GV80 I drove was no base-spec, though, as it had the E-Supercharger, boosting its starting price to $89,145. The vehicle's lone option, $650 worth of Bering Blue Paint, brought the final price to $89,795. It's a small price to pay for something that looks this good — it's nearly a concept car for the road, if you ask me. If you think of the GV80 Coupe as a piece of art rather than a car, then it's a hell of a deal, and it's even fairly in line with alternatives from Germany like the Mercedes-Benz GLE450 Coupe ($82,650), Audi Q8 Premium ($78,295), BMW X6 40i xDrive ($78,750) and Porsche Cayenne Coupe ($97,450). It's worth the premium over the latter four based on looks alone.

According to recent reports, of course, if you look at it compared to the normal GV80, things fall apart, but this is a car meant to speak to your heart, not your head. Just take a second to look at the mess your head's gotten you into throughout your life. Perhaps it's time to let your heart make some decisions.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, BYD is one of the many Chinese car companies trying to rack up orders, and its Denza brand has now recreated a famous Volkswagen commercial from two decades ago that involved a diesel-powered SUV and a jumbo jet.
  • In a recent development, I vividly remember when I saw the original clip 20 years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chinese automakers are trying to capture as much of the European car market as possible, and they’re resorting to clever marketing tricks that legacy automakers have used in the past to attract buyers.

In a recent development, BYD is one of the many Chinese car companies trying to rack up orders, and its Denza brand has now recreated a famous Volkswagen commercial from two decades ago that involved a diesel-powered SUV and a jumbo jet. Only this time, Denza has an ace up its sleeve, and it’s quite impressive.

In a recent development, I vividly remember when I saw the original clip 20 years ago. A blue Volkswagen Touareg V10 diesel towed a 171-ton jet aircraft down the same Dunsfold runway in the United Kingdom where the old "Top Gear" episodes used to be filmed.

Industry observers note that now, the Denza B5 (or Bao 5 in some markets) plug-in hybrid SUV is back at the same place to do the same stunt, but adapted for a 2026 where everything seemingly needs to be bigger, more over the top, and more in-your-face. (I blame TikTok.).

So, we have a Chinese PHEV that uses two electric motors and a 1.5-liter gas engine. It’s all-wheel-drive, its 31.8-kilowatt-hour battery can deliver up to 56 miles of all-electric range on a full battery, and it has two mechanical locking differentials. This last part is key. The battery can be fast-charged at up to 100 kW, and the total system output is a healthy 536 horsepower, with most of that oomph being provided by the two e-motors.

We also have a 207-ton jumbo jet that got a quick repositioning for no other purpose than pure entertainment.

Here comes the interesting bit: While Volkswagen’s original stunt kept all four of the Touareg’s wheels in place—you know, how a car usually works—BYD decided to put its PHEV SUV to the test by gradually removing some wheels.

Sources indicate that the first run was done with all four wheels in place, followed by a three-wheeled run with 2.2 tons of ballast. For the final act, both right wheels were removed, and the ballast reached 5 tonnes. During the three runs, the Denza B5 towed the Boeing 747-400 over one mile, and best of all, it used exclusively electric power.

The point of it all? Promote the new SUV to the UK market, where the Land Rover Defender is among its biggest rivals. Unlike the Defender, however, which is now based on a unibody design and is primarily combustion-powered, the Denza B5 sits on a bespoke ladder-frame chassis and more substantially electrified. It has a gas engine that acts mainly as a generator for the high-voltage battery. The battery cells are directly integrated between the chassis rails.

It has been revealed that if you're thinking about trying this stunt at home, just know the vehicle needed a few modifications to pull it off. BYD added a custom towing attachment, removed some seats to make room for the ballast, and added stabilizers to make up for the missing wheels.

#604. Tech Report: History Of The AMC Javelin: The Alternative Pony Car

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2586 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Tech Report: History Of The AMC Javelin: The Alternative Pony Car

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in 1971, a minor player in the American automotive industry accomplished something extraordinary.
  • The upstart AMC had been building cars in Wisconsin, across Lake Michigan from the Detroit giants that the tech giant would later beat at their own game.
  • Sources indicate that it's tempting to tell the Javelin's story as one of failure, mostly because that's how we tend to remember the cars that don't survive long enough to earn a prominent place in our shared automotive history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in 1971, a minor player in the American automotive industry accomplished something extraordinary. After years of long-shot competition against companies with vastly more significant resources, American Motors Corporation won the Trans-Am championship. The following year, it did it again.

The upstart AMC had been building cars in Wisconsin, across Lake Michigan from the Detroit giants that the tech giant would later beat at their own game. Yet, not long after the metaphorical credits would have rolled following that fairytale ending, the car responsible for those victories would be no more. The car was the AMC Javelin, and by the end of 1974, it was gone.

Sources indicate that it's tempting to tell the Javelin's story as one of failure, mostly because that's how we tend to remember the cars that don't survive long enough to earn a prominent place in our shared automotive history. The icons become institutions, celebrated and remixed into anniversary editions, nostalgic ad campaigns, and generations of increasingly expensive collectibles. Everything else is a footnote.

But the Javelin's existence has more to say than the handful of years in which it was made, as its brief run coincided remarkably with a transformative shift in the broader history of the automobile in the United States. It arrived in 1968, when American prosperity seemed limitless, and disappeared just as the country was beginning to confront the limits of that optimism.

Along the way, the Javelin became something its creators could have scarcely imagined. Its story is one of ambition, ingenuity, and the kind of underdog triumph that's impossible not to root for. Except, it's also about the difference between reaching a dream and being able to hang onto it.

In the early '60s, the American automobile was clearly becoming more than just a way to get around. The baby boomers were getting old enough to drive, and cars weren't just for families anymore. Women took to the road in increasing numbers, and multi-car households became more common. As a growing market with more disposable income showed an appetite for cars that were more fun and even had a little personality, carmakers were eager to oblige.

In a recent development, ford led the way. The company introduced the Mustang at the Latest York World's Fair on April 17, 1964. The Mustang had a long hood and short rear deck that fundamentally changed the posture of what a fun car could be and started at just $2,368. Available options and configurations could accommodate buyers interested in anything from a free-spirited runabout to a serious performance car.

It has been revealed that ford expected to sell 100,000 Mustangs a year. It took 22,000 orders on the first day, and first-year sales exceeded 400,000 cars. The era of the American pony car had arrived, but that meant more than just the Mustang.

According to recent reports, plymouth had actually beaten Ford to market with the Barracuda, but Ford gets the credit for turning the segment into a sensation. Chevy answered with the Camaro, Pontiac arrived with the Firebird, and the Mercury-branded Cougar followed its Ford sibling into production.

The pony car offered buyers individuality, excitement, and an invitation to have fun with cars in ways that went beyond simply buying a family sedan with a needlessly-large V8. American Motors didn't have one.

According to recent reports, american Motors Corporation built a reputation around economical, everyday cars since the company was established by a merger of the Nash-Kelvinator Corporation and the Hudson Motor Car Company, which, in 1954, represented the largest merger in United States history. As America embraced the fun, newly introduced Mustang and its early pony car contemporaries, AMC was struggling with a stodgy and decidedly unexciting reputation.

Enter the 1968 Javelin, a sporty coupe developed under AMC design chief Richard Teague after he had personally advocated for AMC to get in on the pony car segment and start shaking off the buttoned-down, no-fun image. The car had a long hood and daring proportions that clearly made a play at the burgeoning market without being a copy of any that existed so far. In-period advertising called out the Mustang by name, leaning into the rivalry and calling out the Javelin's differentiating features like large, contoured bumpers, hand-finished roof joints, and extra room inside.

Underpinning what some would say is one of the most attractive muscle cars ever forgotten was the basic architecture of AMC's Rambler American, a car that was explicitly built to minimize operating costs and compete with the rise of economical imports. Yet, AMC was able to take the bones of one of the least exciting vehicles on the road at the time and use it as a jumping-off point that could do more than turn heads. Engine choices included a 232-cubic-inch inline-6, 290 and 343 V8s, and, eventually, a 390-cubic-inch V8 producing 315 gross horsepower. A 390-powered Javelin SST tested by Car and Driver reached 60 mph in 6.9 seconds.

People noticed. AMC had first set out to sell just 35,000 Javelins but ended up building more than 50,000 in that first year.

Sources indicate that the Mustang might have been leading the herd when it came to pony cars, but AMC wasn't content to spend the Javelin's existence playing catch up and running ads touting its superior headroom or trunk space. Even if the firm couldn't compete with Detroit's marketing or development budgets, it could at least try to out weird the competition.

According to recent reports, for 1969, AMC introduced its "Substantial Bad" paint colors: Big Bad Blue, Big Bad Green, and Big Bad Orange. These were absolutely eye-piercing finishes that came with body-colored bumpers and complementary hardware options like (fake) exhaust shields, stainless steel trim, and a roof-mounted spoiler. Unlike almost everything AMC had produced up until that time, subtlety was not part of the package (and it remains one of the classic coupes that looks sick with window louvers).

Recent findings suggest that in 1970, the manufacturer doubled down, with 100 Javelin SSTs built as replicas of the cars in the Trans-Am racing series, finished in the over-the-top red, white, and blue livery of AMC's competition cars. There was not a unique high-performance engine under the hood, and the replicas came with the same 390-cubic-inch V8 available on the SST. So, aside from a ram-air hood and performance-oriented gearing, this was a car that was all about appearances.

Sources indicate that that appearance was spectacular to be sure, though some of those 100 Trans-Am replicas ended up being repainted back into submission, presumably because drivers were getting more attention on the street than they bargained for. All that remarked, AMC saw that the Javelin had the potential to be a lot more than just a pony car dressed up like a race car. It was headed to the races, and the organization had every intention of winning.

Of course, there's a difference between having the willingness to sell customers a replica race car from the factory and actually competing on the track. Perhaps the likes of Ford and Chevrolet represented immovable racing incumbents, but AMC wasn't going to concede the point.

In 1967, the firm commissioned Ronnie Kaplan Engineering to prepare a handful of Javelins for the Sports Car Club of America's Trans-Am series, which included Mustangs and Camaros backed by Substantial Three resources and some of the best drivers in the world. The Javelins were powered by modified versions of AMC's existing V8s, bored out from a factory-stock 290-cubic-inches up to just over 304, but they were still no match for the competition in a straight line.

In a recent development, despite the horsepower handicap, drivers Pete Revson and George Follmer drove AMC to six second-place finishes and landed third overall in the 1968 manufacturers' championship. It was a promising start, but the team remained a distant third behind the two well-funded factory-backed teams of Chevy and Ford. The following year, Kaplan's team failed to maintain the momentum and the series was roundly dominated by Penske Racing and its driver, Mark Donohue, driving for Chevrolet.

AMC had demonstrated that it could compete on the racetrack, but the little red, white, and blue Javelin had gone two seasons without a victory. It would have to do something differently if the firm wanted a real shot at beating Ford and Chevy at their own game.

Sources indicate that penske and Donohue were two people who had just spent consecutive racing seasons beating up on AMC and its Javelin, but it turns out that they were also something else: free agents. Fresh off of delivering back-to-back manufacturers' championships for Chevrolet, the pair agreed to revise loyalties and see what they could do with the upstart Javelin. Donohue was anything but a mere hotshot racing driver. He had studied engineering at Brown University, and in addition to being behind the wheel, he was also team manager and chief engineer. Together, Penske and Donohue took to the engineering side of the problem first, starting out by questioning the Javelin's bored-out V8. What if instead of stretching AMC's 290 to the limit, they started with the firm's newer 360 V8, reducing its stroke to meet the series' displacement limit while producing enough horsepower to challenge Chevrolet?

Sources indicate that winning is what happened. Donohue drove the Javelin to the car's first three first-place finishes in 1970, and, for the first time, AMC managed to pick off one of its two massive factory rivals, pushing past Chevrolet and finishing second behind Ford. The Javelin wasn't just an oddball outsider hoping to deliver the occasional upset to establishment rivals. It was a serious car capable of winning against the best Detroit had to offer.

Sources indicate that of course, while Donohue and Penske were out winning races, AMC also had to continue being a tech giant that makes and sells cars. For 1971, AMC released a substantially redesigned Javelin that was longer, lower, wider, and more visually striking. Bulging front fenders caught the public's eye, not to mention that of Donohue, who appreciated the breathing room the upcoming design would give to race tires on his Trans-Am cars.

According to recent reports, it was here that the AMC AMX shifted from its previous status as its own model in the AMC lineup, becoming a trim package for the up-and-coming Javelin. This latest Javelin AMX could then be equipped with AMC's 401-cubic-inch V8, rated at 330 gross horsepower. And yet, somehow, this was just the beginning. The following year, AMC tapped fashion designer Pierre Cardin for an outrageous aesthetic overhaul that included colorful stripes taking over the interior, and, indeed, what was once the most conservative automaker was now creating the wildest muscle car graphics in the business. Along the way it built one of the era's automotive special editions that was truly special.

People were taking notice, including the Alabama State Police, which placed an order for 100 of the 401-powered Javelins for use as cruisers. The Javelin had finally helped AMC shrug off its dull reputation as the company that brought America the Rambler.

Sources indicate that in 1971, American Motors finally reached the goal it'd been chasing since the Javelin started racing. Mark Donohue won seven of that season's 10 Trans-Am races and delivered AMC's first manufacturers' championship. The firm that had gotten its start building painfully sensible transportation had finally conquered one of America's most prestigious racing series. The following year, Roy Woods Racing took over the AMC effort, with George Follmer winning four races, becoming the first officially recognized driver's champion of the series, and bringing home the manufacturers' championship for a second time.

After four straight years of throwing the Javelin squarely at the fiercest competition of the day, AMC had done it. But even so, this previously unthinkable victory came at a time when the foundation of the Trans-Am series was beginning to shift. Other manufacturers, Ford and Chevy included, had withdrawn factory support for the Trans-Am series the year before. They were still on the racetrack, but without the intense backing that had pushed the teams forward through previous seasons. Still, AMC was up against some of the fastest cars that the most formidable manufacturers had fielded the previous season, and some of the private teams were anything but amateurs -– it was the private Penske team that brought Chevrolet those back-to-back championships in the first place, after all.

It has been revealed that the Javelin had reached the top. A team of engineers, drivers, and ambitious tech giant people had turned the unlikely descendant of the Rambler into a championship-winning machine. The achievement was nothing short of extraordinary, only it happened just as the mountain was beginning to empty.

Sources indicate that the Javelin came of age in an America where the future seemed limitless, with more horsepower, unimaginable freedom, and an endless supply of cheap gasoline to keep it all roaring forward. But while the Javelin was winning car races and AMC was experimenting with wild paint colors plus Pierre Cardin aesthetics, the country itself was starting to feel different.

Recent findings suggest that the Clean Air Act of 1970 introduced ambitious fresh emissions requirements, effectively tapping the brakes on what made the pony car segment sing. In '73 the oil embargo sent petroleum prices through the roof, and Americans who had never given a thought to a seemingly bottomless supply of oil  were suddenly weighing what they were going to do if gas ran out. The era of giant V8s drinking fuel right from the tap with no concern for tomorrow was coming to an end.

The extraordinary irony for AMC was that the boring, practical reputation it had worked so hard to overcome was exactly what the market was starting to demand. Sensible, economical transportation was back in style, and despite years of running the other direction with the Javelin, the company was well-positioned to capitalize on the shift, with cars like the Gremlin and the Hornet ready to meet the moment. AMC had finally built a performance champion, but its greatest opportunities lay in leaving it behind.

Industry observers note that in 1971, the Javelin was taking its victory lap on the national stage. Just three years later, it would be offered for the last time. 1974 marked the end of AMC's unlikely hero, leaving incumbent mainstays like the Mustang, Camaro, and Firebird to carry the segment forward into uncertain times.

According to recent reports, AMC could have stayed in the game, navigating the latest landscape as rivals were attempting, but the Javelin would have required significant updates to meet 1975 safety regulations, including an estimated $12 million investment in bumpers alone. The time had come to move on.

Recent findings suggest that that following year, Mark Donohue crashed while practicing for the Austrian Grand Prix. He had seen the potential in AMC's alternative pony car, joining the team to both engineer it into contention and to sit behind the wheel. Donohue died following emergency brain surgery after the wreck, and so 1975 marked the loss of both the Javelin itself and an icon who was central to what it had become.

AMC had done what it set out to do. It had built a car exciting enough for the times, challenged the biggest carmakers in the country, and won it all, twice. Yet, after all that, it would turn out that what America needed just then wasn't a better Mustang after all. It needed a better Rambler.

This EV-Swapped 1967 Porsche 912 Has 300 HP And A Split Battery Pack

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world.
  • According to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving.
  • There's some clever engineering here, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world. It started out doing electric powertrain swaps for classic Range Rovers, which it still does. But it also has a bespoke program now, under which it will develop custom EV swaps for customers for any sort of car they want. In this specific case, Inverted stuffed some batteries and an electric motor into an old Porsche 912. Interestingly, this is the third powertrain that's been in this Porsche.

According to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving. So they took their car to Inverted and the team got to work. The end result is a car that looks exactly like a normal Porsche 912, with all of its gorgeous old-school styling, but drives like a modern EV.

There's some clever engineering here, too. The 62 kWh battery pack is more than enough to propel the vintage Porsche's featherweight body a fair ways. However, that's a lot of weight to hang over the rear axle. Air-cooled Porsches were already prone to lift-off oversteer, so they don't need any more. So Inverted came up with an interesting solution: split the pack into two parts. On section is mounted out back where the engine used to be, and the other is under the hood. It means the electric 912's weight balance is actually better than the original car's.

Recent findings suggest that inverted claims that this EV 912 has around 250 miles of range, and it can DC fast charge at 75 kW. The latter might seem weak in the world of modern EVs, but it's perfectly fine in a classic like this. This is a daily driver, not a long-distance cruiser. So 250 miles is more than enough for daily usage, and plugging it in overnight to charge will get the owner a fresh battery in the morning.

The rear-mounted electric motor makes 300 horsepower, so it's much more potent than the original 912 four-cylinder engine which made around 90 horsepower. Inverted notes it can hit 0-60 mph in four seconds, which kicks the ass of the stock vehicle. The original 912 took about 13 seconds.

According to recent reports, this isn't just a powertrain swap, either. Its interior is completely redone and it's gorgeous. The gauges look like vintage Porsche gauges but they're modified for EV used. For example, the classic Porsche central tachometer was replaced with a power percentage gauge. The fuel gauge is now an analog battery charge gauge, too. It's just lovely.

This is an awesome project and one that would make for an incredible daily driver. It has modern Porsche levels of performance, with modern EV levels of range, in a stylish vintage package. Seems perfect.

Waymo has apparently run into some complications with its robotaxis on highways in California, and it has pulled its robotaxis off of highways across the United States as a result. The main glitch is that Waymo robotaxis have entered active construction zones. (Yikes!).

It has been revealed that earlier this week, in response to the Waymo vehicles driving into active construction zones, California required that Waymo stop operating its robotaxis on highways for the time being. Sources indicate that in addition to the above concerns, Waymo robotaxis have not operated appropriately at times when manual traffic control has replaced traffic lights. Waymo issued an patch recently following a crash that occurred as a result of this problem. “The ‌manual ⁠traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better responds to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on November 6.”.

Sources indicate that so, yes, Waymo robotaxis still aren’t perfect. However, Waymo continues to point out that its vehicles are much safer statistically than human-driven vehicles, as these vehicles are traveling far more miles between accidents than average human American drivers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LDEQ issued air permit to the facility despite serious flaws in permit.
  • Sources indicate that donaldsonville, Louisiana — Today, RISE St.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LDEQ issued air permit to the facility despite serious flaws in permit.

Sources indicate that donaldsonville, Louisiana — Today, RISE St. James Louisiana and Sierra Club filed a lawsuit challenging Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality’s decision to issue an air permit to Hyundai-POSCO for its proposed steelmaking facility. The groups claim that the air permit must be vacated because LDEQ did not conduct an environmental justice analysis, nor did the agency give full and careful consideration to mitigation measures like electrified components and green hydrogen, or to the environmental costs of Hyundai’s added pollution in an already overburdened area, as is required by the Louisiana state constitution and the Clean Air Act.

According to recent reports, throughout 2026, Sierra Club, working with other experts and local groups, submitted a series of comments to LDEQ in an effort to bring to light the errors, miscalculations, and omissions in the permit application. Despite some improvements to the permit application, made by Hyundai Steel following public pressure, the final air permit issued by LDEQ authorizes the facility to emit substantial quantities of greenhouse gases, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter, carbon monoxide, lead, mercury, ammonia, and other pollutants. Many of these pollutants cause significant and irreversible damage to human health even at low levels.

In a recent development, the area around the planned facility already bears a toxic air pollution burden greater than 96% of the rest of the country, and ranks high across a range of environmental and socioeconomic indicators. The Hyundai Steel Plant is one of multiple polluting facilities planned as part of the 17,000-acre Riverplex MegaPark in an area known as Cancer Alley in Ascension Parish, Louisiana.

In response, the petitioners issued the following statements:.

For that reason, we are asking the Court to reverse LDEQ’s final decision and vacate the permit for Hyundai Steel’s proposed facility.”.

According to recent reports, mekaylyn Lavigne, Modeste Coordinator for RISE St. James, said: “I was born and raised in the small and peaceful community of Modeste. Although this region is now known as Cancer Alley because many chemical plants have polluted our air and water, my family and neighbors still enjoy sitting on our porches, watching birds and wildlife, and fishing. #598. Industry News: Is the Energy Crisis Accelerating the Clean Energy Transition? 4 Takeaways from the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1281 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica

Industry News: Is the Energy Crisis Accelerating the Clean Energy Transition? 4 Takeaways from the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.
  • The International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security.
  • What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

The International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security. The report finds that the push to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels is accelerating electrification and the shift toward domestic energy sources, including renewables. Yet electricity demand is surging, grids are struggling to keep pace, and concerns about energy security are also giving coal a longer life in some countries. The IEA warns that the pursuit of energy security alone won’t deliver the emissions reductions needed to meet global climate goals.

What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts? Nick Wayth, global director of the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, explains four key takeaways from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

Recent findings suggest that Q: How close will current and proposed policies get us to the COP31 pledge to raise electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035? What changes are needed to bridge the gap?

In a recent development, the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reinforced the case for electrification as a way for countries to diversify their power sources and reduce dependence on imports, improving energy security and affordability. While the world’s reliance on fossil fuels hasn’t changed substantially, there’s been a real shift in how countries think about the risks of that dependence—and the benefits of electrification. But progress is too slow. The IEA projects that under current and proposed policies, electricity will account for only 29% of final energy consumption by 2035. That’s only half the increase needed to reach the COP31 target of 35%.

Much of the technology is already available. The IEA estimates that nearly half of fossil fuel demand in road transport and more than a third of demand for low- and medium-temperature industrial heat could be electrified at a competitive cost today. The challenge is creating the conditions for businesses and households to make that switch.

To reach the target, countries need to develop detailed plans for shifting transport, heating, and heavy industry toward electricity and invest in transmission and distribution. Governments can help keep their industries competitive by making it more attractive for businesses to switch from gas to affordable electricity. Some countries are doing this successfully already. Germany, for example, has reduced electricity taxes for manufacturers and has subsidized grid charges, helping lower electricity costs for businesses.

Q: The IEA projects rapid growth in electricity demand from both air conditioning and data centers. How do the challenges posed by these two sources of demand differ?

Energy demand from AI and data centers has dominated public attention this year, but by 2035 the global growth in electricity demand from cooling is forecast to be about 70% greater than from data centers. Notably, the IEA finds that global demand for cooling buildings is overtaking demand for heating them for the first time in history.

Energy demand from data centers is concentrated in the U.S., China, and the EU. By contrast, demand for cooling is widespread, especially in emerging and developing economies where much of the population is vulnerable to extreme heat, an increasing threat to human life.

According to recent reports, under current and proposed government policies, cooling is projected to account for 12% of global electricity consumption by 2035. But during periods of peak demand, when millions of air conditioners are running at once, it could reach around 30% of the electricity needed. Electricity grids must be able to cope with these spikes in demand, even if they occur only occasionally. Without better planning and more efficient cooling, countries could face costly grid upgrades—or risk power outages during extreme heat.

Recent findings suggest that this is why policymakers and utilities need to anticipate future electricity demand and blueprint investments in grid infrastructure accordingly. But building more isn’t the only solution. Governments and utilities should also invest in energy storage and other grid flexibility measures that enable them to adapt to fluctuating supply and demand as needed.

Industry observers note that Q: The energy crisis is accelerating clean electrification in some countries but also encouraging greater reliance on fossil fuels in others. What does the IEA’s outlook tell us about the future of oil, coal, and gas—and the risks of investing in new fossil fuel infrastructure?

The report reveals that global oil demand is expected to level off by 2030 under current and proposed policies. The slowdown in China’s oil demand, driven largely by electric vehicle adoption, is expected to continue. Other fast-growing economies, such as India, despite electrifying transport, are nonetheless projected to increase their demand for oil.

In a recent development, the current energy crisis is reinforcing these differences in strategy. Some countries are investing in electrification to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, while others are turning to domestic fossil fuels.

The energy crisis has given coal demand a short-term boost, and the IEA now expects coal use in 2035 to be higher than it projected just a year ago. Even so, under current and proposed government policies, global coal demand is expected to fall by 14% between 2025 and 2035, driven largely by a decline in coal-fired power generation, particularly in China. But coal use in industry is projected to fall by just 5%, highlighting the challenge of reducing dependence on the fuel.

Countries need to be cautious about investing in infrastructure that may not be needed. The IEA estimates that about 400 billion cubic meters (bcm) of new liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity is under construction and could come online by 2035. Yet under current and stated government policies, export capacity could significantly exceed demand in 2035 by70 bcm. That surplus raises the risk of underused infrastructure and investments that fail to pay off.

Industry observers note that the IEA estimates that the world will need at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines over the next decade to meet growing electricity demand and connect new sources of power, including renewables. Another 15 million kilometers of existing lines will need to be upgraded or replaced. Both will require substantial investment.

In a recent development, the biggest challenge is delivering these changes fast enough. Major grid projects can take 5 to15 years to plan, secure permits for, and complete—far longer than many renewable energy projects. Governments need to speed up permitting and grid connections, improve coordination between utilities and developers, and encourage investment before demand materializes. One encouraging example is the EU’s recent provisional agreement to streamline permitting for grid projects.

Equally important is to invest in ways to use existing assets more efficiently. Grid-enhancing technologies can speed up connections by allowing existing power lines to carry more electricity, reducing the need to build latest infrastructure. And increasingly, governments and utilities are seeing the importance of making grids more flexible—building in capability and strategies to balance supply with demand in real time. Brazil, for example, pays large electricity people to temporarily reduce consumption when the grid is under strain. Businesses that fail to deliver the agreed reductions can lose payments or face suspension from programs. By combining energy storage, demand-response programs, smart grid controls, distributed energy generation, and other flexibility strategies, energy planners can meet growing demands and increase resilience while reducing the need to build more grid infrastructure.

Courtesy of WRI. By Sarah George, Senior Manager, Strategic Communications, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition; and Francisco Boshell, Global Lead, Decarbonized Energy Consumption, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition.

#596. How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1462 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica

How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.
  • Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.
  • Recent findings suggest that but access is only the first step.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.

Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.

Recent findings suggest that but access is only the first step. A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable. An electric irrigation pump is unlikely to raise a farmer’s income if crops can’t reach buyers. And a small business may gain little from electricity if it lacks financing to buy the equipment it needs to expand.

For energy to improve people’s lives, it must be affordable, sufficient, and reliable—and people and businesses must be able to put it to productive use.

Recent findings suggest that the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) calls for “universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services” by 2030. But the two indicators used to track its universal-access target focus only on whether people have access to electricity and whether they primarily rely on clean fuels and technologies. They do not address reliability, affordability, or economic impacts.

Recent findings suggest that other approaches already offer a fuller picture. The World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program developed the Multi-Tier Framework to measure electricity access beyond connections, including whether electricity is available when needed, adequate for the equipment people want to use, reliable and affordable. While the framework is used by some countries to assess these broader dimensions of energy access, such measures are not the default, as many countries rely on the U.N.’s official global indicators.

As governments consider what should follow the SDGs after 2030, they should make multidimensional energy-access measures a regular part of national surveys and use the results to track progress globally. Since access alone does not necessarily deliver better livelihoods, improved measures of access could also be paired with indicators of whether energy is delivering the development outcomes it is intended to support. These could include whether clinics and schools can function as intended, farmers can increase yields and incomes and businesses can grow revenues and employment.

Together, these measures could shift energy planning from the largely supply-side question of how many people have access toward the demand-side questions of what people and institutions need energy for and whether the energy system enables them to meet these needs.

The examples below show why looking beyond connections matters in practice.

According to recent reports, national electrification rates can mask large differences in where electricity is available within a country. Addressing those gaps requires looking beyond national averages to identify the households, businesses, and public facilities that lack access.

Recent findings suggest that in 2023, WRI, working closely with Uganda’s Ministry of Health, used WRI’s Energy Access Explorer (EAE)—an online mapping tool that combines energy data with information on infrastructure, public services, and economic activity—to assess the electricity needs of health facilities. The analysis found that 675 facilities serving more than 3 million people had no electricity, either grid or off-grid, yet all were in areas with significant solar energy potential. The analysis helped identify places where solar power could fill the energy gap.

In Ethiopia, the Ministry of Water and Energy and the World Bank used EAE to help design a financing program for off-grid electricity. The analysis identified 145 priority woredas, or districts, where investments could reach more than 19 million people. Having this location-based data helped translate national energy-access goals into decisions about where public financing should be directed.

Ethiopia also illustrates why simple access figures can overstate the level of service people receive. A 2025 national energy-access survey found that 65% of households had access to at least one source of electricity. However, just 44% of the population received at least a basic level of electricity service, enough for uses such as lighting and charging a phone for at least four hours a day.

Simply having an electricity connection is not enough if the supply lacks the capacity or voltage stability to operate the equipment people need.

Industry observers note that in the Gumla district in Jharkhand, India, villages that had gained household grid connections still lacked enough power for many businesses to function. WRI found that the single-phase electricity supplied was insufficient for productive uses such as milling and oil pressing. Beginning in 2015, Mlinda Charitable Trust, a nonprofit, installed solar mini-grids that supplied three-phase electricity, allowing local enterprises to run equipment, including rice and wheat hullers, oil expellers, flour mills, and pulverizers.

Governments should assess not only whether communities are connected but also whether the electricity supplied can meet the capacity and power-quality requirements of the services and equipment people need—and plan grid upgrades or complementary systems accordingly.

According to recent reports, A connection provides limited benefit if households, businesses, or public facilities cannot pay for enough energy to meet their needs. Measuring meaningful access therefore also means asking whether the energy is affordable for the people and institutions expected to use it.

In Ethiopia’s Berbere district, farmers initially used petrol-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, but high fuel and maintenance costs meant these were too expensive for many to keep using. Petrol cost $91 to $203 per hectare a year, while repairs and the cost of transporting fuel added further expenses.

Industry observers note that WRI and the Danish nonprofit DanChurchAid later installed two solar-powered pumps serving 48 farming households. The solar systems have no fuel costs, while maintenance costs are less than $10 a year, compared with more than $1,300 for petrol pumps. But the two pumps’ combined $19,200 upfront cost was beyond what most farmers could afford out of pocket. Governments and funders should therefore assess both the ongoing cost of using energy and the upfront cost of the technologies needed to use it, and provide financing or targeted support where high initial costs remain a barrier.

Being connected to the grid does not mean electricity will be available whenever it is needed. WRI researchers documented power cuts lasting three to 12 hours a day at two health facilities in Jharkhand, with outages worsening during the monsoon season. The facilities relied on diesel generators and small battery backups during outages.

In 2017, after solar photovoltaic systems and larger batteries were installed, the facilities were able to keep wards and offices running and power other essential equipment during grid outages, reducing their reliance on grid electricity.

Tracking the frequency and duration of outages would give a clearer picture of whether electricity is dependable enough to support essential services.

Even when energy is available, adequate, affordable, and reliable, it may not translate into better livelihoods. People also need equipment, financing, and access to markets to put energy to productive use.

Industry observers note that in Uganda, WRI Africa and partners used EAE to identify $15 million in potential investments in renewable energy technologies, including solar-powered irrigation systems and equipment for cooling and milling, that could benefit more than 28,000 farmers. Some organizations identified through that work have since secured funding for related projects. Masaka District Farmers Association, for example, received an IKI Small Grants award for an irrigation project that equipped 150 hectares of coffee-growing land with drip irrigation and worked with 1,500 smallholder farmers.

In Berbere, solar-powered irrigation has enabled farmers to harvest three to four times a year and grow higher-value crops. In their first season, many farmers earned four to 10 times as much from onion, pepper, and cabbage sales as they had previously earned in a year from staple crops.

Tracking these outcomes alongside measures of energy access can help show whether investments are translating into higher productivity and incomes.

Making greater use of existing multidimensional measures, alongside complementary indicators of development outcomes, could change not just how governments report progress but also how they plan and direct investment.

Rather than starting with how many fresh connections a project can deliver, governments and funders would ask what people and institutions need energy for, what prevents them from using it effectively, and which investments could remove those barriers. In some places, that may mean extending electricity supply. In others, it could mean improving reliability, lowering costs, or helping farmers and businesses obtain the equipment and financing needed to use energy productively.

It has been revealed that energy is essential to improving human well-being, but it is only one part of what drives development. Like water, health care or education and energy is necessary but not sufficient. Treating access as a starting point rather than an end goal—and measuring whether people can use, afford, and rely on the energy they receive—would give governments a clearer picture of whether energy investments are improving people’s lives.

It has been revealed that courtesy of WRI. Experts: Dimitris Mentis, Harsha Meenawat.

Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, Volkswagen is marking the 50th anniversary of the GTI by showing how uncompromising an electric GTI with motorsport ambitions can be. The concept car will be presented to the public next week at the Essen Motor Show (27 November to 6 December 2026). Its performance figures meet a two-door silhouette and flared wings as well as a large front splitter, diffuser and rear wing. The result: a powerful appearance and maximum downforce for fast laps. At the same time, the concept vehicle provides a preview of how the GTI idea can be further developed in the electric age.

Kai Grünitz, Member of the Board of Management for Technical Development, Volkswagen Brand and Brand Group Core: “The GTI has been one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years. This year, we launched our GTI as an electric vehicle in series production for the first time. With the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, we are showing how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world. Our platform strategy and MEB+ give us the technological freedom to make even extreme concepts possible.”.

Designed for performance. The design of the newly introduced ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the production model, the 166 kW (226 PS) ID. Polo GTI. In both models, the drive power is transmitted to the front axle. In the 270 kW (367 PS) ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, this power delivery is controlled – thanks in part to an electronically regulated front differential lock (VAQ) – so that the model reaches 100 km/h from a standstill in just 4.7 seconds with Launch Control. Like the drive system, the electrical infrastructure has also been adapted to the high performance of the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept. The 52 kWh high-voltage battery can provide up to 290 kW at short notice, enabling a top speed of 240 km/h. The DCC (adaptive chassis control) has also been tuned for use on the racetrack and ensures precise handling and high traction in conjunction with the front differential lock. The new ceramic brakes of the one-box brake system are also designed for high performance.

Dynamics are visible in the design. On the exterior, the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept follows the powerful clarity of the ID. Polo GTI production model, while at the same time incorporating design elements that underline the motorsport characteristics. Particularly striking features are the two-door instead of four-door silhouette, pronounced flaring of the wings by 50 millimetres in each case, a large motorsport splitter at the front, a wider rear end, a fresh diffuser and a rear wing in carbon fibre that protrudes above the roof line.

It has been revealed that two-seater. Reduced to racing. The interior is also tailored to the racetrack, and only the basic layout of the overall cockpit has been adopted from the production model. This means there is no infotainment system, for example. The focus is solely on ergonomics and driving. The driver and front passenger sit on Recaro racing bucket seats with red 5-point harnesses. The rear and luggage compartment have been completely cleared. Instead of a rear seat system, a rollover bar painted in the GTI colour Tornado Red is integrated above and behind the front seats. The dash panel, side trims and many other details are covered in dark ArtVelours microfibre fabric with red topstitching – work that has been carried out with great precision by Volkswagen trainees. In many areas – in keeping with Volkswagen tradition – the young employees were directly involved in realisation of the concept vehicle by the Development department and designers.

550 instead of 290 newton-metres. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept features the high-torque APP550 motor. The special technical challenge here: this motor is actually intended for the rear of large models such as the ID. Tiguan or ID.7. It therefore had to be fitted into the smaller ID. Polo as front-wheel drive and additionally combined with an electronic front differential lock. Thomas Schmall, Member of the Board of Management Volkswagen AG for Technology, and CEO of Volkswagen Group Components: “The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept demonstrates just how emotive electric mobility can be: This is made possible by our APP550, one of the most efficient electric drives in its class. Manufactured over one million times at the Group Components plant in Kassel, this drive was actually developed for larger vehicle classes. Integrating it into the Polo required millimetre precision and is a powerful example of engineering skill and teamwork at Volkswagen, from Development and Design through to our trainees who worked on the project.”.

In a recent development, GTI from the master of modular platforms. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the modular electric drive (MEB+) platform with front-wheel drive. Volkswagen has used the basic technical layout of the production model and taken it to a new level of performance with a 104 kW (141 PS) more powerful electric drive. The result is the most dynamic interpretation of a front-wheel drive ID. model to date. At the other end of the scale is the Mission Efficiency, which is also based on the ID. Polo and set four world records as a particularly efficient near-production electric vehicle. Both concept vehicles show the large bandwidth offered by electric drive systems from maximum sportiness to outstanding efficiency.

Industry observers note that 2026 is the year of the GTI. Following the Golf GTI EDITION 50, the upcoming ID.3 GTI (sales start early 2027) and the new ID. Polo GTI (available to order since October), the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is making its debut this year as the fourth new model under the umbrella of the iconic GTI product brand. No other compact sports car family has been as successful worldwide for half a century now – with more than 2.5 million units sold – as the GTI models.

energyRe Will Continue as Construction Manager Through Commercial Operation; Sale Reflects Strength of the Company’s South Carolina Development Platform; Transaction Expected to Close in First Quarter of 2027.

energyRe today revealed that it has agreed to sell 100% of a portfolio of utility-scale solar projects in South Carolina to Enel Green Power North America, Inc. (EGPNA). The projects have a combined total capacity of roughly 317 MWdc of fresh generating capacity across the Palmetto State. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to customary conditions, including required U.S. regulatory approvals.

“This transaction is a strong validation of the projects we have built in South Carolina and of the team that developed them,” remarked Ryan Brown, Chief Operating Officer at energyRe. “Enel Green Power is a world-class owner and operator, and we are pleased to hand these projects to a partner that shares our commitment to delivering reliable, affordable power to South Carolina homes and businesses. Our team will remain on the ground as construction manager to see these projects through to commercial operation.”.

As part of the transaction, energyRe will continue to serve as construction manager through commercial operation.

energyRe has broken ground on approximately 450 MW in the last year and has nearly 700 MW in operation or late-stage development. The manufacturer’s 1.8+ GW portfolio spans 20 projects in South Carolina, North Carolina, Nebraska, and Oklahoma.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • JJA ESS has launched its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations.
  • It has been revealed that according to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service.
  • A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JJA ESS has launched its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations. The platform is hosted in the company’s own cloud environment, giving the team direct responsibility for data policies, access permissions, and future updates.

It has been revealed that according to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service. Further requirements will follow.

A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery. A QR code and a unique identifier based on the ISO/IEC 15459 series connect the data record to the battery, enabling access to information throughout its entire lifecycle. This can include product identity, material composition, CO₂ footprint, recycled content, performance and durability, condition, supply chain due diligence, and end-of-life disposal. Taken together, these data points support consistent information management from product identification to the end of the product lifecycle.

It has been revealed that for manufacturers, the challenge lies not simply in creating a QR code. The data must be traceable back to its source, up-to-date, and accessible in accordance with regulatory and business requirements. Companies must also manage access to sensitive information and comply with regulations governing cross-border data transfers and trade secrets. This balance is particularly relevant for companies operating in multiple markets. When companies utilize a third-party platform, its functionality, access to data fields, and interoperability can be determined by the provider’s configuration and service model.

Sources indicate that JA ESS developed the platform internally and hosts it in its own cloud environment. Data policies, access permissions, and future platform updates are managed by the JA ESS internal team. This team ensures compliance with EU regulations regarding data access, presentation, and updates, while also giving JA ESS greater control over data management. The platform can also evolve as regulatory requirements change and real-world applications provide further insights.

Sources indicate that JA ESS is the energy storage business unit under the JA brand. As a central component of JA’s energy storage strategy, JA ESS offers a wide range of FTM and BTM applications with safe, efficient, intelligent, and customized solutions for the large-scale, commercial, and industrial sectors as well as the residential market.
