#409. 2027 Subaru Forester Wilderness Hybrid Is The Happy Wanderer

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1520 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

2027 Subaru Forester Wilderness Hybrid Is The Happy Wanderer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Subaru has a knack for making its vehicles incredibly capable right out of the box, but it also knows how to add extra garnishes to take things to the next level, like when it Wilderness-ified the standard Forester by bumping up the ride height and giving it all-terrain tires, more underbody protection, tougher exterior body panels and a slew of copper accents.
  • The hybrid powertrain offers more power, better fuel economy and a more refined drivetrain experience than the standard Wilderness' 2.5-liter boxer four-cylinder, while also affording the Forester a bit more off-road capability thanks to the added torque of an electric motor.
  • It makes it a bit hard to understand why the regular Forester Wilderness exists at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Subaru has a knack for making its vehicles incredibly capable right out of the box, but it also knows how to add extra garnishes to take things to the next level, like when it Wilderness-ified the standard Forester by bumping up the ride height and giving it all-terrain tires, more underbody protection, tougher exterior body panels and a slew of copper accents. Now Subaru is taking that notch up another notch by hybrid-ifying the Wilderness-ified Forester, resulting in — you guessed it — the 2027 Forester Wilderness Hybrid.

The hybrid powertrain offers more power, better fuel economy and a more refined drivetrain experience than the standard Wilderness' 2.5-liter boxer four-cylinder, while also affording the Forester a bit more off-road capability thanks to the added torque of an electric motor. Making things even sweeter is the fact that choosing the hybrid only adds $1,000 to the Forester Wilderness' MSRP, a delta that Subaru says will be overcome in just 2 years, or about 30,000 miles.

It makes it a bit hard to understand why the regular Forester Wilderness exists at all. The added fuel efficiency and comfort mean the Forester Wilderness Hybrid can do a seemingly endless amount of driving, exploring and wandering around, and it's absolutely happy to do so.

Recent findings suggest that full Disclosure: Subaru flew me out to central California, put me up in a very nice hotel and fed me, all so I could drive the 2027 Forester Wilderness Hybrid. They sourced me a lovely 2026 Ascent Touring to drive all the way from Chicago to New York when every flight in the U.S. was grounded, and I faced the prospect of spending a few days sleeping on the floor at O'Hare. For that reason, I am eternally grateful to both Aaron Cole and Miranda Jimenez.

There isn't much of a difference between the Forester Wilderness and Forester Wilderness Hybrid outside of the hybrid powertrain, but it does a hell of a lot to transform the character of Subie's compact crossover. Like in the non-Wilderness Forester Hybrid, Subaru teamed up an Atkinson-Miller-cycle 2.5-liter boxer four-cylinder with two motor-generator units inside the continuously variable transmission. One is used to stop and start the gas engine and charge the battery, while the other handles regenerative braking and sends actual drive power to all four wheels. They're fed by a 1.1-kWh battery that lives where the spare tire once was, which may be disappointing to some off-road enthusiasts who also love busting tires. However, that positioning means the hybrid has the same exact amount of rear cargo room as a regular Forester, which normal people are going to appreciate.

It has been revealed that they're also going to appreciate the extra power. The Forester Wilderness Hybrid pumps out 194 horsepower, a 14-hp improvement over the normal Forester Wilderness. Subaru gives no combined torque figures, but the gas motor puts out 154 pound-feet, and the electric motor produces its own 199 lb-ft. Either way you slice it, the numbers are stronger than the 178 lb-ft of torque from the normal Forester Wilderness. In typical Subaru fashion, the symmetrical all-wheel-drive system sends internal-combustion power to all four wheels — unlike the RAV4, which has no mechanical connection between the front and rear wheels — and that makes a huge difference off-road.

According to recent reports, gas mileage has never been a Subie strong suit, but the hybrid's fuel economy is also much improved to go along with its added performance. According to the EPA, the Forester Wilderness Hybrid will get 33 mpg city, 29 mpg highway and 31 mpg combined, improvements of 9 mpg, 1 mpg and 5 mpg, respectively. The EPA-expected driving range is also bumped up from 432 miles to 515 miles. Happy wanderer, indeed.

In a recent development, the Forester Wilderness' lovably ugly looks are still present, and the hybrid maintains the same 9.3 inches of ground clearance as its gas-only counterpart. It also gets the same 235/60R17 Yokohama Geolander All-Terrain tires, raised roof rails with 800 pounds of capacity, bronze interior and exterior design elements, and redesigned front and rear bumpers with increased approach, departure and breakover angles.

Hill descent control and Subaru's X-Mode system with Snow/Dirt and Deep Snow/Mud settings mean it's pretty much impossible to get this thing stuck; those two modes can basically be summed up as stuck and absolutely biffed. They allow the Forester Wilderness Hybrid to do pretty much anything off-road; at the very least, it can do things far beyond what anyone would expect from a car without a locking rear differential.

The majority of the time I drove the Forester Wilderness Hybrid was without any pavement below me on the seemingly endless acreage of Rancho Quien Sabe, and I've got to say, it was nearly boring in the way the SUV saw any obstacle in front of it and just traversed it without fuss or hesitation. The Forester happily trudged along, unbothered by what sort of terrain it was forced to deal with. In the rare moments where I found myself a bit more stuck than I thought I should be, all that was needed was a little bit of extra power, and the added torque of the electric motor pulled me out with ease. Aiding in that was the 180-degree front view monitor that helped me see where I was going, but while it was undoubtedly helpful, I can't help but think the resolution left a bit to be desired.

Industry observers note that I'm no fool, and I know that for all of its off-road prowess, the Forester Wilderness Hybrid will spend the majority of its life on road. Luckily, it's quite good there. Subaru did a good job of insulating the cabin so not too much road noise or rattly boxer sounds enter the cabin, and the more powerful drivetrain means it's even better at getting up to speed than the slightly anemic normal Forester Wilderness. It also comes as standard with all sorts of safety features, courtesy of Subaru's EyeSight suite of tech like emergency lane-keeping assist, emergency steering assist, blind spot detection, rear cross-traffic alert, reverse automated braking, and full-speed adaptive cruise control. (I was able to truly experience the highs of EyeSight during my 820-mile drive home in the Ascent).

Sources indicate that changes to the Forester Wilderness Hybrid are decidedly minimal on the inside, too. Drivers are still treated to a 10-way power seat, and in front of the steering wheel is a fairly customizable 12.3-inch gauge cluster screen that can display a full-screen map. Beside that in the middle is an 11.6-inch vertical infotainment screen, which is getting harder and harder to justify as the years pass — especially now that the new Outback is out, and its system is so good. Luckily, you can hook up wireless Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, but even they are a bit laggy, and glare is still prevalent when it's super sunny.

Screen woes aside, the animal-free interior is fairly well appointed for this type of vehicle. Dual-zone climate controls, a panoramic-ish sunroof, TomTom navigation, a heated steering wheel, four heated seats, a power tailgate, all-weather floor mats and an 11-speaker Harman/Kardon stereo are all standard on the Forester Wilderness Hybrid.

Space is also very solid for the class. I had more than enough room to fit comfortably behind myself at 6-foot-1, and there's 33.1 cubic feet of room behind the second row for all of your Outdoor Activity Crap. If you somehow need more room for your Outdoor Activity Crap, drop the second row, and that space increases to 64.1 cubic feet. If that somehow still isn't enough for your Outdoor Activity Crap, you can strap 800 pounds to the roof (statically). There are enough interesting materials choices and quality-feeling items that you won't feel too silly about the cost.

Subaru claims the 2027 Forester Wilderness Hybrid starts at $41,970, including destination, and that's pretty much where pricing ends, as well. Outside of a few optional paint colors, there aren't any packages you'll be able to add to the Wilderness Hybrid. What you see is what you get. Nice and easy. And as I mentioned before, it's just $1,000 more than the standard Forester Wilderness. There's a hard deal to beat.

The Forester Hybrid Wilderness has a real can-do attitude to it. It's a real billy goat of a car — one that takes a licking and keeps on kicking, happily coming back for more. When driving, it was as if the Forester was whistling a little tune to itself as I mashed the throttle, forcing it to traverse up a hill a compact crossover has no business going up.

No, it doesn't have the best infotainment in the world and it's not a classically "beautiful" vehicle, but it has something most cars don't: character. The Forester Wilderness Hybrid wants to get lost with you, and all you need to do is make sure you've got the time to get lost with it, because with over 500 miles of driving range, you can get lost for a long, long time.

#408. From Social Leasing to Social Fleets: A Proposed Law Lends Credibility to the Goal of One Million Affordable Electric Cars

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (592 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica

From Social Leasing to Social Fleets: A Proposed Law Lends Credibility to the Goal of One Million Affordable Electric Cars

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Social leasing could soon change in scale, name, and business model.
  • Several presidential candidates have made reaching one million vehicles (or even more) one of the hallmarks of their campaigns¹.
  • The current system cannot simply be scaled up twentyfold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Social leasing could soon change in scale, name, and business model. The bill introduced by MP Christine Arrighi aims to create a public service offering one million “low-cost electric vehicles” (ALM). Scheduled for December 3rd in the National Assembly, its examination is expected to place at the heart of the debate a now crucial question: how to make social leasing sustainable and widespread?

Several presidential candidates have made reaching one million vehicles (or even more) one of the hallmarks of their campaigns¹. While this convergence is excellent news, the battle of figures says nothing about how to achieve this goal.

The current system cannot simply be scaled up twentyfold. Its cost per vehicle, intermittent financing, imperfect social targeting, lack of a guaranteed solution after three years, and the resale risks borne by dealerships are all structural limitations. The 2026 edition also revealed its dependence on Renault and Stellantis, which can at any time restrict volumes to favor more profitable traditional sales.

It has been revealed that the proposed law changes its approach. Sponsored by MP Christine Arrighi, it draws inspiration from the proposals of T&E France and Bernard Julien, stemming from their study on the future of social leasing, published in June 2026.

In this new model, the government would directly purchase the vehicles at an average net cost of €15,000. These vehicles would be kept for twelve years in a public fleet and leased successively to one or more households for an average monthly rent of €150 before being resold. The day-to-day management of the fleet would be delegated to groups of public or private operators within the local areas.

Sources indicate that the initial investment to build the fleet would be financed by borrowing, with a maximum outstanding amount of €7.8 billion in 2035. Lease payments and resales, supplemented by €350 million in annual public support (equivalent to the current social leasing budget), would cover service costs and repay the debt within eighteen years. By then, the system would be self-financing, and the state would own one million cars worth approximately €10 billion.

Industry observers note that “This model is much more beneficial for public finances,” explains Diane Strauss, director of T&E France. “It requires an initial funding effort, but it eventually pays for itself. Instead of subsidizing at a loss, we build up an asset that generates its own revenue. This is what makes the move to a million vehicles financially viable.”.

In addition to providing long-term protection for low-income motorists against rising and volatile fuel prices, the proposal represents a genuine industrial planning policy. The announcement of a public order for two million vehicles over twenty years (including fleet renewal) would indeed give the French automotive sector the visibility necessary to invest and prepare for the future.

According to recent reports, “This will also allow us to direct our production towards the vehicles that households truly need: affordable, fuel-efficient, repairable electric cars, produced in France and Europe,” concludes Léo Larivière, automotive transition expert at T&E France. “This proposal must now open a substantive discussion among all stakeholders. It is high time to prepare the next steps for one of the rare examples of policies that reconcile climate, social justice, and industrial planning.”.

It has been revealed that ¹ Raphaël Glucksmann and Marine Tondelier aim for one million vehicles. Jean-Luc Mélenchon proposes a public fleet of 1.4 million cars by 2032, and François Ruffin raises the target to three million. Gabriel Attal and Dominique de Villepin also advocate expanding social leasing, without specifying a target.

Industry observers note that residents of Newly introduced Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief. A dangerous menace to society has been taken off the streets after police apprehended a 75-year-old man accused of leading deputies on a high-stakes electric bike chase at speeds reaching a blistering 16 mph (26 km/h).

According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.

What followed was apparently the world’s slowest police chase.

Mitchell reportedly continued riding along the beach, eventually exiting onto city streets, where he allegedly rode against traffic before making it back to his home. Deputies followed him, and when Mitchell attempted to retreat into his garage, he reportedly resisted arrest by grabbing onto a golf cart and refusing to let go.

The ordeal ended with Mitchell in custody, facing four charges, including felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area. His bond was set at $4,000.

And just like that, another dangerous electric bicycle criminal was brought to justice. This was clearly a success story like no other, and American streets are now safer.

Sources indicate that now, before anyone gets too worked up, let’s be clear: I’m not suggesting that e-bike riders should be allowed to ignore traffic laws, endanger pedestrians, or flee from police. Reports indicate that Mitchell was riding recklessly around beachgoers, including children, and that’s certainly something worth addressing. And once he allegedly decided to flee from deputies, he turned what could have been a minor infraction into a much more serious situation.

But can we also acknowledge how absurd this whole thing is?

We’ve reached a point where a 75-year-old man riding a bicycle at 16 mph can end up the subject of a police pursuit and felony charges, while we’ve largely accepted that multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and seriously injure people on our roads as an unavoidable cost of modern transportation.

Sources indicate that every day, drivers speed through neighborhoods, roll through stop signs, stare at their phones, and operate vehicles capable of killing pedestrians with a moment’s inattention. Or perhaps I shouldn’t say ‘capable’, but rather that they do. 40,000 people every year die in the US from car violence. Yet somehow, electric bicycles have become one of the great transportation menaces of our time, despite contributing much, much less to major bodily harm or death.

And yes, there are absolutely legitimate concerns about dangerous riding. I’ve repeatedly argued that we need better enforcement, especially when it comes to teenagers riding high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths. Those aren’t electric bicycles, and treating them as such has created a real problem for everyone.

But if we’re going to devote police resources to cracking down on dangerous two-wheeled behavior, perhaps we could start there instead of turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century.

What is absurd is that he didn't simply stop and follow the officer's directions to slow down. If he is going to try to flee from the police by riding dangerously including going against traffic then he should face charges. As presumably a first time offender, he'll be given probation if he agrees not to do it again.

To be fair, Mitchell’s alleged behavior after being stopped certainly didn’t help his case. But the larger point remains: our priorities around road safety have become wildly distorted.

We’ve normalized the dangers of cars so thoroughly that we barely blink at the daily carnage they cause, yet we’re increasingly treating comparatively low-speed electric bicycles as an existential threat to public safety.

Industry observers note that I’m all for enforcing sensible e-bike rules. I’m all for throwing the book at major infractions and scofflaws who pose a public menace. But I’m also for applying a little perspective.

Because if a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph is among our most pressing transportation safety concerns, then I have some very good news about the state of our roads. But unfortunately, there is no good news to share today.

Industry observers note that the first American-made electric BMW is now being assembled at the manufacturer’s plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina. It’s a significant moment for the German automaker in the U.S., but it’s just the beginning of a much larger initiative, which will include no fewer than six U.S.-built EVs by the end of the decade.

According to recent reports, roughly 70 iX5 electric SUVs are rolling off the assembly line every day, alongside gas, diesel, and hybrid-powered models. All X5 powertrain versions are based on the same architecture, enabling the car manufacturer to share the same assembly line for multiple fuel types.

2027 BMW iX5 production in Spartanburg, South Carolina.

According to recent reports, initially, BMW’s goal was to build no fewer than 100,000 iX5s in 2027 in Spartanburg, but that target has reportedly been revised to 60,000, according to Automotive News. The automaker has not provided production volume estimates for the iX5, but a firm representative stated that roughly one in four X5s will be electric for the near future.

In a recent development, “Currently, the market is looking like 20-25 percent EVs for the immediate three months,” noted Kavit Antani, general manager of vehicle assembly. “As the market sees these vehicles come through, it might shift.”.

Suppliers have reportedly been given a target of 175,000 EVs in 2028 and 2029, but that’s still a long way from now, and judging from what has happened in the American electric car market in the previous two years, the target could shift significantly.

The batteries that power the upcoming iX5 come from a new plant 15 miles away in Woodruff, where the first mass-produced packs started their journey to Spartanburg to be fitted to finished chassis earlier this week.

It has been revealed that the first Gen6 cylindrical cells used in completed packs will be sourced from AESC in China, BMW confirmed for Automotive News, but the German automaker will switch suppliers toward the end of the decade. LG Energy Solution will supply the car manufacturer’s facilities in the U.S. with locally made cells, while Samsung SDI will supply European factories.

In a recent development, BMW is not backing down from its plan to build six EVs in America by 2030. The iX5 is the first, and it will likely be followed by the iX7, iX6, and a performance-oriented iX5 M, according to BMW Blog.

It has been revealed that the 2027 BMW iX5 is powered by a 144-kilowatt-hour battery that can be recharged from 10% to 80% in 22 minutes. Its estimated range sits at an impressive 450 miles, while its dual-motor powertrain delivers 570 horsepower and 594 pound-feet of torque. Pricing starts at $79,800.

We know you're an automotive enthusiast if you're a regular Jalopnik reader, which means you probably have a pretty good recollection of the very first time you ever drove a car. I'm not certain what the statute of limitations is for driving a car without a license, so hopefully you don't perjure yourself by sharing your story, because we want to hear all about it! Share the story of the first time you ever drove a car in the comments section below.

RuPaul actually inspired this question. On social media he recently told the story of the first time he ever drove a car at 11-years-old, when he stole the keys to his dad's 1966 Toyota Corona and drove it around Cerritos, California. RuPaul describes himself as someone who's obsessed with cars, and I know most of us Jalops would describe ourselves in a similar fashion. That's why we want to know the story of the first time you ever drove a car.

I'm not sure that I've even shared this story with my friends or family, but sharing it here seems like a good idea. I don't remember my exact age at the time, but I know I was in middle school, so it was definitely before I should have legally been behind the wheel. Still, I'd been practicing my driving in my conscious and unconscious mind for at least a decade before this, so I felt ready.

One fateful summer day at Model Boat Shop (don't laugh, it was really fun), a friend's older sister came to pick him up, but her boyfriend was the one who drove. Along with my brother, our conniving, car-obsessed minds hatched a brilliant proposal to strongarm this poor high school kid into letting us drive his green second-generation Nissan Altima. We convinced him it would earn him brownie points with his girlfriend if he'd let her little brother and his friends drive his car, and he bought it, hook line and sinker.

He took us to a nearby parking lot and let us loose, and I have the most distinct memory of doing incredibly safe and not-at-all dangerous acceleration runs and panic brake evaluations in that parking lot while the owner of the car looked on in horror. Thankfully nobody got hurt and nobody got sued, but that joyous memory was the first time I drove a car. What's your story?

Recent findings suggest that commercial property owners invest in solar and battery storage to manage energy costs and strengthen resilience. One question can shape that investment from the start. Who pays when equipment needs repairs years after installation?

Solar Insure today expanded its SI-Commercial Suite with two fresh warranties. SI-Commercial Battery is a 20-year limited warranty for commercial battery storage systems, and SI-Commercial Total covers solar and battery storage under one warranty. Together with the existing SI-Commercial Solar warranty, these additions allow Certified Providers to offer protection tailored to each project, whether it includes solar, battery storage, or both. It’s about giving property owners greater confidence not just in the installation, but in the years of ownership that follow.”.

A failed inverter or declining battery capacity can lead to costs an owner did not budget for. Even when a manufacturer covers replacement equipment, the owner may still be responsible for labor and service costs. The expanded suite helps Certified Providers explain which repair expenses are covered so customers can evaluate their potential repair costs alongside system performance and installation price.

“Commercial battery owners are making a long-term investment, but some of the most significant expenses can emerge years after installation,” noted Dean Chiaravallotti, Chief Revenue Officer at Solar Insure. “A battery replacement or unexpected repair can change the financial picture of a project. When providers can explain how they address those costs before the customer signs, they help buyers make a more informed investment decision. That’s the value we’re bringing to commercial storage.”.

Sources indicate that solar companies must become Solar Insure Certified Providers to offer SI-Commercial warranties. Certification includes a review of the company’s qualifications, business practices, and commitment to customer service.

Recent findings suggest that for qualifying claims, Solar Insure pays covered repair costs directly to the Certified Provider or service provider performing the work. If the original installer is no longer available, Solar Insure helps coordinate next steps, which may include identifying another qualified service provider. When a property changes hands, coverage transfers to the new owner at no cost.

According to recent reports, “A lot can change over the life of a commercial energy system. Properties change hands, service providers change, and equipment eventually needs attention,” remarked Chiaravallotti. “Property owners need to know what happens w          hen those changes occur. Our goal is to give them a clearer path forward, with protection and support that extend well beyond the original installation.”.

Solar companies can contact Solar Insure to learn about becoming a Certified Provider. Commercial property owners can speak with a Solar Insure Certified Provider about which warranty fits their project.

In a recent development, solar Insure is a leading provider of solar and storage warranties, focused on protecting long-term system performance and elevating accountability across the renewable energy industry. Through rigorous provider certification and governance, Solar Insure delivers durable protection that residential and commercial installers can stand behind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you wake up tomorrow as the esteemed Lord Mayor of London, you’ll want to make a properly dignified entrance. To make sure your arrival turns the right heads, Electrogenic has taken the Mayor’s 1973 Roll-Royce Phantom VI and turned it into a properly traditional standard-bearer with modern electric power.

The stately, stylish, and silent electric Rolls-Royce car made its public debut at last month’s Salon Privé weekend at Blenheim Palace, where it joined a growing fleet of classic Rollers that have received Elctrogenic’s electric conversion, including the stunning Mulliner-bodied 1929 Phantom II that we covered back in 2023.

It has been revealed that for this project, Electrogenic carefully removed the internal combustion-based engine, transmission, and fuel system from the City of London Corporation’s official ’73 Phantom VI limo and replaced it with a 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motor putting out 310 Nm (~230 lb-ft) of torque. Sharp-eyed readers will note those numbers are significantly lower than what you’d expect from the 6.2L L410 V8 fitted with twin SU carburetors (as it was in the standard ’73 IV), but since those numbers were never officially published, we would say that the power available from the upcoming electric drivetrain is similarly adequate for Mayoral use.

Power for the electric motor comes from a 62 kWh li-ion battery fitted under the hood bonnet, and offers more than enough range to get the Lord Mayor to their appointments in and around the city.

To ensure the heads of the heads of the city don’t bob in an undignified manner while on parade, Electrogenic added a “ceremonial” drive mode that trims power and torque and softens the throttle map, so the chauffeur can more easily hold the crawling pace demanded by civic processions and state occasions.

“We were honored to be asked to electrify this significant motor car, and to play a part in the City of London Corporation’s journey to net zero,” indicates Steve Drummond, chief executive of Electrogenic. “When it was released in the late 1960s, the Rolls-Royce VI was the most refined and dignified limousine on the road. Now, thanks to electrification, its core character has been enhanced further: it is whisper quiet, effortless to drive with swift performance, and emits zero tailpipe emissions.”.

Only Phantom VIs were built, with this 3 meter-long coach-built limousine having been commissioned during the mayoralty of Alderwoman Dame Susan Langley DBE, the 697th Lord Mayor of the City of London. The Phantom was converted as part of the Corporation’s broader effort to achieve a net zero carbon emissions goal from its own operations in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In just over two years after the manufacturer was founded, it already has 224 operational sites across dozens of states.
  • According to recent reports, the company on Wednesday opened its largest and fanciest charging location in the U.S., in Westminster, California.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ionna, the electric vehicle charging consortium backed by major U.S. automakers including General Motors and Toyota, is growing its footprint in the U.S. at an astonishing pace.

In just over two years after the manufacturer was founded, it already has 224 operational sites across dozens of states. Now, it’s announcing a new flagship location, better access for the growing pool of Tesla drivers, more powerful stations, and discounted charging rates for Jeep, Dodge, and Fiat EV drivers.

According to recent reports, the company on Wednesday opened its largest and fanciest charging location in the U.S., in Westminster, California. The new Rechargery has 22 stalls and is full of amenities.

Recent findings suggest that it has canopies over the charging bays, outdoor seating, and a dedicated driver lounge. That's not it. You also get an arcade machine and round the clock access to Wi-Fi, coffee machine, and restrooms.

Seth Cutler, the CEO of Ionna, told InsideEVs in an interview that the tech giant partnered with Amazon to build a 900-square-foot convenience store at the location which features the e-commerce giant’s Just Walk Out technology.

It lets customers tap their card while entering and directly walk out after shopping without having to stand in line or physically pay through a payment terminal.

“We're moving really fast to build this network up and provide a differentiated experience for customers,” Cutler said.

Sources indicate that he added that multiple EVs can simultaneously charge at their maximum speeds at this station. Because it is backed by a whopping 4 megawatts of grid power, there are practically no power constraints for every day EV drivers.

In a recent development, “You could have 10 Lucid Gravitys and they can all pull 400 kilowatts,” Cutler said. “There’s only load management at the charger level,” he added.

Sources indicate that that charger-level limit comes from how the hardware is set up. Each Ionna charging tower can deliver up to 400 kW, and each tower has two cables serving two parking spots.

If only one car is plugged in, the charger can dispense the full 400 kW, as long as the car can accept that speed. If two cars are plugged into the same tower, they share that 400 kW between them. The towers don’t draw from each other, so one busy tower never slows down the one next to it.

Recent findings suggest that that means drivers can get back rapidly on the road and the chance of long queues building up are less. In other words, you spend more time driving and less time charging.

The firm is also preparing for future EVs that push the boundaries of ultra-fast charging speeds, at least for non-Chinese automakers.

According to recent reports, cutler said groundwork had already started to build 500-kilowatt stations in the U.S. Its current network comprises 400 kW-capable Alpitronic Hyperchargers, which are plenty quick by their own right.

He didn’t say when and where exactly these new chargers will open, but he added that the probable timeline is 2028 when more EVs on the market will actually be able to benefit from such high charging speeds.

Only a handful of EVs in the U.S. can currently accept even 400 kilowatts, let alone 500 kW. The Lucid Gravity, Porsche Cayenne Electric, and the BMW iX3 are capable of accepting 400 kW.

The upcoming Mercedes AMG GT will be able to charge at 600 kW when deliveries start next year. Owners have reported the Tesla Cybertruck pulling 500 kW for a brief window at the newer V4 Superchargers capable of dispensing such speeds.

That said, Tesla drivers can now get auto charge at Ionna stations using fleet charging manufacturer Presto's app. Plug & Charge is already enabled at Ionna for BMW, General Motors, Toyota, Volvo, Rivian, Ford, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and Volvo.

Downloading another smartphone app, however, might be unnecessary for Tesla drivers who already use the ubiquitous Supercharger network.

Sources indicate that starting in December, Ionna is also offering a 10% discount for EVs under the Stellantis umbrella. So drivers with the Jeep Wagoneer S, Dodge Charger Daytona, and the Fiat 500e will benefit from lower charging rates. If they have a connected services subscription, they get an additional 15% discount at Ionna taking the total to 25%.

Recent findings suggest that and finally, Ionna’s network is now dense enough for coast-to-coast road trips just using Ionna charging stations. That’s something the firm demonstrated this week with multiple drivers that set-off from Fresh York, Raleigh, and Miami among other cities in a journey that culminated in California.

It’s a major achievement that proves that even though EV sales are up and down, the country’s charging network is growing promptly and is now better than ever.

#399. Tesla unveils 7.4 MW Powercore to take on ex-exec Baglino’s Heron Link

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tesla unveils 7.4 MW Powercore to take on ex-exec Baglino’s Heron Link

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit.
  • Industry observers note that it’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027.
  • According to recent reports, update: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center aims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW (9 MVA) continuously at 34.5 kV, with grid-forming support up to 10 MVA of peak power.

Industry observers note that it’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027. That’s the same year Heron Power, the startup founded by Tesla’s former top engineer Drew Baglino, aims to start volume production of its own solid-state transformer, the Heron Link.

According to recent reports, update: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center aims. We’ve updated the article with the new details.

Tesla first said it would build its own transformers in September 2025, when it unveiled Megapack 3 and Megablock. Megablock connects four Megapack 3 units to a transformer and switchgear, but Tesla shared next to nothing about the transformer itself.

Powercore is that missing piece. Tesla unveiled it today through its Tesla Megapack account on X:.

Introducing PowercoreSolid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak powerMade in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf.

About an hour later, Tesla followed up with a much longer post on X laying out the full spec sheet:.

It also packs a built-in solid-state medium-voltage breaker that Tesla claims clears faults up to 1,000x faster than a conventional breaker. There’s no flammable oil, and it’s modular, so components can be serviced in the field without swapping the whole unit.

Tesla is pitching one product for three markets: battery storage, utility-scale solar, and 800 Vdc data centers. For Megablock, Powercore replaces the current two-step setup, where Megapack’s inverters output 480 V AC before a separate transformer steps it up to medium voltage. Tesla notes that old architecture had twice the losses. For solar, Powercore works as a central inverter for today’s 1,500 Vdc arrays and upcoming 2,000 Vdc systems.

Tesla still hasn’t shared pricing, customers, or a factory location. It only says Powercore will be made in the US “of U.S. and imported parts” with first units operating in 2027.

Industry observers note that the idea behind a solid-state transformer is simple enough. A typical solar or battery project uses low-voltage inverters to convert DC into AC, then a major oil-filled, iron-core transformer to step that up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit does both jobs with silicon carbide power electronics, which means less gear, a smaller footprint, and active control over voltage and frequency. That control is what “grid-forming” means: the unit can help hold the grid steady instead of just following it.

And with lead times on conventional transformers stretching into years as data centers and renewable projects pile into interconnection queues, there’s real demand for an alternative.

You can’t look at Powercore without thinking of Heron Power.

Baglino spent 18 years at Tesla and finished as SVP of powertrain and energy, in charge of batteries, motors, power electronics, and energy products. He left in April 2024 and launched Heron Power in 2025 to build solid-state transformers.

It has been revealed that he brought a lot of Tesla’s power electronics talent with him. As we reported when Tesla first announced its transformer plans, Heron hired engineers who led power electronics design for Powerwall 3, the next-gen Megapack, and Superchargers, along with the person who ran Tesla’s power electronics controls team for charging and energy products.

It has been revealed that since then, Heron has raised a $38 million Series A, a $140 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and Breakthrough Energy Ventures, and a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital. Former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn sits on its board, and Tesla co-founder JB Straubel is an investor.

In a recent development, it’s also building Heron Factory One, a 286,000-square-foot plant in Morgan Hill, California, designed to make 10,000 Heron Links a year. That’s over 40 GW of annual capacity, with commercial production planned for late 2027.

It has been revealed that and the customers are lining up. Vantage reserved more than 1 GW for its data centers, Intersect reserved 1.5 GW, LG Energy Solution Vertech is integrating Heron Link with its US-made battery systems, and RWE signed a pilot to install Heron Links at a Texas battery storage site in April 2027. Baglino says Heron has 50 GW of orders in the pipeline.

Here’s how the two compare based on what each tech giant has disclosed:.

Industry observers note that on paper, Powercore is the bigger box, and now it has the better numbers too. At 7.4 MW continuous, it carries about 50% more power per unit than the 5 MW Heron Link, and its 98.86% peak efficiency edges out Heron’s 98.6%. But Tesla’s figure is a peak number, and Heron doesn’t label its own as one, so it’s not quite apples to apples. Neither manufacturer has shared pricing.

Tesla is also going straight at Heron’s data center pitch. Powercore converts medium voltage directly to 800 Vdc, the rack architecture Nvidia is pushing, and Tesla says it’s working with Nvidia on 800 Vdc designs. Heron’s data center version does the same 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion with built-in storage, and data centers make up about a third of its business. Tesla’s answer to the storage piece is Megapack on the DC bus, and it says it already has 10 GWh of Megapack running at data centers.

This one is a little awkward for Tesla.

A significant chunk of the people who designed Tesla’s power electronics over the last decade now work at Heron, and the guy who ran the whole org is its CEO. Tesla’s energy business also lost its longtime leader, Mike Snyder, last month, according to the WSJ.

Recent findings suggest that this is all wrong. Tesla started developing this 3 years ago. Before Heron. The team selling Powercore is same as Megapack that has a way larger customer base than Heron. Also Heron is not a bankable tech giant per project finance terms. So they will struggle to get projects financed through equity and senior debt . Not as Tesla.

According to recent reports, to be fair, Tesla still has plenty of power electronics expertise. Its silicon carbide inverters are in millions of cars and every Megapack. And it has something Heron doesn’t: a massive installed base and a sales channel. Tesla claims it’s almost sold out of Megapacks for 2027, and bundling Powercore into Megablock is an easy upsell. Plenty of developers will take the one-stop shop.

Industry observers note that tesla’s specs now match or beat Heron’s on paper. But Heron has named customers, a pilot site with an install date, and a factory under construction. Tesla has none of those yet. I wouldn’t be surprised if Heron is actually ahead here.

But either way, the transformer shortage is significant enough for both companies to sell everything they can build.

As data centers and latest solar and battery projects pile onto the grid, utilities are scrambling for equipment and passing those costs on to ratepayers. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, is presently losing her seat.
  • Upgrade: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result.
  • Christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, is presently losing her seat.

Upgrade: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result. As of now, with 100% of votes counted, Foxx is losing by 362 votes, but has requested a recount. We’re updating this article with the most current information on the race below.

Christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker. Christian chose his Congressional representative, 83 year old Virginia Foxx.

Foxx is an 11-term Congresswoman in North Carolina, one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation, and was expected to win a 12th term in the heavily republican district, having previously proudly touted an endorsement from an enemy of the US who tried to overthrow the government. Her opponent is Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist and native of the district.

It has been revealed that for the topic of his letter, Christian chose electric cars – which is what makes this story relevant to us here at Electrek. Christian laid out several points about EVs, stating that “they’re better than normal cars. They’re better for the environment. They pay less. And there’s no gas.” (All true! well done Christian).

Christian suggested that electric cars could be incentivized with a $5,000 tax rebate – lower than the $7.5k EVs used to get, but better than the $0 they get federally today (compare to the ~$20k in ignored costs that gas cars still benefit from).

Christian went on to suggest action on climate change, stating “maybe there is still a chance for 6.5 million people to not die anymore and for the weather to get better just maybe glaciers stop melting.” Christian was probably referring to the number of people who die from air pollution globally each year (though several estimates suggest that number is actually higher, and Christian did conflate climate and weather… but we’ll give him a pass on this one, his heart is in the right place).

According to recent reports, christian was proud of his letter, as was his mother, Emily Mango, who said “he researched, cited facts, and made good arguments in his essay – an essay that had nothing to do with politics. He was proud of his essay.”.

But then he got a response, and that’s when things took a turn for the worse. Christian’s mother Emily angrily shared the response on Instagram, where it gained traction.

Emily noted Foxx’s screed was “disrespectful, hostile and unkind” and called it “demoralizing and reprehensible.” She said she had to speak to her son and teach him that this response was “not okay,” and that “nobody should talk to a child like that and nobody should talk to a teacher like that.”.

I’d also add that it’s full of disinformation, and that it even seems to brag about the massive debt that Foxx has imposed on Christian’s generation.

According to recent reports, foxx includes six links, all from propaganda publications that deny the science of climate change. 3 are from from WSJ (2 of which are opinion pieces) and 1 is from Fox, both of which are owned by the same climate denier, Rupert Murdoch. 1 is from Washington Times, a tabloid founded by a religious cult (yes, really), and 1 is from another right-wing climate denying publication, National Review.

Notably, none of the six links have anything to do with electric cars.

In the text of the response, Foxx touts republicans’ “all of the above” energy policy, which is ironic given that the party whose energy policy she touts has spent most of the last year forcing broken dirty coal plants open (which they are still doing after ruled illegal) and trying to shut down clean cheap ones. Apparently “all of the above” is code for “fossil fuels and nothing else.”.

Foxx’s letter does not directly address the strengths of electric cars, despite them being the subject of Christian’s letter. Notably, EVs actually can receive energy from any generation method, whether it be wind, solar, or even coal or gas – whereas gas-powered vehicles can only use one type of energy, oil. Thus, an “all of the above” strategy should probably find EVs the preferable route for transportation.

But in apparent contradiction to Foxx’s surely sincerely held belief that we should pursue an “all of the above” energy policy – which electric cars would help to achieve – she in fact has voted against EVs when given the opportunity.

Foxx claims in her response that she can’t support tax credits on electric cars, because those go to “mostly people with higher incomes who are able to purchase ‘new’ electric cars.”.

But she in fact voted against, and later voted to repeal, incentives which were limited to lower-income-earners and were only available on cars up to a certain MSRP cap. Further, they were available on used vehicles, not just newly introduced ones – suggesting that Foxx doesn’t know what she voted against.

Foxx was one of 218 republicans to vote in favor of a ~$4 trillion giveaway to wealthy elites. Her vote raised electric bills and threatened US energy security and surrendered US manufacturing jobs to China. Some of the money given away to wealthy elites in the bill was clawed back from energy efficiency programs that had been going to regular Americans.

Industry observers note that those energy efficiency programs had been instituted by the Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden-era law which established tax credits for EVs and other efficiency rebates. The Inflation Reduction Act was actually revenue positive, which is to say it reduced the national debt (by $238B), rather than adding to it, because of provisions to increase enforcement against wealthy tax cheats.

But most of the IRA was repealed by the bill that Foxx voted for, meaning the US lost out on those deficit reductions. All in all, the bill Foxx voted for would add $4 trillion to the national debt – which, incidentally, is another point Foxx touches on in her response.

In one sentence, she seems to directly mock Christian, telling him that “YOU and your classmates will be responsible for that debt” as part of a warning about the dangers of government debt.

But I read this sentence as mockery, rather than as a sincere warning, given that Foxx voted to add $4 trillion to the national debt, which she, at 83 years old, knows she will not have to pay off. Christian, who is 10, will likely spend his whole life saddled with the debt Foxx voted for.

He will also have to pay for her inaction on climate change, which will have increasingly worse effects on the world Christian will grow up into. Foxx’s generation has already felt the heat, with the massive floods that devastated her state in 2024, from a hurricane that was made 200x more likely due to climate change. Now, imagine how much worse it could get if Foxx’s policies remained in place until 72 years from now when Christian will be her age.

Foxx then closes out the letter with disparaging remarks about teachers, claiming that they are “too interested in indoctrinating you,” and warning Christian about “propaganda.” Which I guess indicates where Foxx’s attitude comes from – if she has spent her 83 years never trusting anyone who knows more than her about a topic, that would certainly lead to the ignorance reflected in her letter.

Foxx – who somehow has a doctorate in education and right now sits on the Congressional education committee – could have turned this into a nice moment to teach the child who wrote her something about democracy and responsive government, but instead turned it into a moment to teach the world what’s wrong with her.

When we first wrote this article, Foxx had a projected 97% chance of winning in a district which voted for her by a 19% margin in 2024.

But that was before America (and its short memory) was reminded of how incapable republicans are of leading anything.

Sources indicate that after a pile of economic crises caused by Donald Trump’s incompetent “leadership,” and his continued participation in an 8-month-and-counting war of choice that is spiking energy prices worldwide, bringing oil profits to record highs (and attempting to distract the news from talking about the Epstein files, which he is heavily featured in and has tried to cover up), America was once again fed up. And his incompetence took his entire party down with him.

Safe republican seats were flipped around the country in the biggest “wave” election we’ve seen in recent times, with the Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate.

And it looks like Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a Wilkes county native and former journalist, who also ran against Foxx in 2024, will now get his chance to represent the people of North Carolina’s 5th district… assuming a recount goes in his favor.

The situation in North Carolina is particularly interesting, given that republicans had done an emergency redraw of district lines in an attempt to cheat their way to winning more seats.

Generally, district lines get redrawn after each Census, which happens on the decade mark, rather than mid-decade. But republicans saw ahead of time that they were likely to lose the House due to their unpopularity, and wanted to fudge the numbers in several states instead of going for a fair fight.

Recent findings suggest that foxx’s main argument against Christian’s suggested $5,000 EV incentive, is increasing national debt. Yet in just one tax bill, her approval increases the national debt over 10%. This is not Christian’s “responsibility”, this burden is forced on him, along with climate change.

Recent findings suggest that so they engaged in Gerrymandering, a process wherein district lines are redrawn to favor a particular political party. The idea is to put as many of your opponents’ votes into a few safe seats as possible, while spreading out your own votes to a wider range of seats that you win each by a small margin.

Recent findings suggest that but it turns out that republicans were even more unpopular than they thought, and as a result, their Gerrymandering backfired. Those narrow margins they sought ended up flipping more seats than would have otherwise flipped, turning North Carolina almost completely blue in what analysts have called a “Dummymander“. (NC-5 itself was not one of the redrawn districts, though – it just swung 19 whole points to the Dems).

In a recent development, that said: the race is not over yet. The deadline to request a recount is today, and sure enough, Foxx has done so. The current margin is extremely thin, just 0.12% of votes, so things could certainly change in a recount. Foxx also vowed to run again in 2028, hoping for a less hostile political environment. She will be 85 years old at the time of that election.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric vehicle built in the US, promising an estimated up to 456 miles of range, ultra-fast charging speeds, and plenty of Neue Klasse tech.

BMW officially opened its fresh Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) electric vehicle batteries.

The Gen6 batteries will power BMW’s upcoming “X” electric vehicles, starting with the all-latest iX5 SUV.

The iX5 is being built about 15 miles away at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, the organization’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the US.

BMW Plant Spartanburg is churning out around 70 iX5s a day following a $1.7 billion investment in South Carolina to expand the plant for EV production and build the new battery assembly plant in Woodruff.

According to Robert Engelhorn, president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing in Spartanburg, the organization is confident the iX5 will attract buyers, promising 435 miles of range, ultra-fast charging, and its updated Neue Klasse technology and design.

Engelhorn told Automotive News in an interview that “there’s a clear trend globally for EVs,” adding that “We will contribute to this growth from the BMW side.”.

BMW didn’t provide a specific production estimate for the iX5, but suppliers were reportedly told it would be around 60,000 EVs in 2027, down from 100,000 it initially forecasted.

“We stated we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment,” Engelhorn said.

A manufacturer spokesperson confirmed that the iX5 will initially use battery cells from China before switching to US-sourced cells from LG Energy Solutions plant in Arizona by the end of the decade.

With production now underway, the iX5 is expected to begin arriving at US dealerships in early 2027.

The 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800. BMW estimates the 144 kWh battery will provide up to 456 miles of range, up from the 435 miles it previously estimated.

In a recent development, it features BMW’s latest “double-X” light signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights, and turn signals into one unit. The Double-X headlights come standard, but BMW remarked you can switch them for simpler diagonal stripes.

Last month, BMW showcased the i5’s ultra-fast-charging capabilities during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic.

During the demo, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add an impressive up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The electric SUV features a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain setup that delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse design and tech, like the smaller iX3 SUV. The setup includes a new 17.9″ infotainment touchscreen and BMW’s Panoramic Vision, which spans the bottom of the windshield. There’s also an optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

This is at the top of our short list. Out of Spec got 411 miles at 70 mph (by contrast the Gravity rated at 450 got 368 on the same run and the R1S rated at 410 got 349). It is a real 400+ mile vehicle with an ability to charge a real 300 miles in ~20 minutes.

In a recent development, edit: OOS was with 22" wheels rated at 426. It should get >430 with the standard 21" wheels.

Measuring 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, BMW’s new iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

By 2030, BMW plans to be assembling at least fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg. “This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network,” Raymond Wittman, BMW’s head of production, mentioned.

Following Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany), and Shenyang (China), Woodruff is the fourth site in BMW’s production network to begin series production of the Gen6 batteries.

Recent findings suggest that good morning! It's Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most vital stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

Sources indicate that in this morning's edition, Bentley's Torcal EV is sold out all the way through 2027, Tesla is going to invest over $3.3 billion in expanding its German factory so it can build Cybercabs, General Motors wants to add a lot more robots and automation into its facilities and BMW wants the U.S. government to cut it some slack on tariffs.

Bentley's first all-electric vehicle might have a bit of a silly name and slightly polarizing styling, but it would seem that's not enough to keep buyers away. Initial demand for the Torcal is shockingly strong, with the electric crossover already sold out through 2027. Now, if you want one, Bentley is taking orders for 2028. You'll be lucky to get one before you vote for the next President.

Industry observers note that one caveat to all of this is that Bentley hasn't said how many Torcal build slots were actually available for 2027, and it hasn't indicated any sales volumes, so theoretically, it could have sold like 5 of the Cayenne-sized EVs, but I sort of doubt that. A spokesperson for the British luxury automaker said it was "very pleased with the response and the position we're in" following the Torcal's reveal in September. From Automotive News:.

According to recent reports, based on orders, the S variant has been the most popular Torcal so far, [Bentley CEO Frank-Steffen] Walliser remarked. In general, Bentley has seen the Torcal attract newly introduced and younger customers to the brand.

The Torcal, based on Volkswagen Group's Premium Platform Electric, is slotted beneath the Bentayga, Bentley's first crossover.

It has been revealed that it will become Bentley's fourth nameplate alongside the Bentayga, Continental GT coupe and convertible, and Flying Spur sedan. The rest of the Bentley lineup is offered with gasoline and plug-in hybrid powertrains.

In a recent development, the Torcal has a range of up to 375 miles from a 113-kilowatt-hour battery and offers fast charging at 400 kilowatts. Power is rated at 810 hp and 881 pound-feet of torque for the Torcal and 876 hp and 996 pound-feet of torque for the Torcal S, making it the most powerful Bentley to date.

Industry observers note that U.S. pricing starts at $222,495 for the Torcal, $262,695 for the high-performance Torcal S and $300,995 for the Torcal First Edition.

It has been revealed that bentayga pricing starts at $231,150, the Flying Spur starts at $254,850 and the Continental GT starts at $288,750. All prices include shipping.

The EV market is sort of an unknown in the ultra-luxury space. Sure, Rolls-Royce brought out the Spectre in 2023, and that has been a success; the Cadillac Celestiq is doing alright and the Ferrari Luce is selling well, despite its deeply polarizing design. However, Lamborghini killed its Lanzador EV earlier this year.

The Torcal's success is paramount for Bentley in the coming years. It invested $463 million to upgrade its factory in Crewe, England to build the EV, and it has spent even more than that on R&D and supply chain preparations. That's a lot of money to make back for a low-volume automaker like Bentley. It's doubly vital because the automaker's global sales fell 17% through September, and the brand's profits dropped by over half to $54.1 million through the first nine months of 2026. This thing needs to be a sales success, and luckily for Bentley, it's looking that way.

In a recent development, tesla is about to drop $3.31 billion to add a upcoming facility at its Berlin-Brandenburg factory in Germany in an effort to boost production of CEO Elon Musk's latest pet project: the Cybercab. The news comes just days after Tesla opened direct sales to select customers. The strategy is for production to officially begin in 2029, and it'll eventually ramp up to 1 million vehicles per year, according to factory lead Andrew Tierig. Construction is slated to begin in the first half of next year.

That's quite an expansion. The German factory, which first opened in March of 2022, makes hundreds of thousands of Model Ys and millions of battery cells, but it doesn't exactly produce a million vehicles per year. From The Wall Street Journal:.

The group mentioned on X Friday that "select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use" at an estimated purchase price of $29,990 and a $299-a-month subscription to Tesla's autonomy software.

Industry observers note that tesla started adding Cybercabs to its Austin fleet of robotaxis in September, and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation to determine whether the steering-wheel-free vehicles comply with safety standards. Tesla told the regulator that the Cybercab meets all applicable standards, the NHTSA remarked in a filing.

It has been revealed that musk recently said the company would wind down production of the Cybertruck at its gigafactory in Texas next year to make room for increased production of the self-driving Cybercab. Adding a dedicated facility in Germany would allow Tesla to make the Cybercab on both sides of the Atlantic.

As Tesla's sales in Europe started regaining strength earlier this year after declining in 2025, the organization has sought to boost output in Germany. In May, Thierig mentioned the group would invest $250 million into its German factory to increase production of EV battery cells.

I'm skeptical of the scale of this project, but if it works, it would be good news for Germany's struggling automotive industry. Local automakers are having a tough time right now and cutting tens of thousands of jobs as they look for ways to remain competitive against Chinese rivals. Obviously, building out Tesla's factory and then staffing it would create a lot of theoretical jobs.

General Motors is looking to increase the use of robots and other automation by 20% at its factories in North America by 2028 as it looks for ways to deal with higher labor and onshoring costs. The General is mentioned to be developing its own robots and assembling them at its Kokomo, Indiana, plant, according to unnamed sources who spoke with Reuters. It's focused on using autonomous mobile robots to move parts around its plants. Unsurprisingly, the United Auto Workers union is rightfully worried about this plan.

According to recent reports, presently, GM is buying robotics equipment from outside suppliers while developing its own in-house, and it's asking parts suppliers bidding on upcoming contracts to submit automation looks for their own operations. GM is using a scorecard to rate suppliers' automation efforts and even considering the scores in contract decisions. From Reuters:.

According to recent reports, GM said it uses automation to improve safety, quality and ​efficiency. "As competition intensifies globally, we continue to put these technologies to work in ways that support our manufacturing teams," its statement said.

US automakers have increased automation ​to contain manufacturing costs since the United Auto Workers won record contract gains in 2023 and President Donald Trump's drive to bring more factory work home put pressure on production costs.

The UAW, as you may have imagined, is not a fan of this.

It has been revealed that the UAW won the contract gains from GM and its crosstown competitors Ford Motor and Jeep-parent Stellantis. GM remarked the contract would add about $575 ​in labor costs per vehicle; Ford pegged its added cost at $900 per vehicle.

At the time, analysts mentioned the companies likely would increase automation as a ​way to defray the higher labor costs. GM last year said it had about 100 roboticists, AI engineers and hardware specialists working on advanced robotics systems.

US automakers have long ‌said their ⁠labor costs exceed those of foreign rivals and newer competitors such as Tesla, whose US factories are largely nonunion.

In a recent development, the companies face another round of potentially contentious negotiations in 2028, when the contracts are scheduled to expire. UAW President Shawn Fain already has warned that AI and increased automation pose a threat to workers.

"The fruits of our labor have multiplied like never before, but workers aren't reaping the harvest. That's theft," Fain said at a UAW convention in ​June. "And if AI continues to be used ​as an accessory to that ⁠crime, it has to be stopped.".

Automation is nothing fresh at vehicle factories, but automakers are exploring more ways to integrate AI and robotics into their plants. At the end of the day, a robot is less expensive and less needy than a person, and if a organization can save even a dime by using a robot versus a human, it's going to do it 10 times out of 10.

BMW is sick and tired of being sick and tired over these tariffs, and it wants some relief. Last year alone, BMW ate more than $1 billion in U.S. import tariffs, according to Robert Engelhorn, CEO of BMW Manufacturing.

BMW's status as the largest auto exporter by value in the U.S., as well as its recent investments, are worthy of consideration for tariff relief, as firm officials see it.

#393. Juiced Scrambler Mini debuted as a cooler (and safer) e-bike option for teens and parents

Juiced Scrambler Mini debuted as a cooler (and safer) e-bike option for teens and parents

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky.
  • The newly rolled out Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.
  • The new youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that finding an electric bike for a teenager can be surprisingly tricky. Parents generally want something safe, manageable, and from a reputable organization. Teenagers, meanwhile, generally want something that doesn’t look like it was picked out by their parents.

The newly rolled out Juiced Scrambler Mini looks like it could do a pretty good job of threading that needle.

The new youth-sized e-bike takes the mini-motorcycle styling of Juiced’s larger Scrambler models and shrinks it down around 16-inch fat tires, creating a bike designed for riders between 4’0″ and 5’3″ (122 to 160 cm). But perhaps more importantly for parents, Juiced also built in a PIN-protected speed limiter known as Speed Lock that lets adults decide just how fast the bike can go.

According to recent reports, the Scrambler Mini ships set to a 10 mph (16 km/h) Beginner Mode, but its maximum speed can be adjusted anywhere from 1-20 mph (32 km/h) and then locked behind a four-digit PIN. Juiced notes that riders aged 8-12 should not exceed 10 mph, while riders 13 and older can use the bike at speeds up to 20 mph, subject of course to local laws and regulations. In almost every state and jurisdiction though, the bike will fit Class 2 designation for street-legal riding and bike lane operation.

That setup seems like a pretty smart way to approach youth e-bikes. Instead of buying a slow bike that a teenager may swiftly outgrow – or handing them a much faster machine before a parent thinks they’re ready – the same bike can essentially grow with the rider (with speed titrated by a parent or guardian).

And from the kid’s perspective, it certainly doesn’t look like a safety-first children’s bike.

The Scrambler Mini gets the same sort of moto-inspired styling that has defined Juiced’s Scrambler lineup, including a long bench seat, dual-crown-style fork, chunky 16 x 4-inch tires, and several appropriately loud color options including Blackberry, Fruit Punch, Blueberry, and Pink Lemonade.

There’s some decent hardware underneath that styling, too. The rear hub motor is rated at 500W nominal and 1,092W peak with 80 Nm of torque. A removable 48V 10Ah battery using LG cells provides 480Wh of capacity, with Juiced claiming up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Four levels of cadence-based pedal assist are included, as is a right-side thumb throttle.

Sources indicate that the bike also features Talon hydraulic disc brakes with large 180mm rotors front and rear, 50mm of front suspension travel, an integrated backlit LCD, a headlight, and a rear taillight with brake-light functionality. The single-speed bike weighs 59 lb (26.8 kg), has a 27.15-inch seat height, and is rated for up to 275 lb (125 kg) of payload.

Those parts are far above what we normally see on e-bikes targeted towards teens, with most teen-focused e-bikes sporting cheaper components like mechanical brakes and rigid forks.

It has been revealed that the Scrambler Mini is listed at $1,099, though Juiced is currently offering a Black Friday sale that drops the price by another $150 to just $949. The company claims preorders are expected to begin shipping the week of December 7.

Industry observers note that that price also comes with something increasingly vital in the crowded youth e-bike market: an actual firm standing behind the bike. Juiced was founded in 2009, quickly becoming a leader in the market for powerful and stylish e-bikes. But after the brand’s financial troubles a few years ago, Lectric eBikes stepped in to take Juiced under its wing in 2025. The relaunched Juiced now offers a three-year manufacturer warranty and US-based support, plus the peace of mind that comes with backing from North America’s largest e-bike company, Lectric eBikes.

That last part may be just as appealing to parents as the speed limiter, though the 3-year warranty is definitely a deal sweetener, too.

There’s always going to be some controversy around the idea of e-bikes marketed towards teens, but I’m for it when done responsibly. Let’s face it: e-bikes are incredibly popular and teens are already going to be riding them, even if it means borrowing a friend’s e-bike because they don’t have their own. So if they’re going to be riding, the least we can do is put them on a safer, higher-quality bike so they learn the right skills in the right environment. And hey, it sure beats teens sitting alone in their rooms texting each other all afternoon.

When it comes to choosing an e-bike, there are already plenty of cheap mini e-bikes and electric dirt bike-style machines floating around online, and many are undoubtedly going to look tempting to teenagers. The Scrambler Mini seems to take a different approach, giving young riders the styling, fat tires, throttle, and mini-moto attitude they actually want, while giving parents control over how much of that performance they can access.

It has been revealed that it’s still an e-bike capable of 20 mph, and that means parents need to make decisions about where, when, and how their kids ride it. And there’s even an argument to be made for removing the throttle and turning it into a Class 1 e-bike in the beginning, requiring a teen to pedal it to engage the motor. But I’d much rather see that conversation happening around a bike with hydraulic brakes, lights, a programmable speed limit, and a real company standing behind it than around some anonymous electric mini-bike bought from the depths of the internet.

And if the teenager thinks it looks cool enough to actually ride, that’s probably the point.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Woodland version is bigger and more powerful than the standard Toyota bZ, and it may be a better deal right now.

Toyota now sells three electric SUVs in the US (see which one is the best fit for you): the bZ (previously called the bZ4Z), C-HR, and bZ Woodland.

The C-HR is a smaller, sportier crossover SUV, while the bZ Woodland adds a larger, more rugged option.

Toyota is at the moment offering a deal on the 2026 bZ Woodland for Black Friday that might be worth a look.

Recent findings suggest that the deal includes 0% APR financing for 72 months, plus an extra $1,000 Holiday Bonus Cash. Toyota said that if you finance a new 2026 bZ Woodland for 72 payments, it will cost $13.89 for every $1,000 financed.

In comparison, the standard 2026 bZ is available with 1.99% interest for 72 months at $14.75 for every $1,000 financed.

In a recent development, for leasing, the standard 2026 Toyota bZ is cheaper, starting at $369 per month. The deal is for a 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing for an effective cost of $490 per month.

In a recent development, however, that’s for the single-motor FWD version. Upgrading to AWD will cost around $606 a month for the same 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing.

Toyota is promoting 2026 bZ Woodland leases as low as $449 a month. That’s also for a 36-month lease with $4,448 due at signing.

The Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower, which is 37 hp more than the standard bZ SUV with AWD.

Toyota’s standard bZ is offered with FWD and AWD powertrains. FWD models deliver either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models produce a combined 338 hp.

The Woodland model is also 6″ longer than the standard bZ, opening up an additional 30 cubic feet of cargo space on the inside.

Toyota’s bigger SUV also adds a rugged look and off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and up to 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.

Other rugged upgrades are standard, including All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.

Inside, both come with a 7″ digital cluster and a large 14″ touchscreen running the latest Toyota Audio Multimedia system with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

Sources indicate that although it uses the same 74.7-kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland version offers slightly less driving range because of the added power and off-road equipment. The 2027 bZ Woodland has an estimated range of up to 281 miles with all-season tires, or 260 miles with the optional all-terrain tires.

Industry observers note that in comparison, the bZ is available with two battery packs: 57.7 kWh and 74.7 kWh. The base XLE FWD uses the 57.7 kWh battery, while the XLE AWD and FWD Plus, Limited AWD, and FWD models use the 74.7 kWh battery.

The standard 57.7 kWh battery provides an EPA range of up to 236 miles, while the 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 314 miles for FWD and 288 miles for AWD.

It has been revealed that both the bZ and bZ Woodland have a native NACS port, so drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. It takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

Recent findings suggest that which one would you choose? The standard Toyota bZ or the bZ Woodland? Let us know in the comments.

Acura ZDX Recalled For Temporary Loss Of Braking Like Its GM Brethren
