#347. The BLUETTI Apex 200 Expandable Portable Power Station — CleanTechnica Tested

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1267 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica

The BLUETTI Apex 200 Expandable Portable Power Station — CleanTechnica Tested

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding fresh ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.
  • They recently reached out about a new stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station.
  • Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding fresh ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.

They recently reached out about a new stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station. It packs in a meaningful 2.5 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of storage capacity by itself, but the real magic is that it was built to be modular and can be linked up with additional storage modules to be stacked underneath, connecting directly to the main unit.

Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.

It has been revealed that this modular format is a game changer because it means you don’t need an installer to bolt 300 pounds of batteries to the wall of your house. Instead, you can order them in manageable formats and add more as you need them. Among other things, this capability allows the owner to assemble and disassemble the battery pack that meets their needs when they need it.

If you’re heading out to camp for a week in your RV, you can grab an Apex 200 and one of BLUETTI’s B300K expansion batteries and bring 5.5 kWh of capacity with you on the road. When you get home from the trip, you can put them back into the garage and add that back into the battery capacity for your home.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 serves as a head unit or master controller for the battery stack, while the other battery modules are effectively servants to it. For example, when you’re setting the unit up to charge from a wall outlet or from a set of BLUETTI’s solar panels, which can wire directly into the Apex 200 with MC4 connectors, you simply plug one set of connectors or one AC charging cable into the Apex 200 and it automatically balances the energy storage across however many additional battery packs are plugged into the unit.

According to recent reports, that really simplifies the charging structure and allows you to use the battery exactly how you want to. If you want to just head to the park with two solar panels that are portable, you can do that and have a much more manageable power system, effectively bringing a mini-grid with you on the go.

According to recent reports, we tested the BLUETTI Apex 200 out on a wall charger and, much like most of the other portable power stations on the market, it effectively maxes out the capacity you can actually draw from a wall outlet, which is around 1,600 watts continuous. Even with the best charging cables, you’re going to notice some heat building up in the cable, and BLUETTI has made some concessions for this. The Apex 200 has a switch that allows you to select from different charging modes:.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to solar, the BLUETTI Apex 200 can plug in to solar arrays through either an XT60 connector or the MC4 connectors that wire directly into the unit on the side. Between the MC4 connectors and the XT60 solar input, the unit can pull down 3,000 watts of solar, though you will need to make sure the voltage on your panels lines up with what each of the ports on the unit can handle. When we initially wired our two Bluetti 100-watt solar panels into the unit, we had them wired in parallel, which resulted in just 40 volts being pushed into the unit.

According to recent reports, stacking them in series gave us 80 volts, which pushed it over the minimum 60 volts for the MC4 connectors and allowed the BLUETTI Apex 200 to start charging from the panels. Pushing 2,000 watts maximum of solar power into a 5.5 kWh battery stack is going to take some time to get it charged up, but it’s easy to manage scaling the input power system up to an impressive 2,000 watts to really deliver some meaningful power.

The flexibility is pretty impressive, because it means you can dial the system in to exactly what you need, whether that’s bolting an array to the top of your RV or installing solar panels on the side of your house and then wiring them in a way that’s the most convenient for you.

BLUETTI also makes a larger B500K battery, so you can really pick and choose exactly the right level of storage that you need for your house and the right size battery packs that you want to be able to move around.

The MC4 connectors for solar panels are a little bit troublesome on the BLUETTI Apex 200 because they require a special tool to release the locks that connect the male and female ends of MC4 connectors together. That means if you have your solar panels wired up and plugged into the unit, you’ll need an MC4 connector release tool to disconnect the solar panels from the Apex 200 before you move on. Alternately, you can wire the solar panels up through an XT60 connector, which is a simple plug-and-play adapter for lower voltage solar setups.

When it came time to use the stored power from the BLUETTI Apex 200 and the B300K battery pack, we had to pick up some more high-draw appliances to really put them the the test. We bought a 1,500-watt electric fireplace and 1,500-watt portable heater for a total draw of around 3,000 watts by. We also grabbed an an Instant Pot from the kitchen to pull a bit more juice from the battery stack.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 handled both of the heaters running full blast without a problem. It shared a continuous power output capacity of 3,200 watts. This gets bumped to 3,600 watts when you attach a B300K extension battery. Beyond that, you can even pull a little bit more power, pulling peak usage up to 4,800 watts for a few seconds, because of its peak power handling capacity.

Keeping the larger heater unit attached, we added an Instapot to the the mix, and again the unit had no concerns no matter what power levels we used. It’s a solid stack with impressive stats that actually deliver when you need them to the most.

It has been revealed that BLUETTI has really built an impressive system here with the Apex 200 and its different expansion battery options. A single BLUETTI Apex 200 can be expanded up to 33.3 kWh, and they can even go bigger than that if you need something with more storage.

BLUETTI allows you to link three Apex 200 battery stacks together through their Hub 1 accessory for a total of just under 100 kWh of storage capacity. That can be accomplished by stacking three Apex 200s with a bunch of BLUETTI’s 5kWh B500Ks and then linking them all together through the Hub 1.

It’s a massive system that demonstrates BLUETTI isn’t just building products for a quick sale, but building a much more comprehensive, flexible storage system that you can build at home into the right configuration for your needs with components that act more like LEGO building blocks.

The ability to wire in solar via XT60 connectors and MC4 connectors is exciting, giving homeowners even more options to produce power from the sun for them to run their lives on. The BLUETTI Apex 200 retails for $1,399 USD.

For more information about the BLUETTI Apex 200, the B300K, B500K expansion packs, or their solar panels, head over to their official website.

#346. Bentley’s First EV Is Already Sold Out, And Production Hasn’t Even Started

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (635 w)

Bentley’s First EV Is Already Sold Out, And Production Hasn’t Even Started

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that bentley’s first electric car, the Torcal SUV, looks like a hit already.
  • The British luxury automaker said that all available production slots for next year have already been allocated and that the company is now taking orders that will be delivered in 2028.
  • “Needless to say, we’re very pleased with the response and position we’re in,” a tech giant spokesperson told Automotive News.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bentley’s first electric car, the Torcal SUV, looks like a hit already. Even though production hasn’t started yet, the $220,000+ EV is sold out for 2027, according to Frank-Steffen Wallier, the manufacturer’s head honcho, quoted by Automotive News.

The British luxury automaker said that all available production slots for next year have already been allocated and that the company is now taking orders that will be delivered in 2028. Bentley didn’t say how many EVs it will build in 2027, but the initial customer response has made the marque quite happy with the outcome.

“Needless to say, we’re very pleased with the response and position we’re in,” a tech giant spokesperson told Automotive News.

That’s great news for Bentley, which isn’t doing great in terms of sales and profit. From January through September, it sold 5,970 cars globally, 17% fewer compared to the same period last year. Meanwhile, the profit dropped by more than half to $54.1 million through the first nine months of the year.

The Torcal, which is smaller than the Bentayga SUV, is the brand’s cheapest model, though it still costs a pretty penny. The base Torcal starts at $222,495, followed by the more powerful Torcal S at $262,695, and the Torcal First Edition at $300,995. All things considered, Walliser stated that the smaller size and relatively lower price compared to the Bentayga have attracted fresh and younger customers to the brand.

By comparison, the Bentayga starts at $231,150, the Flying Spur sedan starts at $254,850, and the Continental GT two-door starts at $288,750.

So far, the Torcal S has proved to be the most popular version of the new EV, but when it comes to personalization, the sky’s the limit. “We see cars spec’d north of 300,000 pounds ($397,086),” remarked Walliser. “Individual content does not stop in case of an electric car. There have been some assumptions, and some people have been critical if people would be ready to do so.”.

Industry observers note that based on the same underpinnings as the electric Porsche Cayenne, the Bentley Torcal is powered by a 113-kilowatt-hour battery that can be charged at up to 400 kilowatts. It can go from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes, and the estimated EPA range is expected to be over 300 miles.

Sources indicate that built on the Premium Platform Electric (PPE) architecture, it has two electric motors that make 810 horsepower and 881 pound-feet of torque in the standard Torcal and a whopping 876 hp and 996 lb-ft of torque in the Torcal S. When the model debuted in September, Bentley said it was the most powerful and quietest model to come out of the factory in Crewe.

To make the Torcal a reality, Bentley invested $463 million to upgrade its factory in England, plus at least the same amount for supply chain preparations and research and development, Walliser said.

Despite the electric SUV’s initial success, the British automaker is still heavily invested in gas and plug-in hybrid models, and the Bentayga isn’t going anywhere. “We have a very good combination with Torcal and Bentayga,” Walliser remarked. “The segment definitely has space for two cars.”.

At $27,000, Is This 1974 Lotus Europa JPS A Smokin'-Hot Deal?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, according to the ad, the first owner of today's Nice Price or No Dice Europa owned the car for more than 51 years.
  • At some point in one's life, it's best to take the road less traveled.
  • According to recent reports, capable and seemingly in as-new condition, our 350Z came with a six-speed stick, a top that drops, and a $12,500 asking price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, according to the ad, the first owner of today's Nice Price or No Dice Europa owned the car for more than 51 years. That's some dedication, and the car reveals the love they obviously had for it. We'll have to decide if we love the price the current owner has set for its sale.

At some point in one's life, it's best to take the road less traveled. The well-beaten path may be the safest, but the less popular way might just offer unexpected, memorable adventures. The 2004 Nissan 350Z we looked at on Monday is probably not everyone's first choice when it comes to used sports cars with a semblance of panache. The easy answer is Porsche's Boxster or a Mazda Miata, but that's part of what makes the 350Z such a rogue option.

According to recent reports, capable and seemingly in as-new condition, our 350Z came with a six-speed stick, a top that drops, and a $12,500 asking price. That's plumb right in the middle of 986 Boxster territory, but offering more power and potentially cheaper running costs. That concept didn't escape you all. Comments on the car ranged from "not for me, but a good deal for someone," to "if it were closer to me..." In the end, the vote went the Nissan seller's way, too, earning the Z a solid 76% 'Nice Price' win.

Sources indicate that nissan has never offered a mid-engine car for sale here in the States. In fact, of the major Japanese manufacturers, only Toyota and Honda (through Acura) have gone the (rear) mid-engine route here.

Industry observers note that in the early 1960s, mid-engine layouts were all the rage in racing, with F1, Indy, and GT classes moving to place the driver ahead of the drivetrain. Britain's Lotus was at the forefront of this movement, debuting the mid-engine Type 18 Formula 1 racer in 1960. That car brought Lotus its first F1 checkered flag and World Champion title.

Sources indicate that lotus also dallied with mid-engine GT racers, designing a chassis and body that the firm hoped would be bought by the Ford Motor Company (Lotus had a close relationship with Ford at the time) for the Americans' assault on Le Mans. Ford chose the already race-tested Lola Mk 6 chassis for its GT40 racing program, leaving Lotus with significant engineering expense and little to show for it. Instead of initially building a race car from the proposed chassis, Lotus took the more lucrative route and built a road car: Hethel's first mid-engined model.

The resulting Europa leveraged a design first used on the Elan: a stiff, folded and welded center backbone with the drivetrain and suspension bolted in place, and a fiberglass body mounted atop that in saddlebag fashion. The earliest cars had Renault engines and transmissions, while later cars, like this 1973 Europa Special, used the Ford Kent-based Lotus Twin Cam engine.

Not only does this Europa have the most powerful engine offered in Federalized form, but that 115-horsepower 1,557cc four-cylinder is backed by a standard five-speed manual, still sourced from Renault, originally designed for the French tech giant's 16 model.

This isn't just a "Significant Valve" (denoting a reworked twin-cam head) Europa; it's also one of 100 John Player Specials built to commemorate Lotus's 1972 F1 Championship win. The cars were wrapped in black paint with gold trim, emulating the cigarette pack design of the racer's sponsor, Nottingham, England's John Player & Sons. It's an iconic bit of 1970s chic, and very British. This car still wears its commemorative dashboard plaque, indicating it's number 90 of the 100 cars built.

Industry observers note that while the basic Europa design is a bit odd with its bread van back end, this one appears to be in exceptional condition. Also, being a later edition (dubbed Type 47 by Lotus), it has a reworked engine cover and rear end providing better visibility out the back and slightly improved proportions.

Sources indicate that not only does this Europa appear to be in near-show car condition, but it comes with extensive documentation from the moment it was built (March 1973) to the present day. That paperwork details title transfers between all three owners (the second owner held on to the car for more than half a century), along with all the work that has gone into keeping it on the road and winning awards at car shows. As far as turnkey classics go, there's not much to complain about with this Lotus.

Sources indicate that on the exterior, the black-and-gold color scheme still looks as elegant as ever, right down to the original gold anodized alloy wheels. All the badging, lights, and chrome are present and in excellent shape, which is a plus since parts are getting increasingly hard to find. The interior is just as nice, showing just some scuffing on the driver's seat side as evidence of the car's age.

According to the ad, the engine underwent an extensive rebuild and documentation just 2,000 miles ago, and now runs well when warm. Both the engine and gearbox are numbers-matching for the car. How cool is that after all these years?

According to recent reports, the ad notes a clean title and mileage documented at 34,526. It also touts the car as a "once in a lifetime chance to own a fully documented Lotus." It should be noted that, while advertised in the Los Angeles Craigslist classifieds, the car is actually located a few hundred miles away on the California/Oregon border.

Sources indicate that some classic cars come with a story. Some come with a past veiled in mystery. This Europa comes with a dossier that would make a CIA agent proud. Not only that, but it's a prime example of a significant model in its final, some might argue, most desired form. What might something like that be worth?

According to recent reports, the seller has set a price of $27,000, and since the ad for the car has been posted for almost a month, we now need to give that asking price some thought. What's your take on this original mid-engined marvel out of Hethel and the seller's cash-and-carry price? Is it really worth $27,000? Or is a fairer price yet to be documented in the car's records?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#343. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1413 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month.
  • The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging.
  • It has been revealed that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

It has been revealed that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

Industry observers note that that proposal didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

Industry observers note that the bigger concern is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

According to recent reports, no onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

Sources indicate that for a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

Industry observers note that as we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”.

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

According to recent reports, the Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also states only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Sources indicate that tesla first highlighted what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

Industry observers note that and that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

Recent findings suggest that tesla’s own intends for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

Industry observers note that the other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also declared a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

According to recent reports, neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t revealed one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

It has been revealed that this is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

Industry observers note that that saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

The CyberCab is not a serious or well thought-out product, for any purpose besides inflating someone's ego and being able to tell people it looks like it came from a pre-2000's movie about a dystopian future.

If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it introduces, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is right now basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. Testing at all Louisiana coal plants found unsafe groundwater contamination.

Industry observers note that BATON ROUGE, La. — The Sierra Club, Earthjustice, and the Alliance for Affordable Energy Louisiana decried the Trump administration’s final decision today to put the State of Louisiana in charge of oversight of toxic coal ash waste. The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) has repeatedly allowed coal plants to violate federal coal ash protections.

Coal ash is generated when coal is burned, and massive quantities are stored at coal-burning power plants near Baton Rouge, Alexandria, and Shreveport.

At all three active Louisiana coal plants (Major Cajun 2, Brame Energy Center, R S Nelson), and the state’s one retired plant (Dolet Hills), monitoring data shows that coal ash is contaminating groundwater at levels above federal safe drinking water standards. These toxic chemicals include arsenic, boron, cobalt, lead, lithium, radium, sulfate, and thallium. More than 61% of Louisiana’s population relies on groundwater for all or part of their drinking water supply.

According to recent reports, “Louisianans know all too well that we can’t trust our state regulators to hold polluters accountable, so it’s nonsensical that the Trump Administration just gave LDEQ even more authority to handle something as dangerous as coal ash,” said Darryl Malek-Wiley, a Sierra Club senior field representative in Louisiana. “It’s clear this decision is meant to favor wealthy coal-owning utilities at the expense of our health.”.

According to recent reports, “The Trump administration chose polluters over the people of Louisiana,” remarked Earthjustice senior attorney Mychal Ozaeta. “An alphabet soup of toxic chemicals from burning coal is contaminating groundwater in locations across the state. The right thing to do is make the polluters clean up their toxic mess, and protect sources of drinking water. Instead, the Trump administration is handing over authority to Louisiana’s state government which won’t lift a finger to clamp down on the concerning levels of contaminants poisoning the state’s groundwater.”.

Sources indicate that “Our state regulators are dangerously inadequate in their oversight and enforcement of polluting industries, which has already cost Louisiana our safe air and water. We simply don’t think LDEQ can handle even more responsibilities they won’t take seriously,” said Logan Burke, Executive Director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy.

Public interest groups submitted formal comments to EPA urging the administration to reject Louisiana’s request to handle coal ash oversight in the state.

Coal ash contains arsenic, mercury, chromium, lead, lithium, radium, and other heavy metals, which have been linked to numerous types of cancer, heart and thyroid disease, respiratory illness, reproductive failure, and neurological harm.

As an example of the state’s abysmal track record on coal ash, LDEQ has allowed power plants to close coal ash dumps with ash in groundwater, ensuring that the dumps will contaminate groundwater with toxic chemicals indefinitely. LDEQ should not be in charge of issuing permits that let coal plants continue to violate the law. These permits will shield power plants from federal enforcement and prevent Louisiana residents from stopping coal ash pollution.

According to recent reports, LDEQ is a severely understaffed and extremely lenient environmental regulator. In addition to its coal ash failures, its air monitors are far away from Louisiana’s heaviest air-polluting facilities, and the agency has for years been criticized for approving permits for wealthy polluters, including LNG terminals and a massive Formosa plastics factory. Louisianans know all too well that LDEQ does not protect low-income communities of color, and creates a lax regulatory environment that has enabled disasters like the recent Smitty’s Supply explosion and spill.

Sources indicate that BYD’s latest milestone in Japan would barely register on its sales charts back home in China. Sources indicate that the Chinese automaker announced that its cumulative Japanese passenger-car sales had passed 10,000. Its first 5,000 took roughly two and a half years after deliveries began in January 2023. The next 5,000 took about 15 months. That includes its entire lineup, rather than just its newest and arguably most interesting addition: the Racco electric kei car.

Recent findings suggest that it was bold to challenge Japan’s homegrown manufacturers with something designed specifically for their market and to create the world’s first kei car from a non-Japanese automaker. The Racco’s tall body, tiny footprint, and sliding rear doors follow the familiar Japanese formula for such vehicles. BYD didn’t need to reinvent anything, but its entry needed to be convincing.

Japanese buyers’ initial response to the Racco was encouraging. Rolled out on July 28, it attracted 1,002 orders in two weeks, the fastest order intake of any BYD model in Japan. By the end of August, that had grown to around 1,500. Roughly 80% of buyers chose the range-topping 300 Premium, clearly showing that the cheapest version was less attractive.

BYD credited the Racco with helping deliver record monthly orders across its Japanese lineup in August. Potential buyers who came to see the little EV ended up discovering its other models, too.

Recent findings suggest that BYD offers six passenger-car models in Japan, and every one has a charging port. Five are fully electric: the Racco kei car, Dolphin hatchback, Seal sedan, Atto 3 crossover, and Sealion 7 SUV. The sixth, the Sealion 6 SUV, is a plug-in hybrid combining a gasoline engine with electric propulsion. That makes the entire lineup electrified, with no gasoline-only cars or conventional, non-plug-in hybrids on offer.

Sources indicate that what’s more interesting is comparing the Racco’s sales performance to its main rival, the Nissan Sakura EV, which is also Japan’s best-selling electric car. In October, the Sakura EV sold 878 units, while the Racco sold 607. That’s almost 70% of the volume, marking a 37% rise over September.

In a recent development, the Nissan Sakura EV was Japan’s electric bestseller for a fourth consecutive year in 2025, but it could lose its crown to the Racco, which gives buyers more battery for less money, at least before subsidies. It starts at ¥2.145 million with a 22.4-kWh pack and 130 miles (210 kilometers) of WLTC range, while the Sakura starts at ¥2.449 million with a 20-kWh battery and 112 miles (180 km).

Sources indicate that even the longer-range Racco, with a 35.8-kWh pack capable of 199 miles (320 km), undercuts the entry-level Nissan at ¥2.398 million. The BYD also gets sliding rear doors instead of the Nissan’s conventional ones. What could help the Sakura stay ahead is the larger government subsidy it benefits from, which can make it cheaper to buy despite its higher sticker price.

It’s a tad early to call the Racco a Japanese sensation, but buyers are clearly interested. This newcomer is already selling roughly seven cars for every ten Sakuras in one month, so it definitely deserves attention.

Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution does not just outline the real climate risk that the industry’s current growth trajectory poses, it shares substantive and impactful strategies that states can implement right now to prevent harmful emissions from gas plants while protecting ratepayers from rising costs caused by data center demand.

#335. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1484 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • According to recent reports, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • Sources indicate that just before 4 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators notes Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

According to recent reports, police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Sources indicate that just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Sources indicate that jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report states the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson noted the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

Sources indicate that so that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody mentioned a word about Autopilot.

Industry observers note that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and claims it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

Recent findings suggest that the report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

Recent findings suggest that A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a massive truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Industry observers note that trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

Recent findings suggest that we want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

In a recent development, september may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash reveals how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

In a recent development, compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

Industry observers note that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside.
  • In a recent development, the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck.
  • Sources indicate that late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators notes Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

In a recent development, the crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Sources indicate that late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

Sources indicate that according to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

According to recent reports, charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Recent findings suggest that mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

In a recent development, CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Sources indicate that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

Industry observers note that the rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

In a recent development, two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

According to recent reports, CHP hasn’t remarked whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing upcoming rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

Industry observers note that this is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany.
  • That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one.
  • Plant manager André Thierig declared the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The firm confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a latest production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig declared the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

Industry observers note that if you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we declared a first investment of around € 3b in a upcoming manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

Recent findings suggest that per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the newly introduced production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla prepares to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The manufacturer indicates it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the latest hall will be bigger than the original factory.

Industry observers note that the building isn’t fresh. Tesla laid out a proposal to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

According to recent reports, giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the latest hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

Recent findings suggest that the EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Industry observers note that rules can move in three years. The Commission has mentioned it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Recent findings suggest that tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

Industry observers note that the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU said no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

It has been revealed that this is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Sources indicate that will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

In a recent development, in China, the latest Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

In a recent development, the second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s upcoming Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the fresh version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

According to recent reports, with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

It has been revealed that even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

Sources indicate that the optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

In a recent development, in China, BYD offers the latest Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

Industry observers note that the current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

#328. These Are The Worst Ways You've Abused Rental Cars

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1636 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

These Are The Worst Ways You've Abused Rental Cars

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that while most of us would classify lightweight sports coupes as the ideal driver's car, there's just something enjoyable about an econobox off the rental lot.
  • According to recent reports, we asked our readers last week for the worst things they've done to a rental car.
  • According to recent reports, 1998 Volkswagen Passat from Heathrow Airport on business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while most of us would classify lightweight sports coupes as the ideal driver's car, there's just something enjoyable about an econobox off the rental lot. According to USA Today, the Toyota Corolla is the most rented car in the country. The Nissan Altima is the second. And the reputation of Altima drivers alone should be enough to tell you what kind of shenanigans are possible behind the wheel of that sedan.

According to recent reports, we asked our readers last week for the worst things they've done to a rental car. The responses in the comments section read like a "What Not To Do" poster next to an airport rental desk, or maybe even the fine-print section of the rental contract. Company staff would say you shouldn't enter a rental in an off-road racing event. You shouldn't jump a rental on San Francisco's hills. You shouldn't use a rental to learn how to drive a manual. It sounds like you all had quite a bit of fun behind the wheel of your rental cars, so without further ado, here are the most interesting submitted cases of rental car abuse.

According to recent reports, 1998 Volkswagen Passat from Heathrow Airport on business. I decided to practice my clutchless gear changes. After about 2 hours of stop-and-go traffic around the M25 parking lot along with some faster B roads in Kent, the transmission totally gave out. I phoned them up & fair play, they sent a replacement on a flatbed truck to me & took the broken one away. No questions, no follow-up & I learned a valuable new skill!

In the early 2000s, they used to rent to teenagers. Six of us took turns "jumping" an early-2000s Chrysler Sebring convertible. We found a long stretch of road behind a buddy's house, and we all took a turn seeing who could get the most air. One of the guys got so much air he knocked the oil pan off when he landed. He pulled over and turned it off – everyone left and the guy who rented it called the rental car company to report the car had "mysteriously" started leaking oil, so he parked it on the side of the road. They towed it, apologized, and sent him a upcoming Sebring! We did not jump the 2nd Sebring.

According to recent reports, I flew to Texas to attend my grandmother's funeral. When I landed, the car rental place offered me an upgrade to a Mustang convertible for a mere $5/day!

I took it and got a bright yellow drop-top to drive in Grandma's funeral procession. Got some ribbing from relatives because I didn't put the top down during it, but oh well.

Sources indicate that afterward, I was driving on a highway and ran over some plastic sheeting. It wrapped around the driveshaft and caused a helluva vibration. Wasn't my car, and I didn't have anything with me that I could have used to remove it, so I just drove it that way for another day or so.

When I returned it, I'm pretty sure the u-joints were going to need to be replaced, but they didn't notice, so I got away scot-free!

Sources indicate that I once entered a rallycross event in a rental car. Back in 2007, when my regular rallycross car wasn't available, I rented a base-model Chevy—I can't even remember the specific model —and drove it two hours north to compete in the event. A rallycross is like an autocross but is held on dirt.

I entered in whatever class I was allowed to compete. I removed all the loose stuff and hubcaps, and because I photographers were there, I removed the license plates and tapped over the related organization's decal on the left corner of the trunk lid.

I ran three times that day, and the best time of the three runs determines your finish order. For stock class cars, one of the tricks is to lower tire pressures to around 15-20 lbs. My first run was DNF (Did Not Finish) because, in one particularly tight right-hander that I turned into too hard, I popped the bead on my left tire. Uh oh.

A group of fellow competitors (racers are great) came to my rescue with a jack, a ratchet tie-down strap, and a portable air compressor. After some useful, um, encouraging words, we got the tire bead to re-seat and put 5 lbs more air in the front tires. I finished my other two runs and finished second in class.

According to recent reports, on the way home, I spent about three hours at a car wash and made sure the license plates were in place and the tape was taken off the trunk. That bit of sneakiness paid off; I now have a nice framed photo hanging in my "I love me room" of me slinging dirt in that little Chevy.

Sources indicate that I once rented a minivan to work a remote antenna site. It had less than 1k miles on the odometer. We removed the rear seats, bypassing the security tabs, to haul equipment and materials from the nearest town to the site over 50 miles on firefighting gravel roads through forests and across streams. Many trips were made hauling bags of cement mix, punishing the suspension. We even used it to haul dirt from the site to 'authorized' dumping locations. We had it for a month. When we finished the job, we ran it through a car wash, vacuumed the interior, put the seats back in, replaced the security tabs, and then returned it. We had put another hard 5k miles on it. I heard no complaints from the rental company.

According to recent reports, I'm not one to thrash cars, but my favorite life hack is renting U-Hauls as a regular car rental. 19.95 a day is a steal and the other fees don't come close to rental costs. Vans and trucks have both been great and everyone that realizes what's going on is highly entertained.

I rented a car in San Francisco once when my kids were young and we went around late at night when there was no traffic and hit many hills at speed and had a blast catching air. We found one hill that had the perfect landing and did that one several times with kids laughing hysterically.

According to recent reports, after strapping a Christmas tree to the open top of our Boxster S, we got smart the next year. My wife and I went to Enterprise and rented a F-150 4x4. I opted in for all the insurance and extra coverages. Because the night before our excursion to our favorite tree farm... it rained. I asked the Enterprise clerk what was covered, and he remarked, "Everything, if anything happens, you don't have to pay a dime." I confirmed this with him and asked about what if it's dirty, he replied, "Covered." I smiled, and with a sense of fear, the clerk asked where we were going. I told him Christmas tree shopping.

We headed up to the tree farm, and sure enough, they had a sign that said 4x4 and AWD only. Owning a 2000 TJ in my past, I was no stranger to off-roading. Pushed the 4x4 button on the dash and proceeded. The roads were slippery, the tail slid around a bit, but for the most part the rental F-150 did just fine. We hopped out to cut our tree and sunk to our knees in mud. After an hour of mucking about, we loaded our tree and hopped back in the truck, mud dripping everywhere. On the way out, the truck did have to work on some of the muddier parts of the road. Mud flung into the bed, up the sides, over the hood from the truck in front of us.

We returned the F-150, and the receiving clerk just stared at the muddy F-150. I showed my receipt to him, smiled, and handed him the keys. He asked if there were any problems, and I smiled, "Didn't get stuck once.".

Does it count if I managed the rental fleet? When the "Porsche Drive" program was still active, I managed the program for the dealership I worked in. Porsche Drive was a rental & subscription service where you could rent Porsches from participating showrooms, or pay a monthly subscription that was basically a month-to-month lease. At our peak, we had a fleet of 25 cars: Macans, Taycans, a couple of Caymans & Boxsters, several Cayennes and 911s, and at least one Panamera that almost never got rented. As program manager, I was allowed to sign out cars that didn't have bookings, not unlike a manager's demo.

Sources indicate that I was invited to my friend's wedding, about a 3-hour drive out of town. As I departed in my own car, I noticed a tire-pressure warning. I pulled over to find a nail in one of my tires. I used my onboard compressor to get some air back into it, so I could make a 20-minute detour to my office to sign out a Panamera for the weekend.

The ceremony was wonderful, the reception was great, and while my friends & I were in line for dinner, a lady came up to us, introduced herself, and asked us all where we were from and how we were connected with the bride & groom. Turns out, her daughter is friends with the bride and Mom's playing matchmaker. I guess driving a new Porsche to a wedding gave me an extra glow of confidence, because she very quickly introduced us. The night went on, we hit it off, and we ended up spending the night in the back of the Panamera.

#327. Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1154 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek

Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and notes it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • In a recent development, at 11:43 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and notes it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

In a recent development, at 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

FHP remarked the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

According to recent reports, this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it claims Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

Recent findings suggest that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

Industry observers note that so Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

There’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

This is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a newly introduced record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

Sources indicate that tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

Sources indicate that we’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?
